signals.title: [Bug]: MCP auto-execute (require_approval "never") hijacks client-side tool_use from agentic clients like Claude Code, breaking all non-MCP tools with "Error executing tool"
signals.text: ## What happened? A model configured with an MCP tool reference using `require_approval: "never"` (so the proxy auto-executes it server-side) is deployed behind an agentic client that sends its own tools in the same request, such as Claude Code sending Read/Bash/Edit. The auto-execute loop takes over the entire tool_use turn and tries to execute every tool_use block the model emits, including the client's own non-MCP tools. Those tools are not in the MCP server map, so the proxy raises a KeyError that gets swallowed into `Error executing tool: '<tool_name>'` and fed back to the model. The model retries, fails again, and eventually gives up. From the client's perspective all of its native tools (Read, Bash, etc.) are broken for any request routed to that model What I expected: when `require_approval: "never"` is set, the proxy should auto-execute only the MCP tools it injected. A tool_use whose name does not resolve to a known MCP server should be passed through to the client unchanged so the client can execute it locally, the way a normal tool_use turn works when no MCP tool is present ## User Flow Before a fix 1. A user creates a virtual key and a team in the LiteLLM proxy UI, then registers an HTTP MCP server (say `image_understand`) and grants the team access to it 2. The user attaches the MCP tool to a model via the model's LiteLLM Params, e.g. `{"tools": [{"type": "mcp", "server_url": "litellm_proxy/mcp/image_understand", "require_approval": "never"}]}` 3. The user points an agentic client (Claude Code) at `POST /v1/messages` on the proxy, using that model and that virtual key. The client sends its own tools (Read, Bash, Edit, ...) alongside whatever the proxy injects 4. The model decides to call Read on a local file. The proxy's auto-execute loop intercepts that tool_use, fails with `Error executing tool: 'Read'`, and returns the error text to the model instead of handing the tool_use back to the client 5. The model retries with Bash, gets `Error executing tool: 'Bash'`, and eventually stops with a message saying the tools are unavailable. The user sees tool call failures and the client's native tooling is dead for that model After a fix 1. Same setup as above: MCP server registered, team granted access, MCP tool attached to the model with `require_approval: "never"` 2. The user points Claude Code at `POST /v1/messages` with that model and key, sending its own tools 3. The model calls Read on a local file. The proxy recognizes Read is not one of its MCP tools, returns the tool_use block to the client in the response, and lets the client execute it locally 4. When the model calls the injected MCP tool (`image_understand`), the proxy auto-executes it server-side as before and feeds the result back 5. Both the client's native tools and the injected MCP tool work in the same turn ## Proof the bug occurs I verified the root cause by reading the current main branch (v1.98.0-dev.2). I was not able to capture a full Claude Code trace against my own proxy in time for this report, so the proof below is the code path plus the user-visible symptom. I can add a full end-to-end curl reproduction if the maintainers want one Config / setup: a model with an MCP tool attached via LiteLLM Params ```json {"tools": [{"type": "mcp", "server_url": "litellm_proxy/mcp/image_understand", "require_approval": "never"}]} ``` Version or commit: v1.98.0-dev.2 on main Commands and their full output The auto-execute loop in `litellm/llms/anthropic/experimental_pass_through/messages/mcp_handler.py` extracts every tool_use block without checking whether it belongs to an MCP server ``` # line 38-40 def _extract_tool_use_blocks(response): return tuple(block for block in _get_response_content(response) if block.get("type") == "tool_use") # line 139-158 (abridged) for _ in range(MAX_MCP_TOOL_USE_ITERATIONS): if _get_stop_reason(response) != "tool_use": break tool_use_blocks = _extract_tool_use_blocks(response) if not tool_use_blocks: break tool_results = await LiteLLM_Proxy_MCP_Handler._execute_tool_calls( tool_server_map=tool_server_map, tool_calls=list(tool_use_blocks), ... ) ``` `tool_server_map` is built only from the injected MCP tools (in `_process_mcp_tools_without_openai_transform`). When `_execute_tool_calls` looks up a client-side tool name that is not in that map, it throws KeyError ``` # litellm/responses/mcp/litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py line 675 server_name = tool_server_map[tool_name] ``` That KeyError is caught by the broad except at line 891-905 and turned into the user-visible error string ``` # line 891-905 (abridged) except Exception as e: ... tool_results.append({ "tool_call_id": tool_call_id, "result": f"Error executing tool: {e}", "name": tool_name, }) ``` So a model emitting `tool_use` for `Read` produces `Error executing tool: 'Read'`, which matches what I observed in the proxy spend logs and what Claude Code surfaced as "tool call failed" The symptom from the agentic client side (Claude Code talking to the proxy over `/v1/messages`): the model attempts Read on a file that exists, gets `Error executing tool: 'Read'` back, tries Bash, gets `Error executing tool: 'Bash'`, then tells the user it cannot read files or run commands. A plain curl client that sends no tools of its own works perfectly against the same model, because then every tool_use resolves to an MCP tool. This is why the bug is specific to agentic clients that bring their own tools ## What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ## What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.98.0-dev.2 ## Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [X] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? `GET /v1/batches?limit=` returns HTTP 200 for values outside 1..100. On an account holding 99 batches: | `limit` | Records returned | `has_more` | | --- | --- | --- | | 0 | 20 | true | | -1 | 0 | false | | 1 | 1 | true | | 2 | 2 | true | | 5 | 5 | true | | 101 | 97 | false | | 1000 | 97 | false | OpenAI returns HTTP 400 for values outside 1..100: ```json { "error": { "message": "Invalid 'limit': integer above maximum value. Expected a value <= 100, but got 101 instead.", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": "limit", "code": "integer_above_max_value" } } ``` ### Code as it stands at v1.94.3 `litellm/proxy/batches_endpoints/endpoints.py:574`: ```python async def list_batches( request: Request, fastapi_response: Response, provider: Optional[str] = None, limit: Optional[int] = None, after: Optional[str] = None, user_api_key_dict: UserAPIKeyAuth = Depends(user_api_key_auth), target_model_names: Optional[str] = None, ): ``` No `Query(...)` constraint is attached to `limit`. --- ### User Flow **Before a (hypothetical) fix: a script paginating batch history computes a page size of 0 and receives 20 records** 1. The script sends `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches?limit=100` and processes the returned page 2. Its remaining-count arithmetic yields `0` on the final iteration 3. It sends `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches?limit=0` 4. The response is `200` carrying 20 records, so the script processes 20 records it did not request 5. A separate call with `?limit=101` returns `200` carrying 97 records 6. A call with `?limit=-1` returns `200` carrying 0 records **After a (hypothetical) fix: values outside 1..100 return 400** 1. The script sends `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches?limit=100` and processes the returned page 2. Its remaining-count arithmetic yields `0` on the final iteration 3. It sends `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches?limit=0` 4. The response is `400` with `"Invalid 'limit'"` and `"param": "limit"` 5. `?limit=101` returns `400` 6. `?limit=-1` returns `400` --- ### Proof the bug occurs **Version**: `litellm 1.94.3`, image digest `sha256:b7d979bac2a9e8fbb7d55272ef5f1f4a08ab365de8f78b1800834ca718d4c941`. The account held 99 batches. No provider call is made on this path. **Config the proxy ran with** ```yaml model_list: - model_name: gpt-5-batch litellm_params: model: azure/gpt-5-batch-2025-08-07 api_base: os.environ/AZURE_API_BASE api_key: os.environ/AZURE_API_KEY general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL ``` **Commands and their full output** ``` $ for L in 0 -1 1 2 5 101 1000; do N=$(curl -s "http://localhost:4000/v1/batches?limit=$L" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_KEY" \ | python3 -c 'import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(len(d.get("data",[])), "has_more=",d.get("has_more"))') printf 'limit=%-6s -> %s\n' "$L" "$N" done limit=0 -> 20 has_more= True limit=-1 -> 0 has_more= False limit=1 -> 1 has_more= True limit=2 -> 2 has_more= True limit=5 -> 5 has_more= True limit=101 -> 97 has_more= False limit=1000 -> 97 has_more= False ``` Status code for one of them: ``` $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' 'http://localhost:4000/v1/batches?limit=0' \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_KEY" HTTP 200 ``` The total returned by a single in-range request: ``` $ curl -s 'http://localhost:4000/v1/batches?limit=100' -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_KEY" \ | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print("total:", len(json.load(sys.stdin)["data"]))' total: 99 ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.94.3

signals.title: [Bug]: GET /v1/batches with after= does not advance: 99 batches walked in pages of 10 returned 16 distinct rows and has_more stayed true
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [X] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? On an account holding 99 managed batches, walking `GET /v1/batches?limit=10` and passing the `id` of each page's last item as `after` on the next request: - 15 pages returned 10 rows each, 150 rows total - 16 of those rows were distinct - 83 of the 99 batches did not appear in any page - `has_more` was `true` on every page, including page 15 Two consecutive pages at `limit=3` shared 2 of 3 rows. ### Code as it stands at v1.94.3 `litellm_enterprise/proxy/hooks/managed_files.py:318`: ```python if after: where_clause["id"] = {"gt": after} fetch_limit = limit or 20 if target_model_names: # Oversample so post-fetch model-name filtering still has enough rows. fetch_limit = max(fetch_limit * 3, 100) batches = await self.prisma_client.db.litellm_managedobjecttable.find_many( where=where_clause, take=fetch_limit, order={"created_at": "desc"}, ) ``` `:341`, inside the loop over `batches`: ```python batch_obj = LiteLLMBatch(**batch_data) batch_obj.id = batch.unified_object_id batch_objects.append(batch_obj) ``` `:354`: ```python return build_list_page( batch_objects, has_more=len(batch_objects) == (limit or 20) ) ``` `batch_objects` excludes rows dropped earlier in the same loop when `file_object` fails to parse, and rows excluded by `build_owner_filter`. The two columns involved hold different value shapes: ``` $ psql -U llmproxy -d litellm -t -c \ "SELECT id, unified_object_id FROM \"LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable\" WHERE file_purpose='batch' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3;" d11caa62-27a6-4279-adb2-e70b7f4aa1fe | bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9pZDo0ZDhhNWVmMGY2Y2M5OTZkMmEwYzlmYmEzYTMxMzQ5Mjg0OTYxNWNhM2E2YmJjNGRjOTcyMDQ0Mjg4MTBmMjk0O2xsbV9iYXRjaF9pZDpiYXRjaF8yMDI2MDgxNy0wNTU4LjMyMA d0fc3f0d-4edd-458a-bfe6-601f98a816f6 | bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9pZDo0ZDhhNWVmMGY2Y2M5OTZkMmEwYzlmYmEzYTMxMzQ5Mjg0OTYxNWNhM2E2YmJjNGRjOTcyMDQ0Mjg4MTBmMjk0O2xsbV9iYXRjaF9pZDpiYXRjaF8yMDI2MDgxNy0wNTU3LjAxOQ 32e97180-688a-4e74-a757-bcf9924915af | bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9pZDo2MzA0N2NjOGU1MzU3MWJmMDRiY2E4ODZiYjhiNzljNjg5MmQ5OWIwMjEwZGIzMTdhM2Y3MTVmM2EzZjYyMDQ0O2xsbV9iYXRjaF9pZDpiYXRjaF8yMDI2MDgxMy0xMDMxLjMzNA ``` `id` holds a UUID. `unified_object_id`, the value returned to the caller as `id`, holds a base64 string. The `{"gt": after}` filter is applied to `id`. --- ### User Flow **Before a (hypothetical) fix: an analyst exporting a quarter of batch jobs receives repeated rows and a loop that does not end** 1. They send `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches?limit=10` and receive 10 batches 2. They take the `id` of the last item and send `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches?limit=10&after=<that id>` 3. The second page returns 10 batches, of which 8 appeared on page 1 4. Every page reports `"has_more": true`, so their loop continues requesting pages 5. They stop it after 15 pages. It has collected 150 rows containing 16 distinct batches, and 83 of the account's 99 batches appear on no page 6. Every call in the sequence returned `200` **After a (hypothetical) fix: each page continues from the previous one and the loop ends** 1. They send `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches?limit=10` and receive 10 batches 2. They take the `id` of the last item and send `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches?limit=10&after=<that id>` 3. The second page returns 10 batches, none of which appeared on page 1 4. On the tenth page `"has_more"` is `false`, so their loop exits 5. The 10 pages together contain all 99 batches, each once 6. Every call in the sequence returned `200` --- ### Proof the bug occurs **Version**: `litellm 1.94.3`, image digest `sha256:b7d979bac2a9e8fbb7d55272ef5f1f4a08ab365de8f78b1800834ca718d4c941`. No provider call is made on this path. **Config the proxy ran with** ```yaml model_list: - model_name: gpt-5-batch litellm_params: model: azure/gpt-5-batch-2025-08-07 api_base: os.environ/AZURE_API_BASE api_key: os.environ/AZURE_API_KEY general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL ``` **Commands and their full output** Total from a single request: ``` $ curl -s 'http://localhost:4000/v1/batches?limit=100' -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_KEY" \ | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print("total:", len(json.load(sys.stdin)["data"]))' total: 99 ``` Walk at `limit=10`, passing the previous page's last `id` as `after`, capped at 15 pages: ``` === paginated walk, limit=10, following the id the API returns === page 1: returned=10 has_more=True page 2: returned=10 has_more=True page 3: returned=10 has_more=True page 4: returned=10 has_more=True page 5: returned=10 has_more=True page 6: returned=10 has_more=True page 7: returned=10 has_more=True page 8: returned=10 has_more=True page 9: returned=10 has_more=True page 10: returned=10 has_more=True page 11: returned=10 has_more=True page 12: returned=10 has_more=True page 13: returned=10 has_more=True page 14: returned=10 has_more=True page 15: returned=10 has_more=True true total (single page): 99 rows returned by walk: 150 distinct rows in walk: 16 DUPLICATES: 134 NEVER SEEN by the walk: 83 ``` Two consecutive pages at `limit=3`: ``` page1 ids (first 20 chars): ['bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt', 'bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt', 'bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt'] cursor sent as after= bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt (len 166) page2 ids (first 20 chars): ['bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt', 'bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt', 'bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt'] page2 identical to page1? False overlap count: 2 of 3 ``` The `id` values returned to the caller are 166-character base64 strings. The `id` column the `after` filter compares against holds UUIDs, per the psql output above. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.94.3

signals.title: [Bug]: OAuth2 client_credentials MCP servers never receive client_id/client_secret at runtime — token endpoint always rejects with 400
signals.text: ### What happened? Registering an MCP server with `auth_type: oauth2` / `oauth2_flow: client_credentials` results in `tools/list` failing 100% of the time with: ``` misconfigured: OAuth2 client_credentials grant rejected: token endpoint returned HTTP 400 ``` This happens **regardless of how the server is configured** — via the REST API (`POST /v1/mcp/server` with a nested `credentials: {client_id, client_secret}` object) or via `config.yaml`'s `mcp_servers:` block (with either `os.environ/VAR` or literal values). In every case the token endpoint (a real, independently-verified-working Keycloak `client_credentials` grant) rejects the request, which points to litellm sending an empty or malformed `client_id`/`client_secret`. ### Root cause (traced in source, not guessed) 1. **`LiteLLM_MCPServerTable` (`schema.prisma`) has no `client_id` / `client_secret` columns** — only an encrypted `credentials Json?` blob: ```prisma model LiteLLM_MCPServerTable { server_id String @id @default(uuid()) ... credentials Json? @default("{}") ... } ``` 2. The runtime OAuth2 resolver builds its config from **flat fields on the `MCPServer` Pydantic model**: `litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/outbound_credentials/adapter.py`: ```python config=ClientCredentialsConfig( client_id=server.client_id, client_secret=SecretStr(server.client_secret) if server.client_secret else None, token_url=server.token_url, ... ) ``` 3. **Nothing in the codebase ever copies the decrypted `credentials` blob into `server.client_id` / `server.client_secret`.** Searched the whole `mcp_server` package for any `client_id=<decrypted value>` assignment feeding into an `MCPServer(...)` construction used by the OAuth2 resolver — there is none. `decrypt_credentials()` is only used for master-key rotation (`rotate_mcp_server_credentials_master_key`) and DCR client storage, never to populate the resolver's config. Result: for any server persisted through the database (which is every server registered via the REST API, and — because `general_settings.store_model_in_db: true` is a very common production setting — effectively every `config.yaml`-defined server too), `server.client_id` / `server.client_secret` are **always `None`** at the point the token request is built. Keycloak (or any spec-compliant IdP) correctly returns `400 invalid_request`/`invalid_client` for a `client_credentials` grant with an empty `client_id`. 4. Separately, **`config.yaml`'s `mcp_servers:` loader does not resolve `os.environ/VAR`** for `client_id`/`client_secret`, unlike `model_list.litellm_params`: `litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/mcp_server_manager.py`: ```python client_id=server_config.get("client_id", None), client_secret=server_config.get("client_secret", None), ``` This is a plain dict `.get()` — no `get_secret()` / env-var indirection. The [MCP OAuth docs](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/mcp_oauth) show `client_id: os.environ/MCP_CLIENT_ID` as the documented pattern, but it is silently taken as a literal string, so the literal text `os.environ/MCP_CLIENT_ID` gets sent to the token endpoint instead of the resolved secret. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Register (via REST API or `config.yaml`) an MCP server: ```yaml mcp_servers: my_server: url: "https://my-mcp-server.example.com/mcp" transport: http auth_type: oauth2 oauth2_flow: client_credentials client_id: "<a real, working client_id>" client_secret: "<its real secret>" token_url: "https://idp.example.com/protocol/openid-connect/token" ``` 2. Independently confirm the same `client_id`/`client_secret`/`token_url` succeed with a plain `curl -d grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=...&client_secret=...` — they do (200, valid token). 3. Call `tools/list` against the proxy's `/mcp/` endpoint for this server. 4. Observe `"status": "internal", "http_status": 500"` in `_meta.litellm.ai/server_outcomes`, and in the proxy logs: ``` Failed to get tools from server my_server: 500: misconfigured: OAuth2 client_credentials grant rejected: token endpoint returned HTTP 400 ``` 5. Confirm the grant mechanics themselves are fine by calling litellm's own `_prepare_grant` / `post_client_credentials_grant` directly with the identical config object (bypassing the server-record load path) — this **succeeds** and returns a valid access token. The bug is specifically in how the persisted/config-loaded `MCPServer` record's credentials reach that function, not in the grant logic itself. ### Expected behavior `client_id`/`client_secret` provided at registration time (via API `credentials` object or `config.yaml`, with or without `os.environ/` indirection) should reach the actual token request unchanged. ### Suggested fix - Add `client_id`/`client_secret` columns to `LiteLLM_MCPServerTable` (or decrypt+unpack the `credentials` blob into the `MCPServer.client_id`/`client_secret` fields at every read path that feeds `_client_credentials_spec`), and/or - Apply the same `get_secret()`/`os.environ/` resolution used for `model_list` to the `mcp_servers:` config.yaml loader for `client_id`, `client_secret`, and any other credential-shaped field. ### Environment - **LiteLLM version**: `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-stable`, image pulled/deployed 2026-08-10 (prod) — well after the March 2026 fix for #24522, so this is not that issue. - **What part of LiteLLM is this about?**: MCP Gateway / OAuth2 `client_credentials` - Reproduced independently on two separate deployments (Azure Container Apps and an OpenShift-hosted instance with `store_model_in_db: true`), both via REST API registration and via `config.yaml`. ### Related issues Not a duplicate of #24522 (concurrent stateless teardown — different traceback, different mechanism). Possibly related in spirit to #22755 ("Unable to list MCP tools with OAuth through the UI Dashboard", closed `not_planned`) and #15957, which describe the same outward symptom (OAuth-protected MCP tool listing fails) without this root cause having been identified. --- ## Bug 2: `true_passthrough`/`oauth_delegate` MCP sessions time out despite the upstream call itself completing in milliseconds ### What happened? As an alternative to `client_credentials` (see Bug 1), we tested `auth_type: oauth_delegate` (`true_passthrough`), where litellm is supposed to forward the caller's own bearer token verbatim (via the `x-mcp-{alias}-authorization` header) instead of minting its own. `tools/list` against this server times out inside litellm. ### Root cause (traced in source) - `litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/outbound_credentials/resolver.py`, `_passthrough(self, subject)` (~line 163) forwards `subject.inbound_token` verbatim to the upstream MCP server — this part is correct and matches the caller-supplied-credential design we wanted. - `litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/mcp_server_manager.py` (~line 4200) wraps the actual `client.list_tools()` call in `anyio.fail_after(MCP_TOOL_LISTING_TIMEOUT)`. In our reproduction, this consistently fires before the upstream ever responds. - We isolated the upstream call from litellm's session/connection handling entirely: a standalone script (`debug_passthrough.py`), running inside the same cluster network as litellm and using the same caller token forwarded the same way, hit the internal MCP URL directly and got back **`HTTP 200` in `0.04s`**. The upstream server, network path, and token are all fine — the timeout is happening somewhere in litellm's own MCP client/session plumbing between accepting the passthrough token and actually completing the `list_tools()` round trip. ### Expected behavior `tools/list` over a `true_passthrough`/`oauth_delegate` MCP server should complete in roughly the same time as a direct call to the upstream (tens of milliseconds in our environment), not hit `MCP_TOOL_LISTING_TIMEOUT`. ### Environment Same as Bug 1 (OpenShift-hosted litellm instance, `store_model_in_db: true`). ### Status This is reported with less certainty than Bug 1 — we have not yet traced the exact point inside litellm's session/connection setup where the delay is introduced (as opposed to Bug 1, which we traced to an exact missing assignment). Flagging it here because it blocks the architecturally-preferred alternative to Bug 1. --- ## Bug 3: `client_credentials` grant requests every scope advertised by the realm's discovery document, instead of only the client's assigned scopes ### What happened? With Bug 1's root cause fixed locally (server record correctly populated with a real, independently-verified-working `client_id`/`client_secret`), the *live* litellm instance's `client_credentials` requests to our IdP (Keycloak) still fail — but with a different, more specific error surfaced in the IdP's own audit log (not visible from litellm's side, only from the token endpoint's server-side logs): ``` error="invalid_request", reason="Invalid scopes: basic uma_protection Custom_Scope a2a-chat-ia-mcp-audience roles phone microprofile-jwt openid web-origins offline_access acr email service_account profile address", grant_type="client_credentials", client_auth_method="client-secret", username="service-account-<client>" ``` Client authentication itself **succeeds** here (Keycloak resolves the service-account user, confirming the secret is valid) — the request fails only because of the `scope` parameter litellm sends. The requested scope list is unusually large and includes scopes that are not, and could never sensibly be, assigned to this specific client (`microprofile-jwt`, `web-origins`, `acr`, several other realm-wide default/optional scopes). This looks like litellm is requesting the full `scopes_supported` list from the IdP's OIDC discovery document (`/.well-known/openid-configuration`) rather than a scope the operator configured (or no `scope` parameter at all, which is valid per RFC 6749 §4.4.2 and lets the IdP apply the client's default scopes). ### Expected behavior The `client_credentials` grant should either omit `scope` entirely (letting the IdP apply the client's configured default scopes, which is spec-compliant and what a plain `curl` grant with no `scope` param does successfully against the same client/IdP), or send only an operator-configured scope list — never every scope advertised by discovery metadata. ### Environment Same as Bug 1/2. ### Related issues Not yet searched for a matching open issue — flagging here since it was discovered as a direct consequence of investigating Bug 1. **Update: Bug 3 also breaks the interactive `authorization_code` flow, not just `client_credentials`** Confirmed this is not specific to `client_credentials`. Registering a second server with `oauth2_flow: authorization_code` (same `client_id`, plus an `issuer` so LiteLLM does RFC 8414 discovery instead of using manually-set `authorization_url`/`token_url`) and hitting LiteLLM's own `/{server_name}/authorize` endpoint produces a `307` redirect to the IdP's `/auth` endpoint whose `scope` query param is the **exact same** full discovery scope list: ``` Invalid scopes: basic uma_protection Custom_Scope a2a-chat-ia-mcp-audience roles phone microprofile-jwt openid web-origins offline_access acr email service_account profile address ``` i.e. once `issuer` is set for discovery, LiteLLM builds this over-broad `scope` value for **every** OAuth2 flow it drives (both the M2M token request and the interactive `/authorize` redirect), not just `client_credentials`. Same root cause, hits both the token-request call site and the `/authorize` redirect builder. This was confirmed via a real interactive login attempt — the actual Keycloak login page itself surfaces `Invalid scopes` (same string as the token-endpoint audit log entry seen with `client_credentials`), which rules out this being a `client_credentials`-only or backend-log-only artifact. Cópialo desde el primer ```markdown hasta el cierre y pégalo directo en el comentario de GitHub — al pegarlo ahí se va a renderizar bien.

signals.title: [Bug]: provider_budget_config reports budget_reset_at ~57 years in the future without Redis
signals.text: ### What happened? With `provider_budget_config` and **no Redis configured**, `GET /provider/budgets` reports a `budget_reset_at` roughly 57 years in the future, so a monthly budget effectively never resets. Config: ```yaml router_settings: provider_budget_config: openrouter: budget_limit: 5 time_period: 30d ``` Response: ```json {"providers":{"openrouter":{"budget_limit":5.0,"time_period":"30d", "spend":4.8888e-06,"budget_reset_at":"2083-05-04T16:04:00.635943+00:00"}}} ``` Same result with `time_period: 1mo` (`2083-05-05T15:39:32`), so it is not specific to the period format. Today's date when this was captured: 2026-08-18. ### Root cause `async_get_ttl` means different things in the two cache backends, and `_get_current_provider_budget_reset_at` assumes the Redis meaning: - `RedisCache.async_get_ttl()` returns **remaining seconds** (Redis `TTL`). - `InMemoryCache.async_get_ttl()` returns `self.ttl_dict.get(key)` — and `ttl_dict` stores an **absolute expiry timestamp**: `self.ttl_dict[key] = time.time() + float(kwargs["ttl"])` (`litellm/caching/in_memory_cache.py`). `litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py`: ```python if self.dual_cache.redis_cache: ttl_seconds = await self.dual_cache.redis_cache.async_get_ttl(spend_key) else: ttl_seconds = await self.dual_cache.async_get_ttl(spend_key) if ttl_seconds is None: return None return (datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(seconds=ttl_seconds)).isoformat() ``` Without Redis, `ttl_seconds` is an absolute unix timestamp (~1.79e9), so the result is `now + ~56.7 years` — which matches the observed 2083. The budget limit itself works; only the reported reset time (and therefore the reset window for in-memory deployments) is wrong. ### Suggested fix Either make `InMemoryCache.async_get_ttl` return remaining seconds like the Redis backend does, or convert at the call site: ```python ttl_seconds = await self.dual_cache.async_get_ttl(spend_key) ttl_seconds = ttl_seconds - time.time() # in-memory stores absolute expiry ``` The first option is preferable — `async_get_ttl` returning different units per backend is a trap for any other caller. ### Relevant log output ``` LiteLLM.LoggingError: [Non-Blocking] Exception occurred while success logging File ".../litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py", line 412, in async_log_success_event raise ValueError("custom_llm_provider is required") ValueError: custom_llm_provider is required ``` Separate but related observation while testing the same feature: every request through a `pass_through_endpoints` route raises the above in `budget_limiter.async_log_success_event`, so pass-through traffic is not counted toward provider budgets at all. Happy to file that separately if useful. ### Are you a ML Ops Team? No ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.97.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Feature]: Support native CLI login with OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I searched the existing issues and checked that this issue is not a duplicate. ### Feature description Please support standard native-application login for internal and third-party CLIs through LiteLLM Proxy. A developer should be able to configure only the LiteLLM Proxy base URL, authenticate through the enterprise identity provider in the external system browser with OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code and PKCE, and use a per-user credential without manually provisioning or copying a virtual key. Our concrete deployment is LiteLLM Proxy as the LLM gateway, OneLogin as the identity provider, existing AuthID/Beyond Identity MFA, and an internal Go CLI that launches OpenCode against LiteLLM's OpenAI-compatible routes. We may support other coding agents later. Developers should not need per-developer OneLogin issuer or client configuration. The resulting requests must retain the authenticated user's and team/organization's identity for model access, budgets, rate limits, spend, and auditing. [PR #35234](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/35234) is a related prototype, but this request intentionally leaves the credential architecture, discovery contract, and implementation open. For the first browser-capable CLI increment, the observable behavior should be: 1. The developer configures the CLI with the LiteLLM Proxy base URL. 2. The CLI discovers native OAuth/OIDC support and non-secret client configuration through a documented, versioned contract. 3. Login uses OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code with PKCE `S256`. 4. Authentication opens the external system browser, never an embedded webview. 5. The redirect uses a loopback address with an OS-assigned local port. 6. The normal enterprise SSO and MFA policies run at OneLogin. 7. No client secret is embedded in or distributed with the CLI. 8. LiteLLM Proxy accepts the resulting per-user bearer credential. 9. The CLI securely reuses and refreshes the session where possible. 10. Logout removes the local session. 11. Our Go wrapper can launch OpenCode with the credential without copying a virtual key. 12. Requests remain attributable to the authenticated user and team/organization. 13. Existing API-key users and proxy-mediated login remain compatible. 14. The contract is documented for non-Python CLIs. The implementation may use an IdP token or a LiteLLM session credential, choose the discovery endpoint/schema, and choose the secure-storage mechanism and package layout. It should not depend on the architecture of PR #35234. Out of scope for this issue: - Device Authorization Grant for headless or remote-browser SSH sessions; that can be a follow-up. - Embedded-browser authentication. - Resource Owner Password Credentials. - Direct SAML in the CLI. - DPoP or other proof-of-possession work. - Modifying every third-party coding agent. - Replacing API-key authentication. - Requiring raw IdP access tokens as the only credential design. ### User Flow The hostname `https://llm.example.com` below is sanitized; the route paths are the real routes the client would use. #### Before this feature (today) Today the flow dead-ends before our Go wrapper can start a native browser login, so each developer must separately obtain and store a long-lived virtual key. 1. The developer configures the internal Go wrapper with the LiteLLM Proxy base URL `https://llm.example.com`. 2. The wrapper sends `GET https://llm.example.com/.well-known/litellm-ui-config` and receives the current discovery/config response, which has no documented native-client OAuth/OIDC contract for a non-Python CLI. 3. The developer cannot start an external-system-browser Authorization Code + PKCE login through the proxy URL; the current `lite login` remains proxy-mediated and the default-branch CLI has no browser-native flow option. 4. As a workaround, the developer separately obtains a LiteLLM virtual key and stores it in an environment variable or local configuration for the Go wrapper. 5. The wrapper launches OpenCode only after this manual long-lived-secret handling. 6. OpenCode sends `POST https://llm.example.com/v1/chat/completions` with the manually supplied key and receives the normal OpenAI-compatible response. #### After this feature (ideal user flow) With this feature, the same proxy URL starts a standard native browser login and OpenCode runs with the developer's attributable session instead of a copied virtual key. 1. The developer configures the internal Go wrapper with the LiteLLM Proxy base URL `https://llm.example.com`. 2. The wrapper sends `GET https://llm.example.com/.well-known/litellm-ui-config` and receives a documented, versioned native-client OAuth/OIDC contract with the required non-secret client configuration. 3. The developer runs login; the wrapper opens the external system browser to OneLogin with an Authorization Code request containing a PKCE `S256` challenge, `state`, OIDC `nonce`, and a loopback redirect on an OS-assigned port. 4. The developer completes the existing OneLogin SSO and AuthID/Beyond Identity MFA prompts in the browser and sees a successful return to the CLI. 5. The CLI confirms the authenticated identity without printing any token, and securely stores the reusable session. 6. The wrapper launches OpenCode using that session without asking the developer to copy a virtual key. 7. OpenCode sends `POST https://llm.example.com/v1/chat/completions` and receives the normal OpenAI-compatible response, attributed by LiteLLM Proxy to the authenticated user and team/organization. 8. Later launches reuse or refresh the session where possible; logout deletes the local session. ### How far you got #### Config / setup the proxy ran with I used a disposable checkout of the current upstream default branch and attempted this minimal local configuration: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: fake-openai-endpoint litellm_params: model: openai/fake-model api_key: os.environ/OPENAI_API_KEY api_base: https://fake-api.example.com general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY litellm_settings: drop_params: true telemetry: false ``` Non-secret environment/setup values: ```text PYTHONPATH=<disposable checkout of c2efe9e422b6ce62f0001d847d578d1e7d7ea6e3> OPENAI_API_KEY=<redacted local placeholder; no provider call was made> LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=<redacted local placeholder> Host: 127.0.0.1 Port: 4000 ``` #### Version or commit ```text Default branch: litellm_internal_staging Commit: c2efe9e422b6ce62f0001d847d578d1e7d7ea6e3 LiteLLM CLI: 1.85.0 ``` #### Commands and their full output, up to the step that dead-ends ```console $ litellm-proxy --version LiteLLM CLI 1.85.0 LiteLLM URL: http://localhost:4000 HTTPConnectionPool(host='localhost', port=4000): /health/readiness NewConnectionError("HTTPConnection(host='localhost', port=4000): 61") $ python -m litellm.proxy.client.cli.main login --help Usage: python -m litellm.proxy.client.cli.main login [OPTIONS] Login to LiteLLM proxy using SSO authentication Options: --help Show this message and exit. ``` The local proxy startup attempt stopped before serving HTTP because the existing checkout environment did not have the optional proxy dependency installed: ```console $ litellm --config /tmp/litellm-default-evidence/config.yaml --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4000 ModuleNotFoundError: Missing dependency No module named 'websockets'. Run `pip install 'litellm[proxy]'` $ curl -i --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1:4000/.well-known/litellm-ui-config curl: (7) Failed to connect to 127.0.0.1 port 4000 after 0 ms: Couldn't connect to server ``` The closest browser-native CLI command then dead-ended in option parsing on the current default branch: ```console $ python -m litellm.proxy.client.cli.main --base-url http://127.0.0.1:4000 login --flow browser Usage: python -m litellm.proxy.client.cli.main login [OPTIONS] Try 'python -m litellm.proxy.client.cli.main login --help' for help. Error: No such option: --flow ``` #### What stopped me there The current default-branch CLI has no browser-native login option, so the flow stops before any browser, identity provider, or model provider contact. The local proxy could not be started in the existing environment because its optional proxy dependency was absent, so I did not claim a live discovery response. PR #35234 contains separate prototype evidence; it is not presented here as default-branch behavior. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### LiteLLM is hiring a founding backend engineer, are you interested in joining us shipping to all users? No ### Twitter / LinkedIn details No response

signals.title: additional_drop_params strips fields from message content blocks, not just top-level request params
signals.text: # Bug: `additional_drop_params` strips fields from message content blocks, not just top-level request params ## Description `additional_drop_params` is intended to drop top-level request parameters (e.g., `thinking`, `temperature`) before they're sent to the provider. However, it also recursively strips fields with the same name from **inside message content blocks**, breaking valid conversation histories. ## Reproduction ### Config: ```yaml - model_name: "claude-opus-5" litellm_params: model: "anthropic/claude-opus-5" api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY additional_drop_params: ["thinking", "temperature", "top_p", "top_k"] ``` ### Request: ```python import litellm response = litellm.completion( model="claude-opus-5", messages=[ {"role": "user", "content": "What is 2+2?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": [ {"type": "thinking", "thinking": "The user asks about 2+2. The answer is 4."}, {"type": "text", "text": "4"} ]}, {"role": "user", "content": "And 3+3?"} ], max_tokens=100 ) ``` ### Expected behavior: - The top-level `thinking` request parameter (if present) should be stripped. - The `thinking` **field inside message content blocks** (`messages[].content[].thinking`) should be left intact — it's part of the conversation history, not a request parameter. ### Actual behavior: The `thinking` field is stripped from inside the assistant message content block, turning: ```json {"type": "thinking", "thinking": "The user asks about 2+2. The answer is 4."} ``` into: ```json {"type": "thinking"} ``` Anthropic then rejects this with: ``` messages.X.content.0.thinking: each thinking block must contain thinking ``` ## Impact This breaks **fallback routing** in production. When a primary model fails and LiteLLM falls back to a model with `additional_drop_params: ["thinking"]`, the conversation history (which may contain thinking blocks from prior reasoning model responses) gets corrupted, causing the fallback to also fail. Error observed: ``` Error doing the fallback: {"type":"error","error":{"type":"invalid_request_error", "message":"messages.27.content.0.thinking: each thinking block must contain thinking"}} ``` ## Environment - LiteLLM version: v1.93.2 - Deployment: LiteLLM Proxy (Docker/K8s) - Provider: Anthropic (claude-opus-5) - Router with fallbacks enabled ## Suggested Fix `additional_drop_params` should only strip keys from the **top-level request body** (the kwargs dict passed to the completion call), not recurse into nested structures like `messages[].content[]`. The stripping logic should be scoped to: ```python # Only strip from top-level params for param in additional_drop_params: kwargs.pop(param, None) ``` And should NOT traverse into: - `messages[].content[]` (message content blocks) - `messages[].tool_calls[]` (tool call arguments) - Any other nested message payload structures ## Workaround Remove `"thinking"` from `additional_drop_params` on models that are used as fallback targets. This means clients sending the unsupported `thinking` parameter will get a raw provider error, but fallback routing won't break.

signals.title: [Bug]: Per-user authorization-code credentials are omitted from MCP prompt and resource operations
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? For an MCP server configured with per-user OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code credentials, LiteLLM applies the stored user credential to tool operations but not to prompt or resource operations. After the user completes OAuth, `tools/list` and `tools/call` work. The same upstream server returns 401 for `prompts/list` and `resources/list`, and LiteLLM turns those failures into empty lists. `prompts/get`, `resources/read`, and `resources/templates/list` use the same unauthenticated client-construction path and are affected as well. Expected behavior: every protected MCP operation should resolve and send the same stored per-user OAuth credential. Actual behavior: only the tool paths pass `user_api_key_auth` into `_create_mcp_client`, which is required by the Authorization Code credential resolver. The difference is visible in the v1.97.0 source: - Tool listing passes `user_api_key_auth`: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.97.0/litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/server.py#L1965-L2025 - Prompt and resource listing do not pass it to the manager: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.97.0/litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/server.py#L2130-L2305 - The manager constructs prompt and resource clients without `user_api_key_auth`: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.97.0/litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/mcp_server_manager.py#L3480-L3682 ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Configure an upstream Streamable HTTP MCP server that requires the same bearer token for tools, prompts, and resources. 2. Configure that server in LiteLLM with `auth_type: oauth2` and `oauth2_flow: authorization_code`. 3. Complete the per-user OAuth connection and verify that the credential status reports `has_credential: true`. 4. Connect an MCP client through LiteLLM and call `tools/list`. The protected upstream tools are returned. 5. Call `prompts/list` and `resources/list` through the same connection and user identity. 6. Observe upstream 401 responses in the LiteLLM logs and empty prompt and resource lists at the client. 7. Call a protected prompt or resource directly. These operations also create an MCP client without the per-user credential. ### Relevant log output ```text Failed to get prompts from server protected-mcp: Client error '401 Unauthorized' Failed to get resources from server protected-mcp: Client error '401 Unauthorized' ``` ### Suggested fix Pass `user_api_key_auth` through every prompt and resource manager method and into `_create_mcp_client`, using the same Authorization Code credential-resolution path as tool listing and tool calls. Please cover list, get, read, and resource-template operations with regression tests. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.97.0
signals.author: frdeng

signals.title: Exa AI search: highlights, score, and response metadata (costDollars, requestId) silently dropped in transform_search_response
signals.text: ### Bug description `ExaAISearchConfig.transform_search_response` (`litellm/llms/exa_ai/search/transformation.py`) only reads `result.get("text")` when building each `SearchResult`, so a request with `contents: {highlights: {...}}` returns HTTP 200 with `snippet` empty on every row — the `highlights` Exa actually returned are discarded entirely. `highlightScores` and `score` are dropped the same way, and the response envelope (`costDollars`, `requestId`, `resolvedSearchType`, `searchTime`) is discarded too, even though `costDollars` is the only in-band way to reconcile billed spend against Exa's actual charge. ### Reproduction Measured against `v1.93.0`, but the relevant code path looks unchanged on `main` as of this writing: ```python import litellm resp = litellm.search( model="exa_ai/search", query="...", contents={"highlights": {"numSentences": 2}}, ) print(resp.results[0].snippet) # "" -- empty, even though Exa returned highlights ``` ### Expected behavior - `snippet` should fall back to the joined `highlights` when `text` is blank (Exa returns only the content type you request, so in practice one or the other is populated, not both). - `highlights` / `highlight_scores` (from `highlightScores`) / `score` should be attached to `SearchResult` when Exa returns them — `SearchResult` already declares `model_config = {"extra": "allow"}`, so this is purely additive and doesn't change the shape of a text-only response. - The response envelope (minus `results`) should be attached to `SearchResponse` (e.g. as `provider_metadata`), so callers can reconcile billed cost against `costDollars`. ### Fix We have a fix for this (not yet upstream) that does exactly the above. Happy to open a PR if useful.
signals.author: deepanshululla

signals.title: Anthropic /v1/messages adapter maps metadata.user_id to 'user' only, never to OpenAI's prompt_cache_key
signals.text: ## Summary When bridging Anthropic `/v1/messages` requests to OpenAI-compatible targets (Responses API and Chat Completions), `metadata.user_id` is only mapped to the deprecated OpenAI `user` field. It is never used to populate `prompt_cache_key`, which is the field OpenAI's GPT-5.6+ prompt caching actually keys routing/matching off of. This is documented explicitly in the `/v1/messages → /responses` mapping reference: | Anthropic (`/v1/messages`) | Responses API | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | `metadata.user_id` | `user` | Extracted from the metadata object and truncated to 64 characters | Relevant code: `litellm/llms/anthropic/experimental_pass_through/responses_adapters/transformation.py` (Responses path) and the equivalent chat-completions adapter path both only set `responses_kwargs["user"]` / the chat-completions `user` param from `metadata.user_id`. Neither sets `prompt_cache_key`. ## Why this matters Per OpenAI's own prompt-caching docs: - `user` is being replaced by `safety_identifier` and `prompt_cache_key`; OpenAI explicitly recommends using `prompt_cache_key` instead of `user` to maintain caching optimizations. - For GPT-5.6 and later, you must set `prompt_cache_key` to get reliable exact-prefix matching for both implicit and explicit caching. Without it, requests may still get automatic cache hits, but without the improved matching. Anthropic-native clients that talk to LiteLLM's `/v1/messages` endpoint — Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK, other Anthropic-shaped tools — already send a stable, per-session `metadata.user_id` on every request (Claude Code specifically sends a value that's stable for the lifetime of one CLI session and only changes on restart). This is exactly the kind of value `prompt_cache_key` is designed for (OpenAI's own docs list "session IDs and user IDs" as common `prompt_cache_key` values), but it's currently discarded for caching purposes and only forwarded to the deprecated `user` field. The practical effect: any Anthropic-shaped client routed through LiteLLM to an OpenAI GPT-5.6+ backend gets no cache-routing stickiness benefit from a value it's already sending on every call, with no client-side change possible to fix this (the client has no notion of `prompt_cache_key`, only `metadata.user_id`). ## Request Populate `prompt_cache_key` from `metadata.user_id` (in addition to, or as a config-gated alternative to, the existing `user` mapping) when translating Anthropic `/v1/messages` requests to OpenAI-compatible Responses API / Chat Completions targets. ## Related - Closed issue #28354 and open issue #36091 cover the reverse-direction gap (OpenAI cache-hit usage not being reported back in the Anthropic response shape) — fixing this request-side mapping without also fixing the usage-reporting side would leave callers unable to verify caching is actually happening. Flagging for context, not asking to bundle the fixes.
signals.author: jimmychen-p72

signals.title: cache_control_injection_points has no equivalent for OpenAI prompt_cache_breakpoint on OpenAI-compatible targets
signals.text: ## Summary `cache_control_injection_points` (via `AnthropicCacheControlHook`, introduced in #9996 and extended to the `/v1/messages` path in #30341/#30615 for issue #30293) lets an admin configure, at the deployment level, where a stable-prefix cache boundary should be placed. Today this hook only ever produces Anthropic-shaped `cache_control` blocks. There is no equivalent path that emits OpenAI's GPT-5.6+ `prompt_cache_breakpoint` (per content block) plus `prompt_cache_options` (request-level `mode`/`ttl`) when the deployment actually routes to an OpenAI-compatible target. ## Why this matters OpenAI's GPT-5.6+ caching model supports the same concept — an explicit marker on the last content block of a reusable prefix — as `prompt_cache_breakpoint`, combined with `prompt_cache_options.mode` to control whether the automatic implicit breakpoint stays active alongside it. This is functionally the same admin intent `cache_control_injection_points` already expresses for Anthropic, just via a different wire format on a different provider. Without this, admins running mixed model fleets (Anthropic + OpenAI GPT-5.6 deployments behind the same proxy config pattern) have a working, centrally-configured caching primitive for Anthropic-backed deployments and *no* equivalent centrally-configured primitive for OpenAI-backed ones — caching for OpenAI targets is left entirely to either the client (which, for Anthropic-shaped clients like Claude Code, has no notion of `prompt_cache_breakpoint` at all — see openai/codex#35300 for the same gap in another Anthropic-shaped client, Codex CLI) or to OpenAI's default implicit-mode caching, which the docs note is exact-match-only on GPT-5.6+ and does not do the longest-matching-prefix fallback earlier models had. This means a stable prefix (e.g. a large system prompt + tool definitions, sent identically by an Anthropic-shaped client on every turn) that would reliably cache on Anthropic never gets the same reliable treatment on OpenAI targets, purely because of a proxy-side config gap rather than a client or model limitation. ## Request When a deployment configured with `cache_control_injection_points` routes to an OpenAI-compatible target that supports explicit prompt-cache breakpoints (GPT-5.6+), translate the configured injection point(s) into: - a `prompt_cache_breakpoint: {"mode": "explicit"}` marker on the corresponding outgoing content block, and - `prompt_cache_options` at the request root (at minimum enabling explicit mode; `ttl` currently only supports `"30m"` per OpenAI's docs so may not need to be configurable yet). Leaving the specific implementation approach (extend `AnthropicCacheControlHook` with provider-aware branching vs. a new parallel hook) to maintainer judgment — filing this to capture the gap, not to prescribe the fix. ## Related - #30293 / #30341 / #30615 — established the pattern this issue is asking to extend to OpenAI-compatible targets - #32669 — adds `prompt_cache_breakpoint` as a passthrough param for GPT-5.6 models (request-shape plumbing this issue would build on) - openai/codex#35300 — the same underlying gap (no way to emit `prompt_cache_breakpoint`) from the client side, for a different Anthropic-shaped client

signals.title: [Bug]: search router silently drops provider-specific litellm_params from yaml search_tools entries
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? When a `search_tools` entry in the proxy config carries provider-specific keys in its `litellm_params` (for example `tool_name` for the agentcore provider, or `aws_access_key_id` / `aws_secret_access_key` overrides), those keys are silently dropped. The search router forwards only `search_provider`, `api_key`, and `api_base` from the tool's `litellm_params` to the underlying search call (`SearchAPIRouter.async_search_with_fallbacks_helper` in `litellm/router_utils/search_api_router.py`), so every other key is ignored with no warning, no boot error, and no request-time error Expected: either every `litellm_params` key is forwarded to the provider (the way `model_list` entries forward their `litellm_params` to completion calls), or the proxy rejects unknown keys loudly at boot so an admin finds out their knob is dead The same keys do work when passed per request in the body or set via provider env vars (for agentcore, `AGENTCORE_SEARCH_TOOL_NAME`), which is how the guard behind `tool_name` stays reachable. Only the yaml path is dead. The agentcore example config was corrected in #36331 to stop advertising the yaml knobs; this issue tracks fixing the plumbing itself, which affects all search providers ### User Flow Before a (hypothetical) fix: a proxy admin whose AgentCore gateway target has a custom name configures it in yaml and every search silently uses the wrong tool name 1. They add a `search_tools` entry with `search_provider: agentcore`, their gateway `api_base`, and `tool_name: MyTarget___WebSearch` in `litellm_params`, then start the proxy; boot succeeds with no warning 2. They send POST http://litellm-domain/v1/search/agentcore-search with `{"query": "latest AI developments", "max_results": 5}` 3. The request goes out with the default `web-search-tool___WebSearch` instead of their configured name; on a gateway whose target really has a custom name this comes back as an MCP tool-not-found error, and on a gateway that also has a default-named target it silently searches through the wrong one 4. Nothing in the response or the logs says their yaml `tool_name` was ignored After a (hypothetical) fix: the same config works, or fails loudly 1. They add the same `search_tools` entry and start the proxy 2. They send the same POST http://litellm-domain/v1/search/agentcore-search request 3. The request goes out with `MyTarget___WebSearch` and returns results from their target, or, if the key is deliberately unsupported, the proxy refuses to boot naming the unsupported key ### Proof the bug occurs Config the proxy ran with (proxy booted from PR #36331 at commit `70a4f9a73aabd327b9c06e52bf5d47b437b76430`; the router file involved is untouched by that PR and identical on `litellm_internal_staging`): ```yaml search_tools: - search_tool_name: agentcore-badtool litellm_params: search_provider: agentcore api_base: https://litellm-qa-agentcore-tez4ymmxfc.gateway.bedrock-agentcore.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/mcp tool_name: my-target___ListFiles ``` The agentcore provider rejects any `tool_name` not ending in `___WebSearch`, so this request must fail. Instead it returns HTTP 200 with real web results, against a real AgentCore gateway: ``` curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:26793/v1/search/agentcore-badtool \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-REDACTED' \ -d '{"query": "anything", "max_results": 2}' -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' {"results":[{"title":"Anything","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anything", ...}],"object":"search"} HTTP 200 ``` The proxy debug log shows the outgoing JSON-RPC call used the default tool name, not the configured one, proving the yaml value never reached the provider: ``` -d '{'jsonrpc': '2.0', 'id': 1, 'method': 'tools/call', 'params': {'name': 'web-search-tool___WebSearch', 'arguments': {'query': 'anything', 'maxResults': 2}}}' ``` Control showing the guard itself works when the value arrives via env var: rebooting the same proxy with `AGENTCORE_SEARCH_TOOL_NAME=my-target___ListFiles` exported makes the same request refuse with ``` Invalid AgentCore search tool_name 'my-target___ListFiles': must end with '___WebSearch' (a web-search connector tool). Other gateway tools cannot be invoked through this provider. ``` Fix sketch: forward the tool's full `litellm_params` (minus `search_provider`, which becomes the positional provider) as kwargs from `SearchAPIRouter.async_search_with_fallbacks_helper` into the search call, mirroring how `model_list` `litellm_params` flow into completion calls, with request-body params winning over yaml on key collisions. Needs a check across all search providers that previously-ignored yaml keys don't change behavior for existing configs ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? litellm_internal_staging at 2059033352de (also present at PR #36331 tip 70a4f9a7) ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: SendGridEmailLogger: add Reply-To support via SENDGRID_REPLY_TO_EMAIL env var
signals.text: ## Problem `SendGridEmailLogger` (in `litellm_enterprise/enterprise_callbacks/send_emails/sendgrid_email.py`) constructs the SendGrid v3 Mail Send payload with `from`, `personalizations`, and `content`, but does not include the optional [`reply_to`](https://docs.sendgrid.com/api-reference/mail-send/mail-send) field. This means all notification emails (budget alerts, key creation, user invitations) have Reply-To defaulting to the sender address — typically a `no-reply@` mailbox that nobody monitors. Organizations that use a no-reply sender address have no way to direct recipient replies to a monitored mailbox (e.g. a team distribution list) without forking the callback. ## Root Cause `SendGridEmailLogger.__init__` reads `SENDGRID_API_KEY` and `SENDGRID_SENDER_EMAIL` from environment variables but does not read a `SENDGRID_REPLY_TO_EMAIL` variable. The `send_email` method builds the JSON payload without a `reply_to` key, so the SendGrid API defaults Reply-To to the `from` address. ## Proposed Fix 1. In `__init__`, read an optional `SENDGRID_REPLY_TO_EMAIL` env var: ```python self.sendgrid_reply_to_email = os.getenv("SENDGRID_REPLY_TO_EMAIL") ``` 2. In `send_email`, conditionally add `reply_to` to the payload before the HTTP POST: ```python if self.sendgrid_reply_to_email: payload["reply_to"] = {"email": self.sendgrid_reply_to_email} ``` This is fully backward-compatible — when the env var is unset, behavior is unchanged. ## Environment - LiteLLM version: 1.72.4.dev1 (litellm-enterprise) - SendGrid API: v3 Mail Send

signals.title: [Bug]: A2A chat-completions shim ("model": "a2a/<name>") returns "no healthy deployments" when wildcard model groups exist
signals.text: ### What happened? Calling an A2A-registered agent through the documented chat-completions convenience shim (`"model": "a2a/<agent_name>"`) fails with a `400` "no healthy deployments" error, even though the same agent works correctly when called through the native `/a2a/{agent_id}` JSON-RPC endpoint. Expected: the chat-completions call should route to the agent and return its reply, exactly like the native endpoint does. ### User Flow Before a (hypothetical) fix: a developer wants to call a registered A2A agent from an existing OpenAI-style client without changing its request format 1. They send `POST https://<proxy>/v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "a2a/hermes", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "ping"}]}` 2. The response comes back `400` with body `{"error": {"message": "litellm.BadRequestError: You passed in model=a2a/hermes. There are no healthy deployments for this model. ..."}}` 3. The same agent works fine when they instead call `POST https://<proxy>/a2a/{agent_id}` with a native JSON-RPC `message/send` body — so they know the agent itself is healthy, only this endpoint is broken After a (hypothetical) fix: the same request succeeds 1. They send the identical `POST https://<proxy>/v1/chat/completions` request 2. They get back a normal chat-completions-shaped `200` response containing the agent's reply ### Proof the bug occurs Config: proxy has multiple wildcard model groups configured (e.g. `openrouter/*`, `gemini/*`, `anthropic/*`) alongside a registered A2A agent (`agent_id: 26494700-...`, name `hermes`). Version/commit: `docker.litellm.ai/berriai/litellm:main-stable`, revision `ef84494d52c6708e4e9f4a54ce551a265995ad8f` (pulled 2026-08-16, reproduced again 2026-08-20) ``` $ curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ***" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"a2a/hermes","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"ping"}]}' {"error":{"message":"litellm.BadRequestError: You passed in model=a2a/hermes. There are no healthy deployments for this model. Received Model Group=a2a/hermes\nAvailable Model Group Fallbacks=None","type":null,"param":null,"code":"400"}} HTTP_STATUS:400 $ curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/a2a/26494700-501b-4106-a5c4-76655a9bde2b \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ***" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"repro-1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"ping"}],"messageId":"repro-msg-1"}}}' {"id":"repro-1","jsonrpc":"2.0","result":{"task":{"status":{"state":"TASK_STATE_COMPLETED","message":{"parts":[{"text":"PONG"}]}}}}} HTTP_STATUS:200 ``` Code-level cause (for maintainers): in `litellm/proxy/route_llm_request.py`, the `elif llm_router.default_deployment is not None or len(llm_router.pattern_router.patterns) > 0:` wildcard-fallback branch is evaluated before the `elif _is_a2a_agent_model(data.get("model", "")):` check further down — any proxy with wildcard model groups always matches the first branch, so `a2a/...` model names never reach the A2A routing path. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? main-stable @ ef84494d52c6708e4e9f4a54ce551a265995ad8f

signals.title: Router: cool down deployments that are out of budget (400 usage-limit / 402 insufficient credits are never cooled)
signals.text: ### What happened? `Router` cooldowns are decided by HTTP status in `litellm/router_utils/cooldown_handlers.py::_is_cooldown_required`: ```python if exception_status >= 400 and exception_status < 500: if exception_status == 429: return True # rate limit elif exception_status == 401: return True # auth elif exception_status == 408: return True elif exception_status == 404: return True else: # Do NOT cool down all other 4XX Errors return False ``` That list misses **budget exhaustion**, which is arguably the single most cooldown-worthy condition there is: unlike a rate limit, it does not clear in seconds, and unlike a 401 it is not a config mistake -- the deployment is simply unusable for a while, and the router already knows where to send the traffic instead. Two providers, two statuses, neither cooled down: | Provider | Response when out of budget | Status | |---|---|---| | Anthropic | `{"type":"invalid_request_error","message":"You have reached your specified API usage limits. You will regain access on 2026-09-01"}` | 400 | | OpenRouter | `{"error":{"message":"Insufficient credits. Add more using https://openrouter.ai/settings/credits","code":402}}` | 402 | Effect with `fallbacks=[{"primary": ["fb0", "fb1"]}]`: fallback works, so every request still gets answered -- but the exhausted primary is re-attempted on *every* request for as long as the cap lasts (weeks, per the Anthropic message above), paying its latency each time before falling through. A deployment that is known-dead for a month is retried thousands of times. ### Suggested fix Recognise budget exhaustion as a cooldown trigger: 1. Cool down `402` unconditionally -- "Payment Required" has no transient reading. 2. For `400`, match the provider's exhaustion signature rather than cooling all 400s (which would wrongly park a deployment on a malformed request). The provider adapters already parse these bodies. 3. Ideally honour a stated recovery time: Anthropic returns the regain date in the message, so the cooldown could last until then instead of `cooldown_time`. Happy to send a PR if the maintainers agree with (1) and (2) as the shape. ### Relevant log output ``` litellm.BadRequestError: AnthropicException - {"type":"error","error":{"type":"invalid_request_error","message":"You have reached your specified API usage limits. You will regain access on 2026-09-01..."}} litellm.APIError: OpenrouterException - {"error":{"message":"Insufficient credits...","code":402}} ``` ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: `sambanova` provider flattens content lists to a string, so image_url never reaches the API
signals.text: ### What happened? The `sambanova` provider flattens user content lists into a plain string, so `image_url` parts never reach the API. Vision-capable SambaNova models therefore reply with HTTP 200 as if nothing was attached. `litellm/llms/sambanova/chat.py#L114-L130` calls `handle_messages_with_content_list_to_str_conversion` unconditionally. Its docstring states "SambaNova API doesn't support content as a list - only string content", but the API does accept content lists today. ### Relevant log output / reproduction Same API key, same model, same payload. Only the LiteLLM model prefix differs. The image is a PNG with three vertical bands filled green, magenta and yellow, and the prompt asks for the colours from left to right. | model passed to `litellm.completion` | answer | | --- | --- | | `openai/gemma-4-31B-it` with `api_base="https://api.sambanova.ai/v1"` | names the three colours correctly | | `sambanova/gemma-4-31B-it` | answers that no image is attached | For completeness, video is genuinely unsupported by the API, so this is only about images and other non-text parts: `video_url` returns a 500 `unexpected_error`, and an `image_url` holding a video data URI is rejected with `` `image_url` must start with 'data:image/<jpeg|jpg|png|webp>;base64,' ``. ### Suggested fix Flatten only when the content list carries no non-text parts, or drop the transformation. I can send a PR if the conditional approach is preferred. ### Version v1.97.0, and the same implementation is on `main` @ 007bd43cf.

signals.title: [Bug]: Background health-check DB persistence is not leader-gated and LiteLLM_HealthCheckTable grows unbounded — causes DB storms at scale
signals.text: ## What happened? Two independent defects in the background health-check loop combine to storm the database every cycle (default 15 min) when running `use_shared_health_check: true` with multiple workers: **Bug 1 — DB persistence is not leader-gated:** `SharedHealthCheckManager` correctly gates the **probing** step (only the lock-holder sends health-check requests to LLM providers). But after probing, `_run_background_health_check()` unconditionally calls `_schedule_background_health_check_db_save()` on **every worker** (line ~3499 of `proxy_server.py`). Each worker runs `get_all_latest_health_checks()` — a `SELECT DISTINCT ON` full-table scan — plus per-model INSERTs. With N workers this multiplies DB load by N every cycle. **Bug 2 — HealthCheckTable is append-only with no retention:** `save_health_check_result()` in `PrismaClient` uses `.create()` (INSERT). There is no upsert and no pruning. The table grows unbounded. Because `get_all_latest_health_checks()` uses `DISTINCT ON (model_id, model_name)` ordered by `checked_at DESC`, Postgres must scan **all rows** to find the latest per model — there is no loose index-scan optimization for `DISTINCT ON`. **Combined impact at scale:** In our production environment (360 models, ~10 workers, 15-min cycle), the table grew to **3.9 million rows** in 64 days. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of `get_all_latest_health_checks()` shows: - **4.18 seconds** execution time - **~31 GB** buffer traffic (index + heap) - Scans all 3.9M rows to return 360 When ~10 workers run this simultaneously against a near-idle database (we use Aurora Serverless v2 with auto-scaling), it triggers a cold scale-up to max capacity, which causes connection churn, severs query-engine connections across all tasks, health saves fail, deployments get marked unavailable, and the proxy returns `No deployments available` 500s. We observed a **20.6% 5xx rate** during a 25-minute incident window. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Configure LiteLLM proxy with: ```yaml general_settings: use_shared_health_check: true background_health_checks: true health_check_interval: 900 # 15 min ``` 2. Deploy with multiple workers (e.g. 4+ Gunicorn workers or multiple pods behind a load balancer) and 100+ models in config. 3. Let the proxy run for several weeks. 4. Observe `LiteLLM_HealthCheckTable` row count growing linearly (models × cycles × workers per cycle): ```sql SELECT count(*) FROM "LiteLLM_HealthCheckTable"; -- After 64 days with 360 models, 10 workers: ~3.9M rows ``` 5. Observe that **every worker** calls `get_all_latest_health_checks()` each cycle, not just the leader: ```sql -- Proof of leaderless fan-out: distinct checked_by values within a single cycle SELECT checked_at, checked_by, count(*) FROM "LiteLLM_HealthCheckTable" WHERE checked_at > now() - interval '20 minutes' GROUP BY checked_at, checked_by ORDER BY checked_at DESC; -- Returns rows for EACH pod writing the same models <60s apart ``` 6. At sufficient table size, the `DISTINCT ON` read becomes multi-second, and concurrent execution from N workers causes DB saturation / connection exhaustion. ## Relevant log output ``` # EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the DISTINCT ON read (3.9M rows, 360 models): Unique (cost=0.56..2847163.44 rows=360 width=1389) (actual time=0.194..4183.021 rows=360 loops=1) -> Index Scan using ... on "LiteLLM_HealthCheckTable" (actual time=0.193..3922.574 rows=3900000 loops=1) Planning Time: 0.422 ms Execution Time: 4183.541 ms Buffers: shared hit=31457280 ``` ## Root Cause in Code **`proxy_server.py` ~L3498-3505** — `_schedule_background_health_check_db_save()` is called unconditionally regardless of whether this worker was the health-check leader: ```python # Save background health checks to database (non-blocking) _schedule_background_health_check_db_save( prisma_client, shared_health_manager, _llm_model_list, healthy_endpoints, unhealthy_endpoints, ) ``` **`utils.py` ~L5138** — `save_health_check_result()` uses `.create()` (INSERT), never upserts or prunes: ```python return await HealthCheckRepository(self).table.create(data=health_check_data) ``` **`utils.py` ~L5180-5187** — `get_all_latest_health_checks()` does `DISTINCT ON` over the full table: ```python return await HealthCheckRepository(self).table.find_many( distinct=["model_id", "model_name"], order=[ {"model_id": "asc"}, {"model_name": "asc"}, {"checked_at": "desc"}, ], ) ``` ## Suggested Fix **Short-term (two changes):** 1. **Leader-gate the DB persistence:** `SharedHealthCheckManager` already elects a leader for probing. Expose an `is_current_pod_leader` flag (set True when the pod acquires the lock or falls back to local probe; reset to False on cache hit). Gate `_schedule_background_health_check_db_save()` on it so exactly one pod does the read + write per cycle. When `shared_health_manager is None`, preserve the existing per-pod behavior. 2. **Add retention pruning:** After a successful save, the leader prunes rows older than a retention window (e.g. 7 days) via a batched, bounded DELETE. This caps the `DISTINCT ON` scan cost at O(recent rows) instead of O(all history). Batching (e.g. 10k rows per pass, max 50 passes) avoids long locks on the first run against a large backlog. **Long-term (architectural):** Replace the append-only `LiteLLM_HealthCheckTable` with a **one-row-per-model upsert** design (a `LiteLLM_HealthCheckLatest` table with `model_id` as primary key, upserted each cycle). This makes the "latest per model" read O(N models) — a simple `SELECT *` — instead of `DISTINCT ON` over unbounded history. History can be kept in the existing table with retention, or dropped entirely. ## What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ## What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.94.3

signals.title: PATCH /update/mcp_semantic_filter_settings returns HTML 504 when enabling semantic filter
signals.text: ## Bug Description When calling `PATCH /update/mcp_semantic_filter_settings` with `enabled: true`, the server successfully saves the settings but returns an HTML 504 error page from the reverse proxy instead of a valid JSON response. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Call `PATCH /update/mcp_semantic_filter_settings` with body `{"enabled": true, "embedding_model": "text-embedding-3-small", "top_k": 10, "similarity_threshold": 0.3}` 2. The settings are actually persisted (verified by `GET /get/mcp_semantic_filter_settings`) 3. But the PATCH response is an HTML 504 page, not JSON ## Expected Behavior Return a proper JSON response (e.g., `200 OK` with `{"status": "success"}` or `204 No Content`). ## Actual Behavior Returns HTML 504 Gateway Timeout from nginx/openresty, even though the update succeeded. ## Workaround Clients must make a subsequent GET request to verify if settings were actually applied. ## Environment - LiteLLM version: 1.86.2 - Reverse proxy: openresty/nginx
