signals.title: fix(proxy): claim batch cost rows atomically so multi-pod polling can't double-bill
signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Every pod polls batch costs without a lock - Two pods bill the same completed batch - Aggregated spend counts that batch twice How it solves it: - Claim each row with an atomic compare-and-swap - Claim after the results fetch, right before billing - Losers skip, and a failed spend log releases the claim ## User Flow Before: an admin running the gateway on more than one pod has one completed batch counted twice in their spend totals, while the logs page shows a single entry for it 1. The admin runs the gateway with two replicas and batch polling enabled, both pointed at the same database 2. They upload a batch input file and create a batch against a managed model, then wait for the provider to finish it 3. Within one polling window both replicas pick up the same finished batch, and each records a charge for it 4. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs, filter to that batch, and see exactly ONE entry, which looks correct 5. Their spend dashboards and any budget the key or user is under nevertheless move by twice that batch's cost, so the totals are wrong with no per-request evidence anywhere to explain why After: the same batch moves the totals once, no matter how many replicas run 1. The admin runs the gateway with two replicas and batch polling enabled, both pointed at the same database 2. They upload a batch input file and create a batch against a managed model, then wait for the provider to finish it 3. Within one polling window both replicas pick up the same finished batch, but only one of them records a charge for it, and the other moves on, logging that the batch was already claimed elsewhere 4. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs, filter to that batch, and see exactly one entry, as before 5. Their spend dashboards and budgets now move by that batch's cost once, matching the single entry they can see 6. If a replica dies while it is working out that batch's cost, another replica picks the batch up on a later cycle and charges it once, instead of the batch being silently dropped An earlier revision of this description claimed the admin would see two spend entries on the logs page. That was wrong, and the capture below shows why: `LiteLLM_SpendLogs.request_id` is the table's primary key, the poller stamps it with the batch's unified object id, and the flush writes with `create_many(..., skip_duplicates=True)`, so the second row is dropped by the database. Only the aggregates move twice. ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-4827 ## Review notes The claim is a compare-and-swap on `batch_processed`, and where it sits in the poll cycle matters as much as the swap itself. That column does three jobs at once: it is the poller's own "already costed" filter, it is what the managed-files deletion guard reads to decide whether a file is still needed, and it is the terminal state a costed batch ends in. Setting it before the results fetch would do two harmful things beyond winning the row. A pod killed between the claim and the spend log would leave the batch marked processed but unbilled, and no later cycle would ever select it again, so that batch's spend would be lost for good. A delete on the batch's input or output file arriving during the fetch would find no referencing batch and go through, taking away the very file the fetch was reading Claiming immediately before the spend log write avoids both. The row stays unprocessed for the whole retrieve, so the deletion guard keeps holding the files, and an interruption anywhere up to that point simply leaves the batch for the next cycle. The cost is that two pods can both fetch and price the same batch in one window, but only the compare-and-swap winner writes a spend log, and that duplicated read is cheap next to charging a customer twice What is left is the gap between the claim and the spend log itself. It is one statement wide and moving the claim cannot close it, because spend logs are queued in memory and flushed in the background, so a hard kill in that window drops the log whether or not the row was claimed first. Trading it for a lease another pod could reclaim would turn the failure mode into a double charge rather than a missed one, which is the bug this PR exists to remove What this fix protects is the aggregated spend. The spend log row was already protected, because the poller stamps a deterministic `request_id` and the table's primary key rejects the duplicate. So before this change the system had half a safety net, and the half it had is the half an operator looks at ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v` - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup: one Postgres carrying the repo schema, and one managed batch created end to end through the proxy's own endpoints rather than inserted by hand, so the row under test is the one the product writes. ``` $ curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4828/v1/files -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-lit4827" \ -F purpose=batch -F target_model_names=openai-batch -F file=@batch_input.jsonl {"id":"bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTphcHBsaWNhdGlvbi9qc29ubDt1bmlmaWVkX2lkLDE1NmIyMmU1...","object":"file",...} $ curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4828/v1/batches -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-lit4827" \ -d '{"input_file_id":"<that id>","endpoint":"/v1/chat/completions","completion_window":"24h","model":"openai-batch"}' {"id":"bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9pZDphOWU0NDJkZGYwOGQ0NDgzNDAxN2UwNDg2MGU0NWVlZDUzMmM1ZmRhNmU4NjE5YTg4OWIzNDY0ZjQ0ZWU5YjdmO2xsbV9iYXRjaF9pZDpiYXRjaF9saXQ0ODI3",...} $ psql -c 'SELECT id, status, batch_processed FROM "LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable";' id | status | batch_processed --------------------------------------+------------+----------------- ec08f5f4-3c35-4d6b-9a1d-7dbbd007abe1 | validating | f ``` Each leg then runs TWO real proxy pods against that one database, on 4828 and 4830, with `proxy_batch_polling_interval: 15`. Each leg asserts before it opens its window, and again before it closes, that the process holding each port is the pid that leg spawned and that its command line names the tree under test, that both pods are still alive, and that the tree on the import path is the intended one: ``` identity at open port 4828: pid 84525 running before_tree identity at open port 4830: pid 84527 running before_tree liveness before the window: 2/2 pollers alive check_batch_cost -> .../before_tree/enterprise/litellm_enterprise/proxy/common_utils/check_batch_cost.py has _claim_job_for_costing: False ``` The measured quantity is `LiteLLM_DailyUserSpend`, which is what the spend dashboards and budget checks read. The `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` row count is shown alongside it deliberately, to make the point that it cannot measure this: its primary key pins it to 1 whether the batch was billed once or twice. ### Before (d556fac56b) #### two pods poll the same completed batch in one window 1. Both pods select the batch and both run the costing path ``` pod A billed: 1 claim-lost: 0 pod B billed: 1 claim-lost: 0 ``` 2. The aggregate the dashboards read counts the batch twice, at twice its token count and cost, while the logs table holds a single row ``` $ psql -c 'SELECT model, api_requests, spend, prompt_tokens FROM "LiteLLM_DailyUserSpend";' model | api_requests | spend | prompt_tokens -------------+--------------+---------+--------------- gpt-4o-mini | 2 | 0.00045 | 2000 $ psql -c 'SELECT count(*) AS spend_rows, sum(spend) FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" WHERE call_type='"'"'aretrieve_batch'"'"';' spend_rows | total_spend ------------+------------- 1 | 0.000225 ``` ### After (1481a8817d) #### two pods poll the same completed batch in one window 1. Both pods select the batch and both fetch its results, and the one that loses the compare-and-swap stops without billing ``` pod A billed: 1 claim-lost: 1 pod B billed: 1 claim-lost: 0 ``` 2. The aggregate counts the batch once, matching the single row in the logs table ``` $ psql -c 'SELECT model, api_requests, spend, prompt_tokens FROM "LiteLLM_DailyUserSpend";' model | api_requests | spend | prompt_tokens -------------+--------------+----------+--------------- gpt-4o-mini | 1 | 0.000225 | 1000 $ psql -c 'SELECT count(*) AS spend_rows, sum(spend) FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" WHERE call_type='"'"'aretrieve_batch'"'"';' spend_rows | total_spend ------------+------------- 1 | 0.000225 ``` ### Why the claim sits after the results fetch, not before it Claiming before the fetch is the obvious fix and it also stops the double count, so neither leg above can tell the two apart: both read 1. The difference only appears when a pod dies while costing. These two legs run the same interruption against a variant that claims before the results fetch and against this PR, SIGKILLing the pod 10 seconds into a 75 second results fetch. #### claiming before the results fetch 1. The row is already marked processed while the results are still being fetched, so the kill lands after the claim ``` pod A entered the results fetch at 32s; interrupting it 10s into a 75s fetch row at the instant of the kill: batch_processed=t pod A SIGKILLed mid results-fetch ``` 2. Another pod polls for 200 seconds and never sees the batch again, because the poll query filters on `batch_processed = false`. The batch is marked done, was never billed, and no pod will ever pick it up ``` survivor billed: 0 $ psql -c 'SELECT model, api_requests, spend FROM "LiteLLM_DailyUserSpend";' (0 rows) $ psql -c 'SELECT id, status, batch_processed FROM "LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable";' id | status | batch_processed --------------------------------------+-------------+----------------- ec08f5f4-3c35-4d6b-9a1d-7dbbd007abe1 | in_progress | t ``` #### claiming after the results fetch (this PR) 1. The row is still unclaimed while the results are being fetched, so the same kill lands before any claim ``` pod A entered the results fetch at 44s; interrupting it 10s into a 75s fetch row at the instant of the kill: batch_processed=f pod A SIGKILLed mid results-fetch ``` 2. Another pod picks the batch up on its next cycle and charges it exactly once ``` survivor billed: 1 $ psql -c 'SELECT model, api_requests, spend, prompt_tokens FROM "LiteLLM_DailyUserSpend";' model | api_requests | spend | prompt_tokens -------------+--------------+----------+--------------- gpt-4o-mini | 1 | 0.000225 | 1000 $ psql -c 'SELECT id, status, batch_processed FROM "LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable";' id | status | batch_processed --------------------------------------+----------+----------------- ec08f5f4-3c35-4d6b-9a1d-7dbbd007abe1 | complete | t ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - The provider is a local stand-in, since a batch's completion window is 24h - Everything else above is live: two real proxies, one real Postgres - Both pods fetch results in a window; only one bills - Schemas lacking `batch_processed` keep old unclaimed behavior - The poller's deterministic `request_id` is deliberate, for correlating a spend row back to the submitted batch. Randomising it to avoid the primary-key collision would break that correlation - Aggregated spend has no idempotency key where spend logs do; that gap is wider than this PR ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/2386b54878924291841e76da29322c9c Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signals.title: fix(router): isolate deployment model info from cached backend metadata
signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Deployment lookups mutated litellm's cached backend model info - Nested metadata leaked from one deployment to its siblings - A `base_model` deployment overwrote that base model's cached info How it solves it: - Deployment lookups now merge into deep copies of cached info - Nothing returned shares objects with `model_cost` or the lookup cache ## User Flow Before: an admin runs two deployments of the same backend model, one with its own metadata, and the other one silently starts reporting the first one's values 1. They configure `claude-a` with `search_context_cost_per_query: {search_context_size_low: 0.999}` and `claude-b` with no custom metadata, both on `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929` 2. They GET https://litellm-domain/model_group/info and both deployments read as configured, `claude-b` at the built-in `0.01` 3. Traffic flows, or they read the metadata again 4. `claude-b` now reports `0.999`, the value only `claude-a` was ever configured with, and so does anything else on that backend model After: the same setup keeps each deployment's metadata to itself 1. They configure the same two deployments 2. They GET https://litellm-domain/model_group/info and both read as configured 3. Traffic flows, or they read the metadata again 4. `claude-a` still reports `0.999` and `claude-b` still reports the built-in `0.01` ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5471 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. signals.title: fix(scim): fail group sync when a member add or user creation fails (LIT-5105)
signals.text:
## TLDR Problem this solves: - SCIM group sync reported success while some members never landed on the team - Larger groups (10+, often 50+) ended up with users missing from teams - A member whose user row failed to create was silently dropped How it solves it: - Group membership adds and removes now propagate genuine failures to the IdP - A member whose user can neither be found nor created fails the request with 500 - Idempotent no-ops (already in team, already absent) are still swallowed - Repeated member ids in one request are created once instead of twice ## User Flow Before: an admin provisions a 50-member group from their identity provider and the IdP reports success, but the team is missing users 1. The admin assigns a 50-member group to the SCIM app and triggers provisioning 2. The IdP sends PUT https://litellm-domain/scim/v2/Groups/{group_id} with all 50 members and gets 200 back 3. The IdP marks every member as provisioned 4. The admin opens https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=teams and the team shows fewer than 50 members 5. The admin has to add the missing users to the team by hand After: the same sync either lands every member or surfaces an error the IdP retries 1. The admin assigns a 50-member group to the SCIM app and triggers provisioning 2. The IdP sends PUT https://litellm-domain/scim/v2/Groups/{group_id} with all 50 members 3. If every member lands, the IdP gets 200 and https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=teams shows all 50 members 4. If any member fails to enroll, the IdP gets a 5xx naming the failed user and retries that sync instead of recording a false success ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5105 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Captured against a live proxy on 127.0.0.1:4171 backed by its own Postgres. The proxy ran from a directory outside every checkout so it could not pick up a repo `.env`, with `PYTHONPATH` pointed at the branch worktree, so the two legs really do serve different code. No LLM provider is involved: SCIM provisioning is a management-plane path, so the whole capture is `/scim/v2/*` plus `/team/info` Every case pushes a 24-member group, comfortably past the size the ticket describes. In cases 2 and 3, 8 of those 24 already have a LiteLLM user row that the pushed member id does not resolve to. Four were onboarded by SSO, so their row is keyed by the identity provider's object id while the group lists them by email, and four arrived through `POST /scim/v2/Users` in lowercase while the group lists them with the casing the directory displays. LiteLLM itself emits group members by email on `GET /scim/v2/Groups/{id}`, so a directory that reads a group back and re-pushes it sends exactly these values The two legs use disjoint user and team ids (`...before...` / `...after...`) so neither leg can inherit rows the other created Shared setup, run identically inside each leg: ```bash API=http://127.0.0.1:4171 V=before # "after" on the second leg # 4 people already onboarded by SSO: their row is keyed by the IdP object id for i in 1 2 3 4; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}
" -X POST $API/user/new \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "{"user_id":"c9p37688-$V-oid-$i","user_email":"c9p37688.$V.sso$i@example.com","user_role":"internal_user"}" done # 4 people already provisioned through SCIM, userName in lowercase for i in 1 2 3 4; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}
" -X POST $API/scim/v2/Users \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/scim+json' \ -d "{"schemas":["urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:User"],"userName":"c9p37688.$V.case$i@example.com","active":true,"emails":[{"value":"c9p37688.$V.case$i@example.com","primary":true}]}" done ``` Both legs printed `200 200 200 200` then `201 201 201 201`, and `select count(*) from "LiteLLM_UserTable" where user_id like 'c9p37688-$V-%' or user_id like 'c9p37688.$V.%'` returned `8` Group pushes are built from a `for` loop over the member list: ```bash members() { local out=""; for v in "$@"; do out="$out{"value":"$v"},"; done; echo "[${out%,}]"; } PAYLOAD=$(printf '{"schemas":["urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:Group"],"id":"%s","displayName":"%s","members":%s}' "$TEAM" "$NAME" "$(members "${MEMBERS[@]}")") ``` Each leg re-printed the identity of the code it was actually serving, so every number below carries proof of which tree produced it: ``` Before After $ grep -c _ensure_group_member_user .../scim/scim_v2.py 0 2 $ grep -c 'raise_on_error=True' .../scim/scim_v2.py 1 3 $ shasum -a 256 .../scim/scim_v2.py 67f9d761 2b566279 $ python -c 'import litellm, os; print(bool(os.environ.get("OPENAI_API_KEY")))' False False $ curl -s $API/scim/v2/ServiceProviderConfig -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' 200 200 ``` ### Before (3a31331435) #### Case 1: a 24-member group where nobody exists yet 1. `curl -s -w '
HTTP %{http_code}' -X POST $API/scim/v2/Groups -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/scim+json' -d "$PAYLOAD"` ``` HTTP 201 {"id":"c9p37688-before-clean","displayName":"C9 Clean Team (before)","members_written":24} ``` 2. `curl -s $API/scim/v2/Groups/c9p37688-before-clean -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" | jq '{id, members_on_team: (.members|length)}'` ``` {"id":"c9p37688-before-clean","members_on_team":24} ``` 3. `curl -s "$API/team/info?team_id=c9p37688-before-clean" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" | jq '.team_info.members_with_roles | length'` ``` 24 ``` #### Case 2: a 24-member group where 8 members already have a user row under another id 1. `curl -s -w '
HTTP %{http_code}' -X POST $API/scim/v2/Groups -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/scim+json' -d "$PAYLOAD"` ``` HTTP 201 {"id":"c9p37688-before-mixed","displayName":"C9 Mixed Team (before)","members_written":16} ``` The push is reported as a success and the group comes back with 16 of the 24 members that were sent 2. `curl -s $API/scim/v2/Groups/c9p37688-before-mixed -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" | jq '{id, members_on_team: (.members|length)}'` ``` {"id":"c9p37688-before-mixed","members_on_team":16} ``` 3. `curl -s "$API/team/info?team_id=c9p37688-before-mixed" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" | jq -r '.team_info.members_with_roles[].user_id' | sort` ``` c9p37688.before.new01@example.com ... 16 lines, new01 through new16 ... c9p37688.before.new16@example.com ``` All 8 people who already existed are missing from the team, and nothing in the response says so 4. `grep -c "Failed to create user" proxy-before.log` ``` 8 ``` ``` ERROR: scim_v2.py:884 - Failed to create user c9p37688.before.sso1@example.com: {'error': 'User with email c9p37688.before.sso1@example.com already exists'} ERROR: scim_v2.py:884 - Failed to create user C9P37688.before.Case1@example.com: {'error': 'User with email c9p37688.before.case1@example.com already exists'} ... 8 lines total ... ``` The proxy knew about all 8 failures and still answered 201 #### Case 3: the same 24-member set pushed with PUT onto an existing group 1. Seed the group with one member: `POST $API/scim/v2/Groups` returns `HTTP 201` 2. `curl -s -w '
HTTP %{http_code}' -X PUT $API/scim/v2/Groups/c9p37688-before-put -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/scim+json' -d "$PAYLOAD"` ``` HTTP 200 ``` 3. `curl -s "$API/team/info?team_id=c9p37688-before-put" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" | jq '.team_info.members_with_roles | length'` ``` 16 ``` Same silent loss on the route an identity provider uses for every re-sync #### Case 4: the same 24 people, addressed by ids that already resolve 1. `curl -s -w '
HTTP %{http_code}' -X POST $API/scim/v2/Groups -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/scim+json' -d "$PAYLOAD"` ``` HTTP 201 {"id":"c9p37688-before-ctl","displayName":"C9 Control Team (before)","members_written":24} ``` 2. `curl -s "$API/team/info?team_id=c9p37688-before-ctl" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" | jq '.team_info.members_with_roles | length'` ``` 24 ``` The 8 people dropped in case 2 are real, enrollable users, so the loss there is a loss of people and not a rejected payload ### After (74a409bf2b) #### Case 1: a 24-member group where nobody exists yet 1. `curl -s -w '
HTTP %{http_code}' -X POST $API/scim/v2/Groups -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/scim+json' -d "$PAYLOAD"` ``` HTTP 201 {"id":"c9p37688-after-clean","displayName":"C9 Clean Team (after)","members_written":24} ``` 2. `curl -s $API/scim/v2/Groups/c9p37688-after-clean -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" | jq '{id, members_on_team: (.members|length)}'` ``` {"id":"c9p37688-after-clean","members_on_team":24} ``` 3. `curl -s "$API/team/info?team_id=c9p37688-after-clean" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" | jq '.team_info.members_with_roles | length'` ``` 24 ``` #### Case 2: a 24-member group where 8 members already have a user row under another id 1. `curl -s -w '
HTTP %{http_code}' -X POST $API/scim/v2/Groups -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/scim+json' -d "$PAYLOAD"` ``` HTTP 500 {"error":{"message":"{'error': "Failed to create user 'c9p37688.after.sso1@example.com' while provisioning group membership."}","type":"internal_server_error","param":"None","code":"500"}} ``` The failure now reaches the caller and names the member it could not provision, so the identity provider retries instead of recording 24 people as synced 2. `curl -s -w '
HTTP %{http_code}' $API/scim/v2/Groups/c9p37688-after-mixed -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN"` ``` HTTP 404 {"error":{"message":"{'error': 'Group not found with ID: c9p37688-after-mixed'}",...,"code":"404"}} ``` 3. `curl -s "$API/team/info?team_id=c9p37688-after-mixed" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" | jq '.team_info.members_with_roles | length'` ``` 0 ``` No half-populated team is left behind claiming to be the group #### Case 3: the same 24-member set pushed with PUT onto an existing group 1. Seed the group with one member: `POST $API/scim/v2/Groups` returns `HTTP 201` 2. `curl -s -w '
HTTP %{http_code}' -X PUT $API/scim/v2/Groups/c9p37688-after-put -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/scim+json' -d "$PAYLOAD"` ``` HTTP 500 {"error":{"message":"{'error': "Failed to create user 'c9p37688.after.sso1@example.com' while provisioning group membership."}",...,"code":"500"}} ``` 3. `curl -s "$API/team/info?team_id=c9p37688-after-put" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" | jq '.team_info.members_with_roles | length'` ``` 1 ``` The group keeps the member it already had rather than being rewritten to a roster that silently lost 8 people #### Case 4: the same 24 people, addressed by ids that already resolve 1. `curl -s -w '
HTTP %{http_code}' -X POST $API/scim/v2/Groups -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/scim+json' -d "$PAYLOAD"` ``` HTTP 201 {"id":"c9p37688-after-ctl","displayName":"C9 Control Team (after)","members_written":24} ``` 2. `curl -s "$API/team/info?team_id=c9p37688-after-ctl" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" | jq '.team_info.members_with_roles | length'` ``` 24 ``` A 24-member sync that can land still lands in full, so the strict path costs nothing when the ids resolve Both legs answered `/health/liveliness` with 200 immediately before and immediately after every case, so no result straddles a restarted proxy ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - A failing member now fails the whole group sync; IdPs retry these - test_update_group_metadata_serialization_issue now mocks membership writes, since its unmocked DB call was previously swallowed by the bug this PR removes Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/79e76557aa114b229b47fd35e18bf1f2 Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signals.title: fix(router): give auto prompt caching deployment affinity (LIT-5535)
signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Auto prompt caching got zero deployment affinity - Multi deployment groups paid cache writes every call - Affinity only worked for client sent `cache_control` How it solves it: - Router now reproduces the auto injected breakpoints - Affinity key matches the messages actually sent - Repeated cacheable prompts pin to one deployment ## User Flow Before: a developer calling a model group backed by two Bedrock deployments of the same Claude model with `enable_anthropic_prompt_caching: true` keeps paying the cache write premium as routing bounces between them 1. The proxy admin configures one `model_name` with two Bedrock deployments of the same Claude model, `litellm_settings.enable_anthropic_prompt_caching: true` and `router_settings.optional_pre_call_checks: ["prompt_caching"]` 2. The developer sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions eight times with the same ~4.1k token system prompt and no `cache_control` of their own 3. The `x-litellm-model-id` header alternates between the two deployments, and every call that lands on a deployment for the first time comes back with `cache_creation_input_tokens: 4106` and `cache_read_input_tokens: 0` 4. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs and see the 1.25x write premium charged once per deployment instead of once per prompt, so a group of N deployments costs N writes for the same prompt After: the same eight calls stay on one deployment, so only the first pays for the write and the rest read the warm cache 1. The proxy admin configures one `model_name` with two Bedrock deployments of the same Claude model, `litellm_settings.enable_anthropic_prompt_caching: true` and `router_settings.optional_pre_call_checks: ["prompt_caching"]` 2. The developer sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions eight times with the same ~4.1k token system prompt and no `cache_control` of their own 3. `x-litellm-model-id` is identical on all eight, the first response reports `cache_creation_input_tokens: 4106`, and calls two through eight report `cache_read_input_tokens: 4106` with `cache_creation_input_tokens: 0` 4. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs shows one write and seven reads, so caching delivers the 0.1x read discount it promises ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5535 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v` - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup, used identically by both legs 1. Two deployments of Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Bedrock, one on the US cross region inference profile and one on the global profile, in the same account and region. `/tmp/lit5535/config.yaml`: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: claude-sonnet-4-5 litellm_params: model: bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 aws_region_name: us-east-1 model_info: id: bedrock-us-inference-profile - model_name: claude-sonnet-4-5 litellm_params: model: bedrock/global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 aws_region_name: us-east-1 model_info: id: bedrock-global-inference-profile litellm_settings: enable_anthropic_prompt_caching: true router_settings: optional_pre_call_checks: ["prompt_caching"] general_settings: master_key: sk-lit5535 ``` 2. Bedrock keeps a separate prompt cache per inference profile, so the two deployments genuinely cannot serve each other's warm prefix. Without this the whole A/B would be vacuous, so it is checked first, straight against Bedrock with no LiteLLM in the path: ```bash python3 -c ' import json prefix = "Distinct preflight two: silver herons wade the shallow estuary while the tide retreats. " * 220 print(json.dumps({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": prefix}, {"cachePoint": {"type": "default"}}, {"text": "Reply with the single word OK."}]}], "inferenceConfig": {"maxTokens": 16}})) ' > /tmp/converse.json for round in 1 2; do for mid in us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0; do echo "round=$round $mid -> $(aws bedrock-runtime converse --region us-east-1 --model-id $mid --cli-input-json file:///tmp/converse.json | jq -c .usage)" done done ``` ``` round=1 us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 -> {"inputTokens":9,"outputTokens":1,"totalTokens":4415,"cacheReadInputTokens":0,"cacheWriteInputTokens":4405,"cacheDetails":[{"ttl":"5m","inputTokens":4405}]} round=1 global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 -> {"inputTokens":9,"outputTokens":1,"totalTokens":4415,"cacheReadInputTokens":0,"cacheWriteInputTokens":4405,"cacheDetails":[{"ttl":"5m","inputTokens":4405}]} round=2 us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 -> {"inputTokens":9,"outputTokens":1,"totalTokens":4415,"cacheReadInputTokens":4405,"cacheWriteInputTokens":0} round=2 global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 -> {"inputTokens":9,"outputTokens":1,"totalTokens":4415,"cacheReadInputTokens":4405,"cacheWriteInputTokens":0} ``` The global profile paid a full write in round 1 even though the US profile had just written the identical prefix, and each profile then read only its own copy in round 2 3. The payload, a ~4.1k token system prompt with no client `cache_control` anywhere, so every breakpoint in the request is one LiteLLM injected. `$NONCE` differs per leg so each leg starts against a cold Bedrock cache: ```bash python3 -c ' import json, sys prefix = f"Runbook {sys.argv[1]}. " + ("The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the riverbank at dawn. " * 240) print(json.dumps({"model": "claude-sonnet-4-5", "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": prefix}, {"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the single word OK."}], "max_tokens": 16})) ' "$NONCE" > /tmp/lit5535.json ``` 4. The eight call loop, printing the deployment that served each call next to its cache accounting: ```bash for i in $(seq 1 8); do body=$(curl -sS -D /tmp/h -X POST http://localhost:4499/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5535' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @/tmp/lit5535.json) printf 'call %s deployment=%-34s %s\n' "$i" \ "$(grep -i '^x-litellm-model-id:' /tmp/h | tr -d '\r' | awk '{print $2}')" \ "$(printf '%s' "$body" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; u=json.load(sys.stdin)["usage"]; print("cache_creation_input_tokens=%-5s cache_read_input_tokens=%-5s prompt_tokens=%s" % (u.get("cache_creation_input_tokens"), u.get("cache_read_input_tokens"), u.get("prompt_tokens")))')" done ``` Both legs run from a directory outside any LiteLLM checkout with `PYTHONPATH` pointed at the tree under test, so the proxy really imports the commit named in the heading. The two trees were diffed before the run and differ in exactly the four files this PR touches ### Before (cb4eb82249) 1. Start the proxy on the parent commit: ```bash PYTHONPATH=/tmp/lit5535/before python -m litellm.proxy.proxy_cli --config /tmp/lit5535/config.yaml --port 4499 --num_workers 1 ``` 2. Confirm the tree really lacks the fix: ```bash grep -c messages_with_default_injections /tmp/lit5535/before/litellm/router_utils/pre_call_checks/prompt_caching_deployment_check.py ``` ``` 0 ``` 3. Run the eight call loop: ``` call 1 deployment=bedrock-us-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=4106 cache_read_input_tokens=0 prompt_tokens=4109 call 2 deployment=bedrock-us-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 3 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=4106 cache_read_input_tokens=0 prompt_tokens=4109 call 4 deployment=bedrock-us-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 5 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 6 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 7 deployment=bedrock-us-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 8 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 ``` Eight identical requests spread across both deployments, and the prompt was written to the cache twice, on call 1 and again on call 3, because the second deployment had never seen it. The affinity check never fired: routing keyed off the unmarked messages while the success event keyed off the marked ones, so the two keys never matched ### After (469a688de9) 1. Start the proxy on this PR's tip, same config, same port: ```bash PYTHONPATH=/tmp/lit5535/after python -m litellm.proxy.proxy_cli --config /tmp/lit5535/config.yaml --port 4499 --num_workers 1 ``` 2. Confirm the tree carries the fix: ```bash grep -c messages_with_default_injections /tmp/lit5535/after/litellm/router_utils/pre_call_checks/prompt_caching_deployment_check.py ``` ``` 1 ``` 3. Run the same eight call loop against a fresh nonce: ``` call 1 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=4106 cache_read_input_tokens=0 prompt_tokens=4109 call 2 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 3 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 4 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 5 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 6 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 7 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 8 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 ``` All eight land on one deployment, the prompt is written once, and `cache_read_input_tokens` is non-zero from call 2 onward. Which deployment wins is still whatever the strategy picks first, the fix only makes the rest follow it ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Only the default Anthropic and Bedrock breakpoints are reproduced - Custom `cache_control_injection_points` still route as before - Before leg warms both caches, so later calls do read ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/d9190d9ed8a04fbfb6fa4c4165f8dbff Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signals.title: fix(jwt): retry JWKS fetches, serve stale keys, and return 503 when the IdP is unreachable
signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - JWKS fetch had no retry, so one IdP blip failed auth - Expired cache dropped still-valid keys with no fallback - Every in-flight request refetched JWKS after TTL lapse - `httpx.ConnectTimeout` surfaced as a 401 with empty detail - A read timeout blamed the database for a JWKS outage - A non-200 JWKS body was cached as if it were keys How it solves it: - Retry transport failures 3 times with a short backoff - Serve the last-known-good JWKS for a bounded, logged window - Enforce that bound on read, so lowering it binds at once - Coalesce concurrent refreshes, and back off per outage window - Raise 503 `auth_provider_unavailable` when the IdP is unreachable - Reject non-200 JWKS responses instead of caching them ## User Flow Before: a developer whose app authenticates with an Okta-issued JWT gets bursts of 401s whenever the connection to the IdP's JWKS endpoint times out 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `Authorization: Bearer <their JWT>` and get 200 back 2. The gateway's cached copy of the IdP signing keys expires 10 minutes later, and the next fetch of the IdP's key endpoint times out 3. The same still-valid JWT now fails, and how it fails depends on how the endpoint is unreachable. A connect timeout comes back as HTTP 401 `{"error":{"message":"Authentication Error, ","type":"auth_error","code":"401"}}`, with no detail at all. A read timeout comes back as HTTP 503 `{"error":{"message":"Service Unavailable, the authentication database is temporarily unreachable. Please retry shortly.","type":"no_db_connection","code":"503"}}`, blaming a database that is perfectly healthy 4. Their client reads the 401 as "bad credentials", so it logs the user out and does not retry, even though the token and the IdP keys never changed. Whoever is on call reads the 503 and goes looking at the database After: the same request rides out the IdP blip, and a genuine outage reads as a retryable server-side failure 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `Authorization: Bearer <their JWT>` and get 200 back 2. The cached copy expires 10 minutes later, and the next fetch of the IdP's key endpoint times out 3. The gateway retries the fetch, then falls back to the signing keys it last saw, so the same request still returns 200 4. If the IdP is unreachable on a true cold start, the response is HTTP 503 `{"error":{"message":"Service Unavailable, the identity provider's JWKS endpoint is temporarily unreachable, ...","type":"auth_provider_unavailable","code":"503"}}`, which their client retries instead of treating as invalid credentials 5. Once the IdP answers again, the very next refresh wins, so a key the admin removed from the JWKS stops authenticating anyone immediately. If the IdP stays down past `public_key_stale_ttl` (1h by default, `0` to fail closed), the old key stops authenticating anyone too and requests get the same 503 ## A JWKS outage failed two different ways, and the ticket only saw one How the failure surfaced depended on how the endpoint was unreachable, and the two shapes took different paths through the code. `httpx.ConnectTimeout` is absent from `DB_CONNECTION_ERROR_TYPES` on the base branch, which carries `ConnectError`, `ReadError` and `ReadTimeout`. A connect timeout therefore falls past the database handler into the generic auth handler and comes back as `401 auth_error` with an empty detail, which is the symptom the ticket reported. A read timeout matches that tuple, takes the database path, and comes back as `503 no_db_connection`, "the authentication database is temporarily unreachable" The second one is the more expensive failure to be on call for. A 401 at least points at authentication. A database error points at a subsystem where there is nothing to find, while the thing actually down is the identity provider's key endpoint. Both are captured live below, and both are replaced by `auth_provider_unavailable`, which names the identity provider and is a 503 the client retries. Adding `httpx.ConnectTimeout` to `DB_CONNECTION_ERROR_TYPES` is what closes the fall-through for every other caller of that tuple ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5524 ## Review notes The stale fallback deliberately trades a bounded window of "the IdP removed this key and we cannot yet tell" for not failing every authenticated request during an outage. Four things bound it: The window is entered only on `httpx.TransportError`, so any HTTP-level answer from the IdP, a 200 with a narrowed key set as much as a 4xx, goes through the normal refresh path and replaces both the active and the stale copy. Revoking a key against a healthy IdP is honoured on the next refresh, not an hour later That transport-error-only scope is the whole basis for calling this fallback safe, and until now nothing enforced it. Mutation testing caught that: widening the `except JWKSUnreachableError` in `_refresh_or_record_outage` to `except Exception` passed the entire suite. Under that one-word change a malformed response, or any bug in parsing, would quietly serve stale keys instead of failing, and the reasoning above would still read as settled while nothing held it up. `test_unparseable_jwks_response_does_not_fall_back_to_the_stale_copy` and `test_jwks_error_response_is_not_cached_over_the_last_known_good_keys` now pin it, so a future refactor that widens that clause fails CI The window's length is `public_key_stale_ttl`, a new config field defaulting to 3600s, and it is measured past the active entry rather than derived from `public_key_ttl`. That is what keeps a long configured `public_key_ttl` from collapsing the fallback to nothing, and what keeps the extra trust at exactly one configured window no matter how the active TTL is tuned. Deployments that cannot accept any unrefreshed key set it to `0` and get a 503 the moment the active entry expires Every stale serve logs a warning naming the `kid` it authenticated, the JWKS url, how long ago that copy was last refreshed, and how long until it stops being trusted, so the exposure is visible while it is happening rather than after the fact That bound is checked on every read against the current setting, rather than being baked into the cache entry when it is written. An operator who lowers `public_key_stale_ttl`, or sets it to `0`, is usually doing it mid-incident, and a Redis-backed cache survives the restart they perform to make it take effect, so a copy written under the old longer setting would otherwise stay servable until it aged out on its own. The one control reached for under pressure has to bind immediately. An earlier revision of this PR got that wrong in an instructive way: it computed the correct remaining lifetime and used it only for the log line, so the warning told the operator a bound that nothing enforced. An observable reporting a limit nobody applies is worse than having no observable, because it reassures. The cache entry's own TTL is now a memory-management concern and the read-time check is the security boundary Token `exp` and every other claim check still apply, so the window caps how long a key stays trusted, not how long a token does Separately, a sustained outage records the failure for 30s per key url. Without that, every request during an outage paid three connect timeouts serialised behind the refresh lock, and the queue grew faster than it drained, so the fallback was inert exactly under the load that motivated it. The cost is that recovery can lag the IdP coming back by up to 30s ## A hole this PR closes that it would otherwise have widened `_fetch_jwks_keys` never checked `status_code`, so whatever the IdP returned was parsed and cached as the key set. A 5xx with a JSON error body became the cached JWKS for a full `public_key_ttl`, and once this PR started writing a longer-lived stale copy, that same error body would have been promoted to trusted signing material for `public_key_ttl + public_key_stale_ttl`, outliving the incident that produced it. A transient IdP error turning into long-lived trusted key material is strictly worse than the outage the ticket describes. Non-200 now raises before anything is cached, and `test_jwks_error_response_is_not_cached_over_the_last_known_good_keys` asserts that both the active and the stale copy still hold the last good keys afterwards ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Run against a live proxy on :4321 with a stub JWKS endpoint on :8899 standing in for the IdP, so the outage is something I control rather than something I wait for. The stub reads a `mode` file per request: `ok` serves the signing key, `hang` accepts the connection and never answers (read timeout), `revoked` serves a JWKS the key has been removed from. Case 5 points `JWT_PUBLIC_KEY_URL` at a blackholed `10.255.255.1` for a connect timeout. Cases 1 to 4 share one proxy lifetime, because the stale window is measured from case 1's refresh Config (`general_settings.litellm_jwtauth`), TTLs shortened so the whole window fits the run: ```yaml admin_jwt_scope: litellm_proxy_admin admin_allowed_routes: [openai_routes, info_routes] public_key_ttl: 20 public_key_stale_ttl: 60 ``` Case 4 is the one that answers the security question Greptile raised. It returns the same 401 on both legs, and that identical result is the finding: a stale copy of the removed key was in the cache and went unconsulted, so the fallback did not widen trust while the identity provider was reachable The same request throughout, a real Anthropic call with a JWT signed by the stub's key: ```bash curl -s -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4321/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat token.jwt)" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"anthropic-sonnet-5","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Reply with the single word: authenticated"}],"max_tokens":16}' ``` ### Before (4af59d7c6e) #### Case 1: healthy IdP 1. `echo ok > mode`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 200`, `{"choices":[{"message":{"content":"authenticated",...}}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":18,"completion_tokens":6,...}}` #### Case 2: IdP stops answering and the cached keys lapse 1. `echo hang > mode; sleep 25`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 503`, `{"error":{"message":"Service Unavailable, the authentication database is temporarily unreachable. Please retry shortly.","type":"no_db_connection","code":"503"}}` 3. The JWKS endpoint is what is unreachable, not the database, so this points the on-call at the wrong subsystem #### Case 3: the outage outlives the stale window 1. `sleep 50`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 503`, same `no_db_connection` body as case 2 #### Case 4: IdP reachable again, signing key removed from its JWKS 1. `echo revoked > mode; sleep 35`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 401`, `{"error":{"message":"Authentication Error, No matching public key found. keys=['http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys'], kid=demo-signing-key","type":"auth_error","code":"401"}}` #### Case 5: cold start against an unreachable IdP (connect timeout) 1. Restart the proxy with `JWT_PUBLIC_KEY_URL=http://10.255.255.1:8899/keys`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 401`, `{"error":{"message":"Authentication Error, ","type":"auth_error","param":"None","code":"401"}}` 3. This is the reported bug verbatim: a 401 with no detail at all, which a client reads as bad credentials and does not retry ### After (74e8eb17fc) #### Case 1: healthy IdP 1. `echo ok > mode`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 200`, `{"choices":[{"message":{"content":"authenticated",...}}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":18,"completion_tokens":6,...}}` #### Case 2: IdP stops answering and the cached keys lapse 1. `echo hang > mode; sleep 25`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 200`, the same real completion. The request rides out the outage on the last-known-good key 3. The proxy log says which key that was and how long it has left: ``` JWT Auth: ReadTimeout fetching http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys (attempt 1/3), retrying: JWT Auth: ReadTimeout fetching http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys (attempt 2/3), retrying: JWT Auth: identity provider unreachable, authenticating kid=demo-signing-key against a stale JWKS copy of litellm_jwt_auth_keys_http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys (last refreshed 42s ago, stops being trusted in 38s). Refresh failed: ReadTimeout fetching http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys after 3 attempts ``` 4. `42s + 38s` is the configured `public_key_ttl 20` + `public_key_stale_ttl 60`, so the bound in the log is the bound in the config #### Case 3: the outage outlives the stale window 1. `sleep 50`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 503`, `{"error":{"message":"Service Unavailable, the identity provider's JWKS endpoint is temporarily unreachable, so the JWT signature could not be verified. Please retry shortly. Error: ReadTimeout fetching http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys after 3 attempts","type":"auth_provider_unavailable","code":"503"}}` 3. The stale copy is gone at the configured bound, so the key stops being trusted. The failure names the identity provider rather than the database, and it is a 503 the client retries rather than a 401 it logs the user out on #### Case 4: IdP reachable again, signing key removed from its JWKS 1. `echo revoked > mode; sleep 35`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 401`, `{"error":{"message":"Authentication Error, No matching public key found. keys=['http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys'], kid=demo-signing-key","type":"auth_error","code":"401"}}` 3. Unchanged from before, which is the point. A stale copy of that key was on hand and was not consulted, because the identity provider answered. Revocation against a healthy IdP is immediate, not delayed by `public_key_stale_ttl` #### Case 5: cold start against an unreachable IdP (connect timeout) 1. Restart the proxy with `JWT_PUBLIC_KEY_URL=http://10.255.255.1:8899/keys`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 503`, `{"error":{"message":"Service Unavailable, the identity provider's JWKS endpoint is temporarily unreachable, so the JWT signature could not be verified. Please retry shortly. Error: ConnectTimeout fetching http://10.255.255.1:8899/keys after 3 attempts","type":"auth_provider_unavailable","param":"None","code":"503"}}` One boundary of this matrix, stated rather than left to be assumed: every case runs at a fixed `public_key_stale_ttl`, so none of them exercises lowering or raising the setting while a copy written under the previous value is still cached. That path is covered by unit tests instead, `test_lowering_public_key_stale_ttl_stops_serving_a_copy_cached_under_the_old_setting`, `test_zero_public_key_stale_ttl_fails_closed_even_for_a_freshly_written_copy` and `test_increasing_public_key_stale_ttl_only_extends_within_the_new_bound` The capture also runs a single-process proxy, so the Redis-backed shared-cache path is likewise unit-tested rather than captured, including `test_stale_copy_written_at_survives_a_whole_number_epoch` for the epoch a JSON round-trip hands back as an int Each leg was checked for cross-contamination rather than assumed: the before leg's proxy log has zero retry warnings, zero stale-serve warnings and zero `auth_provider_unavailable`, against two `no_db_connection` and the bare 401, and the after leg has three retries, one stale serve and two `auth_provider_unavailable`. Both served exactly five requests for five cases on one proxy lifetime ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Stale keys served up to `public_key_stale_ttl` (1h) past the TTL - Requests can keep 503ing up to 30s after the IdP recovers - Stale fallback covers transport failures, not IdP error responses - Refresh locks live per process; the caches are shared ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/bb79bcd7663d484e93a08ed3f725a0c8 Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signals.title: fix(db): apply the configured connection params to the read replica URL
signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Read replica ignored the configured DB pool cap - Reader pool fell back to Prisma's CPU-based default - Only writer and direct URLs got connection params How it solves it: - Reader URL now inherits the writer's pool params - One allowlist keeps schema-affecting params on the writer - Params pinned on the replica URL still win ## User Flow Before: an operator caps DB connections to protect their database, but the read replica opens as many connections as it likes 1. They set `general_settings.database_connection_pool_limit: 3` and `database_connection_pool_timeout: 20`, point `DATABASE_URL_READ_REPLICA` at their reader, and start the proxy 2. They send a few hundred concurrent `GET http://localhost:4592/key/list` with the master key, all returning 200 3. They count live connections on the database and see the reader holding 11 of them, Prisma's `num_physical_cpus * 2 + 1` default, far more than the 3 they configured 4. The database hits its own connection ceiling under load even though the cap they configured says it should not After: the same cap applies to the reader, so the total stays where the operator put it 1. They set the same two settings, point `DATABASE_URL_READ_REPLICA` at their reader, and start the proxy 2. They send the same concurrent `GET http://localhost:4592/key/list`, all returning 200 3. They count live connections and see the reader holding exactly 3, matching the configured cap 4. If they had pinned `?connection_limit=50` on the replica URL themselves, that value is still what gets used 5. A `search_path` they set on the writer, whether on `DATABASE_URL` or through `database_extra_connection_params`, still does not reach the reader, so replica queries keep resolving against the reader's own schema ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5692 ## Review notes Inheritance is an allowlist of pool and timeout params (`connection_limit`, `pool_timeout`, `connect_timeout`, `socket_timeout`, `pgbouncer`), deliberately not a denylist. A denylist over Postgres' open-ended parameter space cannot be completed, and the one you forget is the one that hurts: `options` carries `search_path`, so copying it wholesale would silently repoint every replica query at the writer's schema. An allowlist fails closed, and a parameter nobody has vetted for the reader stays on the writer by default. There is a test pinning exactly that, so flipping this back to a denylist breaks the build rather than quietly widening what the reader inherits. Both startup paths share the one allowlist. That matters for the CLI in particular, because `database_extra_connection_params` is an untyped passthrough whose keys override everything else, so without the filter an operator could route a writer `search_path` to the reader through config rather than through the URL. The CLI does still set `options` on the reader, but it builds that value from the reader's own `options` plus the configured statement and lock timeouts, never from the writer's. History note: this branch carries a staging merge, `0bf8fe09ba`, that was authored by someone other than the PR author, resolving conflicts against the Azure Entra ID token-auth work. The resolution was reviewed independently before being adopted: the `db_url_settings.py` import block is the union of both sides rather than a pick, which matters because taking either side alone yields a module that imports cleanly and fails at runtime, and the reader-parameter allowlist, its two helpers, the CLI call site, and all four regression tests are present and unchanged. ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** (5/5 at d3f801f790) before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup: a real local Postgres, a replica URL pointing at the same database, and `pg_stat_activity.application_name` used purely to tell the two pools apart. The configured cap is 3 throughout. A namespaced port is deliberate: `--port 4000` silently rebinds to a random port when it is busy, so on a shared machine the health check can be answered by an unrelated proxy ```bash docker run -d --name lit5692-pg -p 6592:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=litpw -e POSTGRES_DB=litellm postgres:16 docker exec lit5692-pg psql -U postgres -d litellm -q -c "create schema if not exists writer_schema;" cat > /tmp/lit5692.yaml <<'EOF' model_list: [] general_settings: master_key: sk-1234 database_connection_pool_limit: 3 database_connection_pool_timeout: 20 EOF export LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=sk-1234 DISABLE_SCHEMA_UPDATE=true python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config /tmp/lit5692.yaml --port 4592 & count_conns() { seq 3000 | xargs -P 100 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" http://localhost:4592/key/list & for _ in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do sleep 4 docker exec lit5692-pg psql -U postgres -d litellm -At -F' | ' \ -c "select coalesce(nullif(application_name,''),'(unset)'), count(*) from pg_stat_activity where datname='litellm' group by 1 order by 1;" | tr '\n' ' ' echo done } ``` Case 1 pins the reader's own marker, so the reader pool is directly countable ```bash export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://postgres:litpw@localhost:6592/litellm" export DATABASE_URL_READ_REPLICA="postgresql://postgres:litpw@localhost:6592/litellm?options=-c%20application_name%3Dlitellm_reader" ``` Case 2 pins a `search_path` and a marker on the **writer URL** and nothing on the reader, so writer `options` reaching the reader would relabel the reader's connections too ```bash export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://postgres:litpw@localhost:6592/litellm?options=-c%20search_path%3Dwriter_schema%20-c%20application_name%3Dlitellm_writer" export DATABASE_URL_READ_REPLICA="postgresql://postgres:litpw@localhost:6592/litellm" ``` Case 3 does the same through **config** instead of the URL, which is the passthrough that overrides everything else ```bash export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://postgres:litpw@localhost:6592/litellm" export DATABASE_URL_READ_REPLICA="postgresql://postgres:litpw@localhost:6592/litellm" # add to general_settings in /tmp/lit5692.yaml: # database_extra_connection_params: # options: "-c search_path=writer_schema -c application_name=litellm_writer" ``` ### Before (a9744645ee) #### Case 1: reader pool size against a configured cap of 3 1. Start the proxy with the Case 1 URLs, confirm `curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://localhost:4592/health/liveliness` returns 200 2. Run `count_conns` 3. The reader holds 11 connections, Prisma's own default, ignoring the configured cap of 3 ```text litellm_reader | 11 psql | 1 (unset) | 1 litellm_reader | 11 psql | 1 (unset) | 1 litellm_reader | 11 psql | 1 (unset) | 1 litellm_reader | 11 psql | 1 (unset) | 1 litellm_reader | 11 psql | 1 (unset) | 1 litellm_reader | 11 psql | 1 (unset) | 1 ``` #### Case 2: writer URL search_path must not follow the reader 1. Start the proxy with the Case 2 URLs, confirm liveliness returns 200 2. Run `count_conns` 3. The reader connections stay `(unset)`, so the writer's `options` never reached them, but they climb to 9 rather than the configured 3 ```text litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 5 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 5 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 5 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 6 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 9 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 9 ``` #### Case 3: configured extra connection params must not carry a search_path to the reader 1. Start the proxy with the Case 3 config, confirm liveliness returns 200 2. Run `count_conns` 3. The writer picks up the marker, the reader stays `(unset)`, and the reader holds 13 connections rather than the configured 3 ```text litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 13 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 13 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 13 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 13 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 13 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 13 ``` ### After (0bf8fe09ba) #### Case 1: reader pool size against a configured cap of 3 1. Start the proxy with the Case 1 URLs, confirm liveliness returns 200 2. Run `count_conns` 3. The reader holds exactly 3 connections, the configured cap, and keeps its own `litellm_reader` marker, so the reader's own `options` survived the params being appended ```text litellm_reader | 3 psql | 1 (unset) | 1 litellm_reader | 3 psql | 1 (unset) | 1 litellm_reader | 3 psql | 1 (unset) | 1 litellm_reader | 3 psql | 1 (unset) | 1 litellm_reader | 3 psql | 1 (unset) | 1 litellm_reader | 3 psql | 1 (unset) | 1 ``` #### Case 2: writer URL search_path must not follow the reader 1. Start the proxy with the Case 2 URLs, confirm liveliness returns 200 2. Run `count_conns` 3. The reader now holds exactly 3 connections and its connections are still `(unset)`, so it picked up the cap without picking up the writer's `search_path` ```text litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 3 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 3 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 3 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 3 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 3 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 3 ``` #### Case 3: configured extra connection params must not carry a search_path to the reader 1. Start the proxy with the Case 3 config, confirm liveliness returns 200 2. Run `count_conns` 3. The writer still picks up the marker, proving the setting is live, while the reader is capped at 3 and stays `(unset)` ```text litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 3 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 3 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 3 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 3 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 3 litellm_writer | 1 psql | 1 (unset) | 3 ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Inheritance is an allowlist; unknown params stay on the writer - `schema` and postgres `options` are never inherited - Replica URLs with nothing to add are left byte for byte unchanged ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/2d1f0c3cd9234051a365e54ab1d647d0 Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signals.title: fix(proxy): fail the standalone prisma migration entrypoint on migration errors
signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Failed migration Job still exits 0 - GitOps then deploys against a stale schema - Failed `prisma generate` also exits 0 How it solves it: - Migration entrypoint enforces the check by default - `prisma generate` failure returns its exit code - `ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=false` restores the old leniency - In-proxy startup default stays lenient ## User Flow Before: a platform engineer upgrading the gateway with ArgoCD sees the sync go green even though the database was never migrated, then the app serves errors against an out-of-date schema 1. They bump the gateway chart version and let ArgoCD sync in an air-gapped cluster 2. The pre-upgrade migration Job logs a database error and finishes as Succeeded, exit code 0 3. ArgoCD marks the whole app Healthy and rolls out the new gateway pods 4. They hit the new release, for example POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions, and get 500s from endpoints whose columns do not exist yet 5. Only after they explicitly set `ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=true` and re-sync does the Job fail and stop the rollout After: the same sync stops at the migration Job, so nothing gets deployed against a stale schema 1. They bump the gateway chart version and let ArgoCD sync in an air-gapped cluster 2. The pre-upgrade migration Job logs the database error and finishes as Failed, exit code 1 3. ArgoCD reports the sync as Degraded and does not roll out the new gateway pods, so the old release keeps serving traffic on the schema it matches 4. They fix the database access, re-sync, and the Job succeeds before the new pods start 5. Anyone who wants the previous behavior can set `ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=false` on the Job and get exit 0 on a failed migration again ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5385 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup: point the migration entrypoint at an unreachable Postgres so `prisma migrate deploy` fails, and print the exit code the Job would report ```bash export DATABASE_URL='postgresql://litellm:wrongpw@127.0.0.1:5599/nope' export DISABLE_SCHEMA_UPDATE=false export LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=sk-1234 ``` ### Before (3a31331435480950d7f1a475e17863646700a083) #### Failed migration, default settings 1. Run the migration entrypoint the Helm Job runs ```bash uv run --no-sync python litellm/proxy/prisma_migration.py; echo "exit code: $?" ``` 2. Observed output, the migration fails yet the Job reports success ```text Datasource "client": PostgreSQL database "nope", schema "public" at "127.0.0.1:5599" 2026-08-20 20:12:17,703 - litellm_proxy_extras - INFO - Running prisma migrate deploy 2026-08-20 20:12:24,049 - litellm_proxy_extras - INFO - prisma db error: Error: P1001: Can't reach database server at `127.0.0.1`:`5599` Please make sure your database server is running at `127.0.0.1`:`5599`. LiteLLM Proxy: Using default (v1) migration resolver. LiteLLM Proxy: Database migration failed but continuing startup. Set --enforce_prisma_migration_check or ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=true to exit on failure. LiteLLM: Setup complete. Skipping server startup as requested. exit code: 0 ``` #### Failed migration, ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=false 1. Not applicable before this change: leniency was the only behavior, shown by the case above ### After (da75cd5fb0b595860681008ef550a335be3e8fb8) #### Failed migration, default settings 1. Run the same command ```bash uv run --no-sync python litellm/proxy/prisma_migration.py; echo "exit code: $?" ``` 2. Observed output, the Job now fails so the deploy is blocked ```text Datasource "client": PostgreSQL database "nope", schema "public" at "127.0.0.1:5599" 2026-08-20 20:12:25,510 - litellm_proxy_extras - INFO - Running prisma migrate deploy 2026-08-20 20:12:31,696 - litellm_proxy_extras - INFO - prisma db error: Error: P1001: Can't reach database server at `127.0.0.1`:`5599` Please make sure your database server is running at `127.0.0.1`:`5599`. LiteLLM Proxy: Using default (v1) migration resolver. LiteLLM Proxy: Database setup failed after multiple retries. The proxy cannot start safely. Please check your database connection and migration status. exit code: 1 ``` #### Failed migration, ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=false 1. Opt back into the old behavior ```bash ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=false uv run --no-sync python litellm/proxy/prisma_migration.py; echo "exit code: $?" ``` 2. Observed output, unchanged leniency ```text Datasource "client": PostgreSQL database "nope", schema "public" at "127.0.0.1:5599" 2026-08-20 20:13:29,818 - litellm_proxy_extras - INFO - Running prisma migrate deploy 2026-08-20 20:13:36,293 - litellm_proxy_extras - INFO - prisma db error: Error: P1001: Can't reach database server at `127.0.0.1`:`5599` Please make sure your database server is running at `127.0.0.1`:`5599`. LiteLLM Proxy: Using default (v1) migration resolver. LiteLLM Proxy: Database migration failed but continuing startup. Set --enforce_prisma_migration_check or ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=true to exit on failure. LiteLLM: Setup complete. Skipping server startup as requested. exit code: 0 ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Behavior change: failing migration Jobs now fail loudly - `docker/entrypoint.sh` images also stop on migration failure - Opt out with `ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=false` - Docs check stays red until BerriAI/litellm-docs#972 merges, which documents the variable the gate flagged ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/d6ef92e6d1ea4b39ae7aabb14b4dc2a2 Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signals.title: feat(ui): add per-key Savings tab to key detail page
signals.text: ## What Adds a "Savings" tab to the key detail view, showing the same four savings drivers (compression, prompt caching, auto-router, cache hit rate) and time-series chart as the proxy-wide Cost Optimization view, but filtered to one API key. For org admins, the tab shows the key's full savings across all requests. Non-admins see only their own requests on that key, with a scope note explaining the limitation. ## Root cause `userDailyActivityCall` and `userDailyActivityAggregatedCall` never forwarded an `api_key` query parameter to the backend, even though both handlers already accept and filter by it. ## Implementation **Unbundled scoping:** Extracted `useScopedDailyActivityRange(accessToken, scope: {userId, apiKey?})` so role resolution lives only in the org-wide entry point (`useDailyActivityRange`), not in a per-key caller. Reuse-by-parameter pattern scales to N callers without duplication. **Shared helpers:** Extracted `compressionOf`, `cachingOf`, `autorouterOf`, `savedTokensOf`, `cacheHitRatio` into utils so both UsageTab and KeySavingsTab use identical formulas and cannot diverge. **Shared component:** Extracted `SummaryCard` to avoid CSS/layout divergence. Both tabs render the same four-tile presenter. ## Files - `components/networking.tsx` — Add optional `apiKey` param to both daily-activity call wrappers - `costOptimizationUtils.ts` — Extract shared metrics helpers - `useDailyActivityRange.ts` — Refactor: `useScopedDailyActivityRange` + wrapper. Update test expectations for 6-arg tuple. - `UsageTab.tsx` — Import extracted helpers and `SummaryCard` component - `key_info_view.tsx` — Add "Savings" tab trigger + wiring; lazy-mounted (no keepMounted) - **NEW:** `components/shared/SummaryCard.tsx` — Shared four-tile presenter - **NEW:** `components/templates/KeySavingsTab.tsx` — Per-key view with admin/non-admin scoping - **NEW:** `components/templates/KeySavingsTab.test.tsx` — 7 tests ## Tests - 6121 component tests pass (1 pre-existing failure unrelated to this change) - Build succeeds with no new type errors - KeySavingsTab tests cover mount, loading, empty state, scoping, scope-note visibility ## Prior art / collision notes - PR #37570 (budgets tab) lands in same TabsList hunks as "Savings" tab, but different names → trivial conflict if both merge - PR #37659 (my own) adds fields to DailyActivityRange on different branch → no conflict with this PR's stable interface <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Touches spend-data scoping (who can see proxy-wide vs own-user activity) and forwards `api_key` on daily-activity fetches. Wrong role mapping would under- or over-show savings, though backend still enforces admin view. > > **Overview** > Adds a **Savings** tab on the key detail page with the same compression, prompt-caching, auto-router, and cache-hit figures as Cost Optimization, filtered to one key. > > Daily-activity clients now pass an optional `api_key`. Fetching is split into `useScopedDailyActivityRange` so callers choose `{userId, apiKey}` without the hook re-scoping. Proxy admins query the whole key (`userId: null`); everyone else, including **org admins**, is scoped to their own user id, with a note that shared-key spend from others is omitted. The tab is not `keepMounted`, so the rollup only loads when opened. > > Shared `SummaryCard`, savings metric helpers, and `cacheHitRatio` keep the two surfaces on the same formulas. `spendScopeUserId` / `hasProxyWideSpendView` replace `all_admin_roles` for this endpoint so org admin is not treated as proxy-wide. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 3b592c0ad28453119b6c8806d15be9626cd6e20e. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
