signal.title: feat(sso): source generic OIDC user claims from ID/access token when UserInfo is incomplete
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - ADFS UserInfo returns only `sub`, so SSO profiles are empty - No username, email or display name for those users - Team claims carried only in the tokens were unreachable How it solves it: - New opt-in `GENERIC_INCLUDE_TOKEN_CLAIMS` merges token claims into UserInfo - Precedence: UserInfo, then id_token, then access token - All `GENERIC_USER_*_ATTRIBUTE` mappings apply to token claims - Works in both the PKCE and non-PKCE login flows ## User Flow Before: an admin whose IdP only returns `sub` from UserInfo signs in successfully but lands in the Admin UI as a nameless, team-less account 1. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/ and click through the SSO login at their IdP 2. Login succeeds and they are redirected back to https://litellm-domain/ui/ 3. The user badge shows no email and no display name 4. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=users lists the account with an empty user id and an empty email, so admins cannot tell who it is 5. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=teams shows no team membership, because the team claim their IdP puts in the tokens was never read After: the same login produces a full profile, with the user id, email, display name and teams their tokens carry 1. The proxy admin sets `GENERIC_INCLUDE_TOKEN_CLAIMS=true`, points `GENERIC_USER_ID_ATTRIBUTE` / `GENERIC_USER_EMAIL_ATTRIBUTE` at the claim names their tokens carry (for example `upn` and `email`), and restarts the proxy 2. The user opens https://litellm-domain/ui/ and clicks through the same SSO login 3. Login succeeds and they are redirected back to https://litellm-domain/ui/ 4. The user badge now shows their real display name and email 5. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=users lists the account with a real user id and email 6. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=teams shows the teams their token claim names Their role is unchanged by this PR in both directions, and the Screenshots section shows why: it already resolved from the access token before this change With the toggle unset, every one of these steps behaves exactly as it does today, which the Before and default-configuration runs below demonstrate byte for byte ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-4825 ## Review notes Greptile's one finding was that the new PKCE test replaced two `SSOAuthenticationHandler` methods with `patch.object`, which the repo CLAUDE.md calls out as an anti-pattern. That test now injects dependencies instead: the PKCE verifier cache and the httpx transport are the only doubles, and the request is a real Starlette `Request`, so `prepare_token_exchange_parameters`, `_pkce_token_exchange`, the userinfo fetch and the claim merge all run for real. The rework also makes the test stronger rather than merely tidier. It now asserts that the cached verifier reaches the token endpoint, that `sub` still comes from UserInfo, and that `email`, which exists only inside the access token, reaches the resulting `CustomOpenID`. Four mutations of `ui_sso.py` were checked against it: disabling the opt-in branch, dropping the bearer-credential filter on `received_response`, inverting the merge precedence, and ignoring the exchange-response access token. All four fail the reworked test, and two of them (disabling the opt-in branch, ignoring the exchange-response access token) passed the old one On trusting token claims: `_decode_sso_token_claims` decodes without verifying the signature, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight. Both tokens come from the authorization-code exchange, a direct TLS back-channel POST to the operator-configured token endpoint authenticated with the client secret or PKCE, never from anything the browser hands us. OIDC Core section 3.1.3.7 clause 6 explicitly permits skipping ID token signature validation on that path. It is also not a new trust surface, and the runs below make that concrete rather than theoretical: `user_role` comes back as `proxy_admin` in all three, including at the merge base where this feature does not exist, because `process_sso_jwt_access_token` already decodes the same access token the same way and already derives the role from `GENERIC_ROLE_MAPPINGS_GROUP_CLAIM`. The merge changes which claims the existing attribute mappings can see, not who is trusted to assert them Two claims in an earlier revision of this description were wrong and the runs below corrected them. It said the role was missing before the fix and arrives with it; the role was never missing. It also implied the group claim was unreachable; the group claim already reached the role mapping, and what was actually unreachable was the identity attributes and the team claim ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v` - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (5/5 at `b5c5f178`) `code-quality` and `documentation` were red until https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm-docs/pull/969 documented `GENERIC_INCLUDE_TOKEN_CLAIMS`, because `tests/documentation_tests/test_env_keys.py` checks env vars against litellm-docs **main**. That PR has merged and both jobs are green on `b5c5f178` ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix The condition this PR fixes is an IdP whose UserInfo response is thin while its tokens carry the real claims. That does not require ADFS specifically, so these runs use a local OIDC provider configured to behave that way: `/userinfo` returns `{"sub": "adfs-subject-0001"}` and nothing else, while `/token` returns signed JWTs carrying `upn`, `email`, `display_name`, `groups` and `team_ids`. All three runs drive the real login with curl, against a real proxy on port 4000 backed by Postgres, and read the result out of the user table, which is what `/ui/?page=users` and `/ui/?page=teams` render. Shared setup, exported before each run: ``` DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:pw@127.0.0.1:6396/litellm PROXY_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4000 GENERIC_CLIENT_ID=litellm-proxy GENERIC_CLIENT_SECRET=stub-client-secret GENERIC_AUTHORIZATION_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:9700/authorize GENERIC_TOKEN_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:9700/token GENERIC_USERINFO_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:9700/userinfo GENERIC_SCOPE="openid profile email" GENERIC_USER_ID_ATTRIBUTE=upn GENERIC_USER_EMAIL_ATTRIBUTE=email GENERIC_USER_DISPLAY_NAME_ATTRIBUTE=display_name GENERIC_ROLE_MAPPINGS_GROUP_CLAIM=groups GENERIC_ROLE_MAPPINGS_ROLES="{'proxy_admin': ['litellm-admins']}" ``` The team mapping lives in the database rather than the environment, seeded once as `{"team_mappings": {"team_ids_jwt_field": "team_ids"}}` in `LiteLLM_SSOConfig`, with a `platform-eng` team created so membership has somewhere to land. Every run was launched from a directory outside the repo, so litellm's import-time `load_dotenv()` could not hand any run the checkout's `.env`. Each run prints that check, the exact tree it loaded, a UTC start and end stamp, and a liveliness probe at both ends, so a run that silently straddled two proxies, or that overlapped someone else's cleanup on a shared machine, would be visible rather than averaged in. All three runs below come from one uninterrupted pass between 22:20:38 and 22:21:04 UTC. A note on the hashes, since the branch was rebased after these runs. The capture was taken with the base at `cde134488c` and the PR at `4311b55704`. Both have since moved: the merge base is now `d8a57a1a2b` and the head is `b5c5f178`. The runs still hold, and it is checkable rather than a matter of trust. `git diff cde134488c d8a57a1a2b -- litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/ui_sso.py` is empty, so the file under test is byte-identical across the two bases and the Before run still describes the current base. `git diff 4311b55704 b5c5f178` restricted to the two changed files is likewise empty, so the After runs describe the current head. Re-running would cost a full IdP rig cycle to reproduce the same numbers. The IdP condition, identical for all three runs: ``` $ curl -s http://localhost:9700/userinfo {"sub": "adfs-subject-0001"} ``` ### Before (cde134488c) 1. Confirm the environment is clean and the proxy is the one under test ``` $ python -c "import litellm, os; print(os.environ.get('OPENAI_API_KEY') is not None, os.environ.get('ANTHROPIC_API_KEY') is not None, os.path.exists('.env'))" False False False code under test: .../scratchpad/rig/base/litellm/__init__.py times this tree mentions GENERIC_INCLUDE_TOKEN_CLAIMS: 0 Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:4000 leg START (UTC): 22:20:38 liveliness: "I'm alive!" ``` 2. Drive the real SSO login ``` $ curl -s -c jar.txt -b jar.txt -L -o /dev/null -w 'final_url=%{url_effective} http_code=%{http_code}\n' \ http://localhost:4000/sso/key/generate final_url=http://localhost:4000/ui/?login=success http_code=200 ``` 3. Read the account the login created, which is what `/ui/?page=users` lists ``` $ psql -c "SELECT user_id, user_email, user_role FROM \"LiteLLM_UserTable\" ..." user_id|user_email|user_role <empty>|<null>|proxy_admin ``` 4. Read the team membership, which is what `/ui/?page=teams` shows ``` user_id|teams: <empty>| ``` 5. The identity the proxy actually resolved ``` generic result: id=None email=None first_name=None last_name=None display_name=None picture=None provider=None team_ids=[] user_role=<LitellmUserRoles.PROXY_ADMIN: 'proxy_admin'> extra_fields=None liveliness at end of run: "I'm alive!" leg END (UTC): 22:20:40 ``` The account is unusable: no user id, no email, no display name, no team. Note `proxy_admin` is already present here, at the merge base, with this feature absent. ### After (b5c5f178) First run, default configuration, `GENERIC_INCLUDE_TOKEN_CLAIMS` unset. This is the regression check. 1. Confirm the tree under test now contains the feature ``` code under test: .../worktrees/c9-pr37696/litellm/__init__.py times this tree mentions GENERIC_INCLUDE_TOKEN_CLAIMS: 1 GENERIC_INCLUDE_TOKEN_CLAIMS=false Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:4000 leg START (UTC): 22:20:50 liveliness: "I'm alive!" ``` 2. Drive the same login ``` final_url=http://localhost:4000/ui/?login=success http_code=200 ``` 3. Account, team membership, and resolved identity ``` user_id|user_email|user_role <empty>|<null>|proxy_admin user_id|teams: <empty>| generic result: id=None email=None first_name=None last_name=None display_name=None picture=None provider=None team_ids=[] user_role=<LitellmUserRoles.PROXY_ADMIN: 'proxy_admin'> extra_fields=None liveliness at end of run: "I'm alive!" leg END (UTC): 22:20:52 ``` Identical to Before in every field, which is the evidence for the opt-in claim. Second run, same code, `GENERIC_INCLUDE_TOKEN_CLAIMS=true`. The flag is the only thing that changed. 4. Confirm the flag is the only difference ``` code under test: .../worktrees/c9-pr37696/litellm/__init__.py times this tree mentions GENERIC_INCLUDE_TOKEN_CLAIMS: 1 GENERIC_INCLUDE_TOKEN_CLAIMS=true Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:4000 leg START (UTC): 22:21:02 liveliness: "I'm alive!" ``` 5. Drive the same login ``` final_url=http://localhost:4000/ui/?login=success http_code=200 ``` 6. The account now carries the token-sourced identity ``` user_id|user_email|user_role dana.reyes@corp.example.com|dana.reyes@corp.example.com|proxy_admin ``` 7. Team membership now resolves from the token claim ``` user_id|teams: dana.reyes@corp.example.com|platform-eng ``` 8. The resolved identity ``` generic result: id='dana.reyes@corp.example.com' email='dana.reyes@corp.example.com' first_name=None last_name=None display_name='Dana Reyes' picture=None provider=None team_ids=['platform-eng'] user_role=<LitellmUserRoles.PROXY_ADMIN: 'proxy_admin'> extra_fields=None liveliness at end of run: "I'm alive!" leg END (UTC): 22:21:04 ``` `id`, `email`, `display_name` and `team_ids` all went from empty to the values carried only in the tokens, and the user table now has a real user id, a real email and `platform-eng` membership. `user_role` is `proxy_admin` in all three runs, unchanged, which is the point made in Review notes about this PR not widening what the proxy trusts. ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats (if any) - Opt-in: default configuration matches the merge base exactly - Token claims merge shallowly, per top-level claim name - Signatures are not re-verified; see Review notes for why - Role already resolved from the access token, so it is unaffected - Documented in litellm-docs #969, now merged ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/51be51a556c74eb3aac303c1ae76f668 Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signal.title: fix(jwt): retry JWKS fetches, serve stale keys, and return 503 when the IdP is unreachable
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - JWKS fetch had no retry, so one IdP blip failed auth - Expired cache dropped still-valid keys with no fallback - Every in-flight request refetched JWKS after TTL lapse - `httpx.ConnectTimeout` surfaced as a 401 with empty detail - A read timeout blamed the database for a JWKS outage - A non-200 JWKS body was cached as if it were keys How it solves it: - Retry transport failures 3 times with a short backoff - Serve the last-known-good JWKS for a bounded, logged window - Enforce that bound on read, so lowering it binds at once - Coalesce concurrent refreshes, and back off per outage window - Raise 503 `auth_provider_unavailable` when the IdP is unreachable - Reject non-200 JWKS responses instead of caching them ## User Flow Before: a developer whose app authenticates with an Okta-issued JWT gets bursts of 401s whenever the connection to the IdP's JWKS endpoint times out 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `Authorization: Bearer <their JWT>` and get 200 back 2. The gateway's cached copy of the IdP signing keys expires 10 minutes later, and the next fetch of the IdP's key endpoint times out 3. The same still-valid JWT now fails, and how it fails depends on how the endpoint is unreachable. A connect timeout comes back as HTTP 401 `{"error":{"message":"Authentication Error, ","type":"auth_error","code":"401"}}`, with no detail at all. A read timeout comes back as HTTP 503 `{"error":{"message":"Service Unavailable, the authentication database is temporarily unreachable. Please retry shortly.","type":"no_db_connection","code":"503"}}`, blaming a database that is perfectly healthy 4. Their client reads the 401 as "bad credentials", so it logs the user out and does not retry, even though the token and the IdP keys never changed. Whoever is on call reads the 503 and goes looking at the database After: the same request rides out the IdP blip, and a genuine outage reads as a retryable server-side failure 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `Authorization: Bearer <their JWT>` and get 200 back 2. The cached copy expires 10 minutes later, and the next fetch of the IdP's key endpoint times out 3. The gateway retries the fetch, then falls back to the signing keys it last saw, so the same request still returns 200 4. If the IdP is unreachable on a true cold start, the response is HTTP 503 `{"error":{"message":"Service Unavailable, the identity provider's JWKS endpoint is temporarily unreachable, ...","type":"auth_provider_unavailable","code":"503"}}`, which their client retries instead of treating as invalid credentials 5. Once the IdP answers again, the very next refresh wins, so a key the admin removed from the JWKS stops authenticating anyone immediately. If the IdP stays down past `public_key_stale_ttl` (1h by default, `0` to fail closed), the old key stops authenticating anyone too and requests get the same 503 ## A JWKS outage failed two different ways, and the ticket only saw one How the failure surfaced depended on how the endpoint was unreachable, and the two shapes took different paths through the code. `httpx.ConnectTimeout` is absent from `DB_CONNECTION_ERROR_TYPES` on the base branch, which carries `ConnectError`, `ReadError` and `ReadTimeout`. A connect timeout therefore falls past the database handler into the generic auth handler and comes back as `401 auth_error` with an empty detail, which is the symptom the ticket reported. A read timeout matches that tuple, takes the database path, and comes back as `503 no_db_connection`, "the authentication database is temporarily unreachable" The second one is the more expensive failure to be on call for. A 401 at least points at authentication. A database error points at a subsystem where there is nothing to find, while the thing actually down is the identity provider's key endpoint. Both are captured live below, and both are replaced by `auth_provider_unavailable`, which names the identity provider and is a 503 the client retries. Adding `httpx.ConnectTimeout` to `DB_CONNECTION_ERROR_TYPES` is what closes the fall-through for every other caller of that tuple ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5524 ## Review notes The stale fallback deliberately trades a bounded window of "the IdP removed this key and we cannot yet tell" for not failing every authenticated request during an outage. Four things bound it: The window is entered only on `httpx.TransportError`, so any HTTP-level answer from the IdP, a 200 with a narrowed key set as much as a 4xx, goes through the normal refresh path and replaces both the active and the stale copy. Revoking a key against a healthy IdP is honoured on the next refresh, not an hour later That transport-error-only scope is the whole basis for calling this fallback safe, and until now nothing enforced it. Mutation testing caught that: widening the `except JWKSUnreachableError` in `_refresh_or_record_outage` to `except Exception` passed the entire suite. Under that one-word change a malformed response, or any bug in parsing, would quietly serve stale keys instead of failing, and the reasoning above would still read as settled while nothing held it up. `test_unparseable_jwks_response_does_not_fall_back_to_the_stale_copy` and `test_jwks_error_response_is_not_cached_over_the_last_known_good_keys` now pin it, so a future refactor that widens that clause fails CI The window's length is `public_key_stale_ttl`, a new config field defaulting to 3600s, and it is measured past the active entry rather than derived from `public_key_ttl`. That is what keeps a long configured `public_key_ttl` from collapsing the fallback to nothing, and what keeps the extra trust at exactly one configured window no matter how the active TTL is tuned. Deployments that cannot accept any unrefreshed key set it to `0` and get a 503 the moment the active entry expires Every stale serve logs a warning naming the `kid` it authenticated, the JWKS url, how long ago that copy was last refreshed, and how long until it stops being trusted, so the exposure is visible while it is happening rather than after the fact That bound is checked on every read against the current setting, rather than being baked into the cache entry when it is written. An operator who lowers `public_key_stale_ttl`, or sets it to `0`, is usually doing it mid-incident, and a Redis-backed cache survives the restart they perform to make it take effect, so a copy written under the old longer setting would otherwise stay servable until it aged out on its own. The one control reached for under pressure has to bind immediately. An earlier revision of this PR got that wrong in an instructive way: it computed the correct remaining lifetime and used it only for the log line, so the warning told the operator a bound that nothing enforced. An observable reporting a limit nobody applies is worse than having no observable, because it reassures. The cache entry's own TTL is now a memory-management concern and the read-time check is the security boundary Token `exp` and every other claim check still apply, so the window caps how long a key stays trusted, not how long a token does Separately, a sustained outage records the failure for 30s per key url. Without that, every request during an outage paid three connect timeouts serialised behind the refresh lock, and the queue grew faster than it drained, so the fallback was inert exactly under the load that motivated it. The cost is that recovery can lag the IdP coming back by up to 30s ## A hole this PR closes that it would otherwise have widened `_fetch_jwks_keys` never checked `status_code`, so whatever the IdP returned was parsed and cached as the key set. A 5xx with a JSON error body became the cached JWKS for a full `public_key_ttl`, and once this PR started writing a longer-lived stale copy, that same error body would have been promoted to trusted signing material for `public_key_ttl + public_key_stale_ttl`, outliving the incident that produced it. A transient IdP error turning into long-lived trusted key material is strictly worse than the outage the ticket describes. Non-200 now raises before anything is cached, and `test_jwks_error_response_is_not_cached_over_the_last_known_good_keys` asserts that both the active and the stale copy still hold the last good keys afterwards ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Run against a live proxy on :4321 with a stub JWKS endpoint on :8899 standing in for the IdP, so the outage is something I control rather than something I wait for. The stub reads a `mode` file per request: `ok` serves the signing key, `hang` accepts the connection and never answers (read timeout), `revoked` serves a JWKS the key has been removed from. Case 5 points `JWT_PUBLIC_KEY_URL` at a blackholed `10.255.255.1` for a connect timeout. Cases 1 to 4 share one proxy lifetime, because the stale window is measured from case 1's refresh Config (`general_settings.litellm_jwtauth`), TTLs shortened so the whole window fits the run: ```yaml admin_jwt_scope: litellm_proxy_admin admin_allowed_routes: [openai_routes, info_routes] public_key_ttl: 20 public_key_stale_ttl: 60 ``` Case 4 is the one that answers the security question Greptile raised. It returns the same 401 on both legs, and that identical result is the finding: a stale copy of the removed key was in the cache and went unconsulted, so the fallback did not widen trust while the identity provider was reachable The same request throughout, a real Anthropic call with a JWT signed by the stub's key: ```bash curl -s -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4321/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat token.jwt)" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"anthropic-sonnet-5","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Reply with the single word: authenticated"}],"max_tokens":16}' ``` ### Before (4af59d7c6e) #### Case 1: healthy IdP 1. `echo ok > mode`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 200`, `{"choices":[{"message":{"content":"authenticated",...}}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":18,"completion_tokens":6,...}}` #### Case 2: IdP stops answering and the cached keys lapse 1. `echo hang > mode; sleep 25`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 503`, `{"error":{"message":"Service Unavailable, the authentication database is temporarily unreachable. Please retry shortly.","type":"no_db_connection","code":"503"}}` 3. The JWKS endpoint is what is unreachable, not the database, so this points the on-call at the wrong subsystem #### Case 3: the outage outlives the stale window 1. `sleep 50`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 503`, same `no_db_connection` body as case 2 #### Case 4: IdP reachable again, signing key removed from its JWKS 1. `echo revoked > mode; sleep 35`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 401`, `{"error":{"message":"Authentication Error, No matching public key found. keys=['http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys'], kid=demo-signing-key","type":"auth_error","code":"401"}}` #### Case 5: cold start against an unreachable IdP (connect timeout) 1. Restart the proxy with `JWT_PUBLIC_KEY_URL=http://10.255.255.1:8899/keys`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 401`, `{"error":{"message":"Authentication Error, ","type":"auth_error","param":"None","code":"401"}}` 3. This is the reported bug verbatim: a 401 with no detail at all, which a client reads as bad credentials and does not retry ### After (74e8eb17fc) #### Case 1: healthy IdP 1. `echo ok > mode`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 200`, `{"choices":[{"message":{"content":"authenticated",...}}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":18,"completion_tokens":6,...}}` #### Case 2: IdP stops answering and the cached keys lapse 1. `echo hang > mode; sleep 25`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 200`, the same real completion. The request rides out the outage on the last-known-good key 3. The proxy log says which key that was and how long it has left: ``` JWT Auth: ReadTimeout fetching http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys (attempt 1/3), retrying: JWT Auth: ReadTimeout fetching http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys (attempt 2/3), retrying: JWT Auth: identity provider unreachable, authenticating kid=demo-signing-key against a stale JWKS copy of litellm_jwt_auth_keys_http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys (last refreshed 42s ago, stops being trusted in 38s). Refresh failed: ReadTimeout fetching http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys after 3 attempts ``` 4. `42s + 38s` is the configured `public_key_ttl 20` + `public_key_stale_ttl 60`, so the bound in the log is the bound in the config #### Case 3: the outage outlives the stale window 1. `sleep 50`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 503`, `{"error":{"message":"Service Unavailable, the identity provider's JWKS endpoint is temporarily unreachable, so the JWT signature could not be verified. Please retry shortly. Error: ReadTimeout fetching http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys after 3 attempts","type":"auth_provider_unavailable","code":"503"}}` 3. The stale copy is gone at the configured bound, so the key stops being trusted. The failure names the identity provider rather than the database, and it is a 503 the client retries rather than a 401 it logs the user out on #### Case 4: IdP reachable again, signing key removed from its JWKS 1. `echo revoked > mode; sleep 35`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 401`, `{"error":{"message":"Authentication Error, No matching public key found. keys=['http://127.0.0.1:8899/keys'], kid=demo-signing-key","type":"auth_error","code":"401"}}` 3. Unchanged from before, which is the point. A stale copy of that key was on hand and was not consulted, because the identity provider answered. Revocation against a healthy IdP is immediate, not delayed by `public_key_stale_ttl` #### Case 5: cold start against an unreachable IdP (connect timeout) 1. Restart the proxy with `JWT_PUBLIC_KEY_URL=http://10.255.255.1:8899/keys`, then the curl above 2. `HTTP 503`, `{"error":{"message":"Service Unavailable, the identity provider's JWKS endpoint is temporarily unreachable, so the JWT signature could not be verified. Please retry shortly. Error: ConnectTimeout fetching http://10.255.255.1:8899/keys after 3 attempts","type":"auth_provider_unavailable","param":"None","code":"503"}}` One boundary of this matrix, stated rather than left to be assumed: every case runs at a fixed `public_key_stale_ttl`, so none of them exercises lowering or raising the setting while a copy written under the previous value is still cached. That path is covered by unit tests instead, `test_lowering_public_key_stale_ttl_stops_serving_a_copy_cached_under_the_old_setting`, `test_zero_public_key_stale_ttl_fails_closed_even_for_a_freshly_written_copy` and `test_increasing_public_key_stale_ttl_only_extends_within_the_new_bound` The capture also runs a single-process proxy, so the Redis-backed shared-cache path is likewise unit-tested rather than captured, including `test_stale_copy_written_at_survives_a_whole_number_epoch` for the epoch a JSON round-trip hands back as an int Each leg was checked for cross-contamination rather than assumed: the before leg's proxy log has zero retry warnings, zero stale-serve warnings and zero `auth_provider_unavailable`, against two `no_db_connection` and the bare 401, and the after leg has three retries, one stale serve and two `auth_provider_unavailable`. Both served exactly five requests for five cases on one proxy lifetime ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Stale keys served up to `public_key_stale_ttl` (1h) past the TTL - Requests can keep 503ing up to 30s after the IdP recovers - Stale fallback covers transport failures, not IdP error responses - Refresh locks live per process; the caches are shared ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/bb79bcd7663d484e93a08ed3f725a0c8 Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signal.title: fix(shadow_eval): split slot release from stops so stopped_at means exactly one thing
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - stopped_at does two jobs: index slot marker (sweeps) and stop marker (operators) - Readers must guess which one a stamp means, and every guess has a race - A stop racing a spend-budget crossing can read as natural completion How it solves it: - New internal released_at column takes over slot bookkeeping - Sweeps write only released_at; any stopped_at now means a stop, always - Spend and count arithmetic is only ever consulted for unstamped keys - The migration moves old sweep stamps to released_at and re-anchors the index ## User Flow Before: whether a stamped eval reads "stopped" or "completed" depends on racy arithmetic 1. An admin stops a running eval from http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=cost-optimization just as its spend crosses max_budget 2. An in-flight sample lands moments before the stop is recorded, pushing recorded spend over the cap 3. The eval's card reads "completed", as if it ran its budget out; the admin's stop left no visible trace After: a stamp is a stop, and no spend timing can reinterpret it 1. The admin stops the same eval at the same moment 2. The card reads "stopped" and keeps reading "stopped", whatever the recorded spend says 3. Evals that end by spending their budget still read "completed", before and after the slot sweep runs ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Setup: proxy from this repo against Postgres, config with `auto_router1` (complexity router over gpt-5 family deployments) and a deterministic OpenAI-compatible upstream at :4299. Evals started with per-key `max_budget` (dollars); spend rows are topped up via SQL where noted because the stub's per-call cost is fractions of a cent ```bash curl -sX POST http://localhost:4000/key/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" -d '{"key_alias": "spend-qa"}' curl -sX POST http://localhost:4000/auto_router/shadow_eval/start -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" \ -d '{"api_key_ids": ["<token_id>"], "router_name": "auto_router1", "shadow_percentage": 100.0, "judge_model": "gpt-5-nano", "duration_days": 7, "max_budget": 0.01}' curl -s http://localhost:4000/auto_router/shadow_eval -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" ``` ### Before (1d7f675e52) #### A stamped job's label depends on spend arithmetic 1. Stop a running eval, then land two attempt rows timestamped one second before the stop, taking recorded spend to $16 against a $5 budget 2. GET /auto_router/shadow_eval: the frozen-count read includes the pre-stop rows, and on any leg whose stopped_by write raced or predated the column the derivation reads `"completed"`; the stamp's meaning is decided by arithmetic #### The sweep writes the stop column 1. Let an eval spend past max_budget, then start a new eval on the same key 2. The sweep stamps the finished job's `stopped_at`: slot bookkeeping and stops share one column, which is what forces every reader to guess ### After (71ff91251f) #### Spend exhaustion reads completed with nothing stamped 1. Start with `max_budget: 0.01`, send 2 chats, top spend to $0.0202 2. GET list: status `"completed"`, `spend: 0.0202` of `0.01`, `stopped_at: null`, `stopped_by: null` #### The sweep frees the slot without touching the stop record 1. Start a second eval on the same key: 201; the first job's slot is released 2. GET list: first job still `"completed"`, `stopped_at` still null #### A stop outranks racing spend 1. Stop the running eval: 200, `"stopped"`, `stopped_by` recorded 2. Insert 2 attempt rows dated one second before the stop, recorded spend $16 against the $5 budget 3. GET list: still `"stopped"`; spend is never consulted for a stamped key #### A bare stamp from a pre-released_at pod reads stopped 1. Insert a leg shaped like an old pod's write mid-deploy: `stopped_at` set, no `stopped_by`, spend over budget 2. GET detail: `"stopped"`; a stamp means a stop, unconditionally ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Adds one internal nullable column, released_at; not exposed in the API - The migration moves actor-less sweep stamps off stopped_at, so their jobs keep reading completed - Mixed-version residue: a job swept by a pre-released_at pod mid-deploy reads stopped until its window passes, the safe direction ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: fix(proxy): fail the standalone prisma migration entrypoint on migration errors
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Failed migration Job still exits 0 - GitOps then deploys against a stale schema - Failed `prisma generate` also exits 0 How it solves it: - Migration entrypoint enforces the check by default - `prisma generate` failure returns its exit code - `ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=false` restores the old leniency - In-proxy startup default stays lenient ## User Flow Before: a platform engineer upgrading the gateway with ArgoCD sees the sync go green even though the database was never migrated, then the app serves errors against an out-of-date schema 1. They bump the gateway chart version and let ArgoCD sync in an air-gapped cluster 2. The pre-upgrade migration Job logs a database error and finishes as Succeeded, exit code 0 3. ArgoCD marks the whole app Healthy and rolls out the new gateway pods 4. They hit the new release, for example POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions, and get 500s from endpoints whose columns do not exist yet 5. Only after they explicitly set `ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=true` and re-sync does the Job fail and stop the rollout After: the same sync stops at the migration Job, so nothing gets deployed against a stale schema 1. They bump the gateway chart version and let ArgoCD sync in an air-gapped cluster 2. The pre-upgrade migration Job logs the database error and finishes as Failed, exit code 1 3. ArgoCD reports the sync as Degraded and does not roll out the new gateway pods, so the old release keeps serving traffic on the schema it matches 4. They fix the database access, re-sync, and the Job succeeds before the new pods start 5. Anyone who wants the previous behavior can set `ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=false` on the Job and get exit 0 on a failed migration again ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5385 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup: point the migration entrypoint at an unreachable Postgres so `prisma migrate deploy` fails, and print the exit code the Job would report ```bash export DATABASE_URL='postgresql://litellm:wrongpw@127.0.0.1:5599/nope' export DISABLE_SCHEMA_UPDATE=false export LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=sk-1234 ``` ### Before (3a31331435480950d7f1a475e17863646700a083) #### Failed migration, default settings 1. Run the migration entrypoint the Helm Job runs ```bash uv run --no-sync python litellm/proxy/prisma_migration.py; echo "exit code: $?" ``` 2. Observed output, the migration fails yet the Job reports success ```text Datasource "client": PostgreSQL database "nope", schema "public" at "127.0.0.1:5599" 2026-08-20 20:12:17,703 - litellm_proxy_extras - INFO - Running prisma migrate deploy 2026-08-20 20:12:24,049 - litellm_proxy_extras - INFO - prisma db error: Error: P1001: Can't reach database server at `127.0.0.1`:`5599` Please make sure your database server is running at `127.0.0.1`:`5599`. LiteLLM Proxy: Using default (v1) migration resolver. LiteLLM Proxy: Database migration failed but continuing startup. Set --enforce_prisma_migration_check or ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=true to exit on failure. LiteLLM: Setup complete. Skipping server startup as requested. exit code: 0 ``` #### Failed migration, ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=false 1. Not applicable before this change: leniency was the only behavior, shown by the case above ### After (da75cd5fb0b595860681008ef550a335be3e8fb8) #### Failed migration, default settings 1. Run the same command ```bash uv run --no-sync python litellm/proxy/prisma_migration.py; echo "exit code: $?" ``` 2. Observed output, the Job now fails so the deploy is blocked ```text Datasource "client": PostgreSQL database "nope", schema "public" at "127.0.0.1:5599" 2026-08-20 20:12:25,510 - litellm_proxy_extras - INFO - Running prisma migrate deploy 2026-08-20 20:12:31,696 - litellm_proxy_extras - INFO - prisma db error: Error: P1001: Can't reach database server at `127.0.0.1`:`5599` Please make sure your database server is running at `127.0.0.1`:`5599`. LiteLLM Proxy: Using default (v1) migration resolver. LiteLLM Proxy: Database setup failed after multiple retries. The proxy cannot start safely. Please check your database connection and migration status. exit code: 1 ``` #### Failed migration, ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=false 1. Opt back into the old behavior ```bash ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=false uv run --no-sync python litellm/proxy/prisma_migration.py; echo "exit code: $?" ``` 2. Observed output, unchanged leniency ```text Datasource "client": PostgreSQL database "nope", schema "public" at "127.0.0.1:5599" 2026-08-20 20:13:29,818 - litellm_proxy_extras - INFO - Running prisma migrate deploy 2026-08-20 20:13:36,293 - litellm_proxy_extras - INFO - prisma db error: Error: P1001: Can't reach database server at `127.0.0.1`:`5599` Please make sure your database server is running at `127.0.0.1`:`5599`. LiteLLM Proxy: Using default (v1) migration resolver. LiteLLM Proxy: Database migration failed but continuing startup. Set --enforce_prisma_migration_check or ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=true to exit on failure. LiteLLM: Setup complete. Skipping server startup as requested. exit code: 0 ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Behavior change: failing migration Jobs now fail loudly - `docker/entrypoint.sh` images also stop on migration failure - Opt out with `ENFORCE_PRISMA_MIGRATION_CHECK=false` - Docs check stays red until BerriAI/litellm-docs#972 merges, which documents the variable the gate flagged ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/d6ef92e6d1ea4b39ae7aabb14b4dc2a2 Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signal.title: fix: map Gemini ON_DEMAND_FLEX traffic type to flex service tier
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Vertex AI flex-tier requests are silently billed at standard rate. How it solves it: - Map the `ON_DEMAND_FLEX` traffic type to the `flex` service tier. ## User Flow Before: a developer runs Gemini/Vertex AI requests that opt into flex/shared capacity, and their spend dashboard bills those requests at the standard rate. 1. They send a Vertex AI `generateContent` request that opts into flex capacity. 2. The response comes back served at flex tier (its usage metadata reports the flex traffic type). 3. Their LiteLLM spend for that request is computed at the standard input/output price, with no signal that flex was actually applied. After: the same request is billed at the flex-tier price it was actually served at. 1. They send the same Vertex AI `generateContent` request that opts into flex capacity. 2. The response comes back served at flex tier. 3. LiteLLM now bills that request at the flex-tier price. ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix ![before: 2 failed on ON_DEMAND_FLEX / after: 8 passed](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9830893b-a43e-45fd-9efc-6da6e0bfe016) This is an internal cost-attribution mapping. `_map_traffic_type_to_service_tier` converts the provider-reported traffic type into the service tier that selects the `_flex` / `_priority` cost keys. Before this change the `ON_DEMAND_FLEX` value that Vertex AI reports for flex traffic was absent from the map, so it fell through to `None` (standard pricing). Setup (both sides), in a venv with litellm installed: ``` python -m pytest tests/test_litellm/llms/gemini/test_cost_calculator.py::test_map_traffic_type_to_service_tier -q ``` ### Before (007bd43) Direct call against the unpatched mapping: 1. `_map_traffic_type_to_service_tier("ON_DEMAND_FLEX")` returns `None` (billed as standard). 2. `_map_traffic_type_to_service_tier("FLEX")` returns `"flex"` (only the non-Vertex spelling was mapped). 3. The added regression test fails on the flex cases: ``` E AssertionError: assert None == 'flex' E + where None = _map_traffic_type_to_service_tier('on_demand_flex') FAILED ...::test_map_traffic_type_to_service_tier[ON_DEMAND_FLEX-flex] FAILED ...::test_map_traffic_type_to_service_tier[on_demand_flex-flex] 2 failed, 6 passed in 1.24s ``` ### After (c4383b3) Same call against the patched mapping: 1. `_map_traffic_type_to_service_tier("ON_DEMAND_FLEX")` returns `"flex"` (billed at flex tier). 2. `_map_traffic_type_to_service_tier("FLEX")` / `"BATCH"` still return `"flex"`; `"ON_DEMAND"` still returns `None`. 3. The full test passes: ``` 8 passed, 2 warnings in 0.29s ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ✅ Test ## Caveats (if any) - A fully live Vertex AI flex-capacity request needs Vertex credentials and a flex-priced model; verified at the mapping and unit-test layer. ## QA runbook - tests/test_litellm/llms/gemini/test_cost_calculator.py::test_map_traffic_type_to_service_tier - the Gemini/Vertex traffic type maps to the service tier that selects flex/priority cost keys, and `ON_DEMAND_FLEX` maps to `flex`. - [ ] In a venv with litellm installed, run `python -m pytest tests/test_litellm/llms/gemini/test_cost_calculator.py::test_map_traffic_type_to_service_tier -q` - [ ] Expect 8 passed, including the `ON_DEMAND_FLEX` and `on_demand_flex` cases mapping to `flex` - [ ] Sanity check: this test asserts the exact tier string per traffic type (not just non-None), so an unmapped flex value fails it ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Fixes #37647

signal.title: feat(proxy): add router_model_name to auto-routed response bodies
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Auto-routed model is only in `x-litellm-model-id`, a header - SDKs that hide response headers cannot read the routed model - Streaming makes it worse: no body surface at all How it solves it: - Adds `router_model_name` to the response body - Present on both non-streaming bodies and every SSE chunk - Emitted only when an auto-routing strategy actually picked the model ## User Flow Before: a developer whose app streams chat completions through an auto-router cannot tell which model answered, so their UI cannot label the response 1. They configure a `smart-route` model group backed by a complexity router with `fast-model`, `standard-model`, and `deep-model` tiers 2. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `"model": "smart-route"` and `"stream": true` 3. Each SSE frame comes back with `"model": "smart-route"`, the alias they sent, and nothing naming the tier that actually ran 4. The routed model is in the `x-litellm-model-id` response header, which their SDK does not expose to application code 5. Their UI renders every answer unlabeled, whether a cheap tier or an expensive one served it 6. Sending the same request without `"stream": true` gives the same result: the body names only the alias After: the same developer reads the routed model straight off the body, streaming included 1. They configure a `smart-route` model group backed by a complexity router with `fast-model`, `standard-model`, and `deep-model` tiers 2. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `"model": "smart-route"` and `"stream": true` 3. Each SSE frame comes back with `"model": "smart-route"` and `"router_model_name": "deep-model"`, naming the tier that actually ran 4. They read the routed model from the frame their SDK already hands them, with no access to response headers needed 5. Their UI labels each answer with the tier that served it 6. Sending the same request without `"stream": true` puts the same `"router_model_name"` on the response body A request that names a model group directly, with no auto-routing involved, has no `router_model_name` key at all, so nothing changes for callers who do not use an auto-router ## Relevant issues - The response body `model` field is deliberately restamped back to the client-requested alias on both the streaming and non-streaming paths, which is correct OpenAI semantics, so this adds a separate namespaced key rather than redefining `model` - `router_model_name` carries the model group the router selected, not the raw upstream provider string, so it matches the names an operator wrote in their config - Router fallbacks resolve on the first `__anext__`, after the streaming wrapper is handed back, so each chunk reads the selected group live instead of a snapshot taken before the router had decided. A fallback onto a plain group drops the key, and one onto another auto-routed group reports the new tier - langchain-openai builds `response_metadata` from a fixed key list, so LangChain users read this off the raw chunk rather than off `response_metadata` - Removes a redundant function-local import in the streaming generator that shadowed the module-level one and made the whole name function-local ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v` - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Live proxy on a complexity router with three tiers, hitting real Bedrock and Anthropic models through a gateway. Same five commands both runs Config used: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: fast-model litellm_params: {model: openai/bedrock/global.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0, api_base: os.environ/GW_BASE, api_key: os.environ/GW_KEY} - model_name: standard-model litellm_params: {model: openai/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001, api_base: os.environ/GW_BASE, api_key: os.environ/GW_KEY} - model_name: deep-model litellm_params: {model: openai/bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0, api_base: os.environ/GW_BASE, api_key: os.environ/GW_KEY} - model_name: smart-route litellm_params: model: auto_router/complexity_router complexity_router_default_model: standard-model complexity_router_config: classifier_type: llm classifier_llm_config: {model: fast-model, timeout_ms: 15000} tier_definitions: - {name: CASUAL, description: greetings, chitchat, and quick factual questions with short known answers} - {name: CODING, description: any programming task, code review, debugging, or software design work} - {name: RESEARCH, description: multi-step analysis, proofs, tradeoff studies, or open-ended research-grade reasoning} fallback_tier: CODING tiers: {CASUAL: fast-model, CODING: standard-model, RESEARCH: deep-model} ``` Commands: ```bash P=4405; K=sk-mib-master ask () { printf '{"model":"smart-route",%s"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"%s"}]}' "$2" "$1"; } echo "### 1. non-streaming, auto-routed" curl -s http://localhost:$P/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $K" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "$(ask 'Derive the time "Authorization: Bearer $K" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "$(ask 'Derive the time complexity of binary search and prove the bound' '"stream":true,')" \ | grep -m1 '^data: {' echo "### 3. streaming, a different tier wins, first SSE frame" curl -sN http://localhost:$P/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $K" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "$(ask 'hey there' '"stream":true,')" | grep -m1 '^data: {' echo "### 4. streaming, review a function so the coding tier wins, first SSE frame" curl -sN http://localhost:$P/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $K" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "$(ask 'Review this Python function for bugs: def add(a, b): return a - b' '"stream":true,')" \ | grep -m1 '^data: {' echo "### 5. negative control: direct model group, no auto-routing, key must be absent" curl -s http://localhost:$P/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $K" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"standard-model","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hey there"}]}' \ | jq '{model, has_router_model_name: has("router_model_name")}' ``` Before, at merge base `e07a7129c5`: ``` ### 1. non-streaming, auto-routed { "model": "smart-route", "router_model_name": null } ### 2. streaming, auto-routed, first SSE frame data: {"id":"chatcmpl-cca8a3f7-5661-436e-8d71-35261d4db817","object":"chat.completion.chunk","created":1787262634,"model":"smart-route","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"role":"assistant","content":"# "}}]} ### 3. streaming, a different tier wins, first SSE frame data: {"id":"chatcmpl-68c41926-3e06-4a86-9290-b01f1a4c891f","created":1787262637,"model":"smart-route","object":"chat.completion.chunk","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"content":"Hey","role":"assistant"}}],"provider_specific_fields":{}} ### 4. streaming, review a function so the coding tier wins, first SSE frame data: {"id":"chatcmpl-e866c795-9173-467f-96a4-72861824102f","object":"chat.completion.chunk","created":1787262640,"model":"smart-route","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"role":"assistant","content":"#"}}]} ### 5. negative control: direct model group, no auto-routing, key must be absent { "model": "standard-model", "has_router_model_name": false } ``` `null` in section 1 is jq rendering a key that is not there, matching the `has(...)` check in section 5 After, at PR tip: ``` ### 1. non-streaming, auto-routed { "model": "smart-route", "router_model_name": "deep-model" } ### 2. streaming, auto-routed, first SSE frame data: {"id":"chatcmpl-c27b92d7-c374-49ea-8473-828acec9cd50","created":1787263277,"model":"smart-route","object":"chat.completion.chunk","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"content":"#","role":"assistant"}}],"provider_specific_fields":{},"router_model_name":"deep-model"} ### 3. streaming, a different tier wins, first SSE frame data: {"id":"chatcmpl-f1344858-017f-43ca-81fc-e97175bbac45","created":1787263280,"model":"smart-route","object":"chat.completion.chunk","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"content":"Hey! How's","role":"assistant"}}],"provider_specific_fields":{},"router_model_name":"fast-model"} ### 4. streaming, review a function so the coding tier wins, first SSE frame data: {"id":"chatcmpl-f5be4eb0-975d-4a2d-ac0a-8b6e0122df81","object":"chat.completion.chunk","created":1787263282,"model":"smart-route","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"role":"assistant","content":"#"}}],"router_model_name":"standard-model"} ### 5. negative control: direct model group, no auto-routing, key must be absent { "model": "standard-model", "has_router_model_name": false } ``` Three different prompts route to three different tiers, each one named in the body, and the direct-group control stays clean ### Mid-stream fallback Review raised that a fallback taken during iteration could keep naming the tier that already failed. Reproduced against a `smart-route-fb` group whose RESEARCH tier points at an upstream that completes the HTTP handshake and then resets the socket, which is what makes the router resolve its fallback lazily on the first `__anext__` rather than before the wrapper is handed back. `router_settings.fallbacks` sends `smart-route-fb` to the plain `standard-model` group. Extra config for this run: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: dead-model litellm_params: {model: openai/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001, api_base: http://127.0.0.1:18477/v1, api_key: sk-dead} - model_name: smart-route-fb litellm_params: model: auto_router/complexity_router complexity_router_default_model: standard-model complexity_router_config: classifier_type: llm classifier_llm_config: {model: fast-model, timeout_ms: 15000} tier_definitions: - {name: CASUAL, description: greetings, chitchat, and quick factual questions with short known answers} - {name: RESEARCH, description: multi-step analysis, proofs, tradeoff studies, or open-ended research-grade reasoning} fallback_tier: RESEARCH tiers: {CASUAL: fast-model, RESEARCH: dead-model} router_settings: fallbacks: [{"smart-route-fb": ["standard-model"]}] num_retries: 0 ``` Port 18477 is a raw socket server that answers with `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, then resets the connection with `SO_LINGER`. A refused connection is not enough here: it makes `acompletion` raise before returning the wrapper, so the fallback resolves eagerly and the snapshot is already correct Commands: ```bash P=4405; K=sk-mib-master frames () { grep '^data: {' | head -3 | jq -Rc 'ltrimstr("data: ")|fromjson|{model, router_model_name:(.router_model_name // "<ABSENT>")}'; } echo "### streaming, the auto-routed tier dies after the handshake, router falls back to a plain group" curl -sN http://localhost:$P/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $K" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"smart-route-fb","stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Derive the time complexity of binary search and prove the bound"}]}' | frames echo "### regression, no fallback, the tier is still named on every frame" curl -sN http://localhost:$P/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $K" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"smart-route","stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Derive the time complexity of binary search and prove the bound"}]}' | frames ``` Before, at the reviewed sha `92b057c641`, which snapshotted the selected group once before iteration: ``` ### streaming, the auto-routed tier dies after the handshake, router falls back to a plain group {"model":"standard-model","router_model_name":"dead-model"} {"model":"standard-model","router_model_name":"dead-model"} {"model":"standard-model","router_model_name":"dead-model"} ### regression, no fallback, the tier is still named on every frame {"model":"smart-route","router_model_name":"deep-model"} {"model":"smart-route","router_model_name":"deep-model"} {"model":"smart-route","router_model_name":"deep-model"} ``` Every frame credits `dead-model`, the tier that served none of the content After, at PR tip, reading the selected group per chunk instead: ``` ### streaming, the auto-routed tier dies after the handshake, router falls back to a plain group {"model":"standard-model","router_model_name":"<ABSENT>"} {"model":"standard-model","router_model_name":"<ABSENT>"} {"model":"standard-model","router_model_name":"<ABSENT>"} ### regression, no fallback, the tier is still named on every frame {"model":"smart-route","router_model_name":"deep-model"} {"model":"smart-route","router_model_name":"deep-model"} {"model":"smart-route","router_model_name":"deep-model"} ``` The fallback lands outside any auto-routed group, so the key drops rather than naming a tier that did not run, and the happy path is unchanged. A fallback onto a second auto-routed group reports that group's tier instead, covered by unit tests <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Touches proxy response shaping and router metadata on the hot completion/streaming path. Additive and gated to auto-routed requests, but a stamp/clear bug could mislabel the serving model or leak the field onto ordinary group traffic. > > **Overview** > Adds a body-level `router_model_name` so clients can see which auto-router tier actually served a request. The existing `model` field stays the client alias; the new field is emitted only when an auto-routing strategy actually picked the group. > > The router stamps `_auto_routed_request` on a successful pre-routing hook and clears it on plain-group re-entry (fallbacks reuse the same kwargs). The proxy copies `deployment_model_name` onto dict and object responses, including the fast SSE serializer. Streaming reads the selected group per chunk so a mid-stream fallback drops the key or reports the new tier instead of a stale snapshot. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit b31cd8e7bfb76f46fd41d42f16a9b51b43f1c27d. signal.title: fix(proxy): claim batch cost rows atomically so multi-pod polling can't double-bill
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Every pod polls batch costs without a lock - Two pods bill the same completed batch - Aggregated spend counts that batch twice How it solves it: - Claim each row with an atomic compare-and-swap - Claim after the results fetch, right before billing - Losers skip, and a failed spend log releases the claim ## User Flow Before: an admin running the gateway on more than one pod has one completed batch counted twice in their spend totals, while the logs page shows a single entry for it 1. The admin runs the gateway with two replicas and batch polling enabled, both pointed at the same database 2. They upload a batch input file and create a batch against a managed model, then wait for the provider to finish it 3. Within one polling window both replicas pick up the same finished batch, and each records a charge for it 4. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs, filter to that batch, and see exactly ONE entry, which looks correct 5. Their spend dashboards and any budget the key or user is under nevertheless move by twice that batch's cost, so the totals are wrong with no per-request evidence anywhere to explain why After: the same batch moves the totals once, no matter how many replicas run 1. The admin runs the gateway with two replicas and batch polling enabled, both pointed at the same database 2. They upload a batch input file and create a batch against a managed model, then wait for the provider to finish it 3. Within one polling window both replicas pick up the same finished batch, but only one of them records a charge for it, and the other moves on, logging that the batch was already claimed elsewhere 4. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs, filter to that batch, and see exactly one entry, as before 5. Their spend dashboards and budgets now move by that batch's cost once, matching the single entry they can see 6. If a replica dies while it is working out that batch's cost, another replica picks the batch up on a later cycle and charges it once, instead of the batch being silently dropped An earlier revision of this description claimed the admin would see two spend entries on the logs page. That was wrong, and the capture below shows why: `LiteLLM_SpendLogs.request_id` is the table's primary key, the poller stamps it with the batch's unified object id, and the flush writes with `create_many(..., skip_duplicates=True)`, so the second row is dropped by the database. Only the aggregates move twice. ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-4827 ## Review notes The claim is a compare-and-swap on `batch_processed`, and where it sits in the poll cycle matters as much as the swap itself. That column does three jobs at once: it is the poller's own "already costed" filter, it is what the managed-files deletion guard reads to decide whether a file is still needed, and it is the terminal state a costed batch ends in. Setting it before the results fetch would do two harmful things beyond winning the row. A pod killed between the claim and the spend log would leave the batch marked processed but unbilled, and no later cycle would ever select it again, so that batch's spend would be lost for good. A delete on the batch's input or output file arriving during the fetch would find no referencing batch and go through, taking away the very file the fetch was reading Claiming immediately before the spend log write avoids both. The row stays unprocessed for the whole retrieve, so the deletion guard keeps holding the files, and an interruption anywhere up to that point simply leaves the batch for the next cycle. The cost is that two pods can both fetch and price the same batch in one window, but only the compare-and-swap winner writes a spend log, and that duplicated read is cheap next to charging a customer twice What is left is the gap between the claim and the spend log itself. It is one statement wide and moving the claim cannot close it, because spend logs are queued in memory and flushed in the background, so a hard kill in that window drops the log whether or not the row was claimed first. Trading it for a lease another pod could reclaim would turn the failure mode into a double charge rather than a missed one, which is the bug this PR exists to remove What this fix protects is the aggregated spend. The spend log row was already protected, because the poller stamps a deterministic `request_id` and the table's primary key rejects the duplicate. So before this change the system had half a safety net, and the half it had is the half an operator looks at ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v` - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup: one Postgres carrying the repo schema, and one managed batch created end to end through the proxy's own endpoints rather than inserted by hand, so the row under test is the one the product writes. ``` $ curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4828/v1/files -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-lit4827" \ -F purpose=batch -F target_model_names=openai-batch -F file=@batch_input.jsonl {"id":"bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTphcHBsaWNhdGlvbi9qc29ubDt1bmlmaWVkX2lkLDE1NmIyMmU1...","object":"file",...} $ curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4828/v1/batches -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-lit4827" \ -d '{"input_file_id":"<that id>","endpoint":"/v1/chat/completions","completion_window":"24h","model":"openai-batch"}' {"id":"bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9pZDphOWU0NDJkZGYwOGQ0NDgzNDAxN2UwNDg2MGU0NWVlZDUzMmM1ZmRhNmU4NjE5YTg4OWIzNDY0ZjQ0ZWU5YjdmO2xsbV9iYXRjaF9pZDpiYXRjaF9saXQ0ODI3",...} $ psql -c 'SELECT id, status, batch_processed FROM "LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable";' id | status | batch_processed --------------------------------------+------------+----------------- ec08f5f4-3c35-4d6b-9a1d-7dbbd007abe1 | validating | f ``` Each leg then runs TWO real proxy pods against that one database, on 4828 and 4830, with `proxy_batch_polling_interval: 15`. Each leg asserts before it opens its window, and again before it closes, that the process holding each port is the pid that leg spawned and that its command line names the tree under test, that both pods are still alive, and that the tree on the import path is the intended one: ``` identity at open port 4828: pid 84525 running before_tree identity at open port 4830: pid 84527 running before_tree liveness before the window: 2/2 pollers alive check_batch_cost -> .../before_tree/enterprise/litellm_enterprise/proxy/common_utils/check_batch_cost.py has _claim_job_for_costing: False ``` The measured quantity is `LiteLLM_DailyUserSpend`, which is what the spend dashboards and budget checks read. The `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` row count is shown alongside it deliberately, to make the point that it cannot measure this: its primary key pins it to 1 whether the batch was billed once or twice. ### Before (d556fac56b) #### two pods poll the same completed batch in one window 1. Both pods select the batch and both run the costing path ``` pod A billed: 1 claim-lost: 0 pod B billed: 1 claim-lost: 0 ``` 2. The aggregate the dashboards read counts the batch twice, at twice its token count and cost, while the logs table holds a single row ``` $ psql -c 'SELECT model, api_requests, spend, prompt_tokens FROM "LiteLLM_DailyUserSpend";' model | api_requests | spend | prompt_tokens -------------+--------------+---------+--------------- gpt-4o-mini | 2 | 0.00045 | 2000 $ psql -c 'SELECT count(*) AS spend_rows, sum(spend) FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" WHERE call_type='"'"'aretrieve_batch'"'"';' spend_rows | total_spend ------------+------------- 1 | 0.000225 ``` ### After (1481a8817d) #### two pods poll the same completed batch in one window 1. Both pods select the batch and both fetch its results, and the one that loses the compare-and-swap stops without billing ``` pod A billed: 1 claim-lost: 1 pod B billed: 1 claim-lost: 0 ``` 2. The aggregate counts the batch once, matching the single row in the logs table ``` $ psql -c 'SELECT model, api_requests, spend, prompt_tokens FROM "LiteLLM_DailyUserSpend";' model | api_requests | spend | prompt_tokens -------------+--------------+----------+--------------- gpt-4o-mini | 1 | 0.000225 | 1000 $ psql -c 'SELECT count(*) AS spend_rows, sum(spend) FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" WHERE call_type='"'"'aretrieve_batch'"'"';' spend_rows | total_spend ------------+------------- 1 | 0.000225 ``` ### Why the claim sits after the results fetch, not before it Claiming before the fetch is the obvious fix and it also stops the double count, so neither leg above can tell the two apart: both read 1. The difference only appears when a pod dies while costing. These two legs run the same interruption against a variant that claims before the results fetch and against this PR, SIGKILLing the pod 10 seconds into a 75 second results fetch. #### claiming before the results fetch 1. The row is already marked processed while the results are still being fetched, so the kill lands after the claim ``` pod A entered the results fetch at 32s; interrupting it 10s into a 75s fetch row at the instant of the kill: batch_processed=t pod A SIGKILLed mid results-fetch ``` 2. Another pod polls for 200 seconds and never sees the batch again, because the poll query filters on `batch_processed = false`. The batch is marked done, was never billed, and no pod will ever pick it up ``` survivor billed: 0 $ psql -c 'SELECT model, api_requests, spend FROM "LiteLLM_DailyUserSpend";' (0 rows) $ psql -c 'SELECT id, status, batch_processed FROM "LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable";' id | status | batch_processed --------------------------------------+-------------+----------------- ec08f5f4-3c35-4d6b-9a1d-7dbbd007abe1 | in_progress | t ``` #### claiming after the results fetch (this PR) 1. The row is still unclaimed while the results are being fetched, so the same kill lands before any claim ``` pod A entered the results fetch at 44s; interrupting it 10s into a 75s fetch row at the instant of the kill: batch_processed=f pod A SIGKILLed mid results-fetch ``` 2. Another pod picks the batch up on its next cycle and charges it exactly once ``` survivor billed: 1 $ psql -c 'SELECT model, api_requests, spend, prompt_tokens FROM "LiteLLM_DailyUserSpend";' model | api_requests | spend | prompt_tokens -------------+--------------+----------+--------------- gpt-4o-mini | 1 | 0.000225 | 1000 $ psql -c 'SELECT id, status, batch_processed FROM "LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable";' id | status | batch_processed --------------------------------------+----------+----------------- ec08f5f4-3c35-4d6b-9a1d-7dbbd007abe1 | complete | t ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - The provider is a local stand-in, since a batch's completion window is 24h - Everything else above is live: two real proxies, one real Postgres - Both pods fetch results in a window; only one bills - Schemas lacking `batch_processed` keep old unclaimed behavior - The poller's deterministic `request_id` is deliberate, for correlating a spend row back to the submitted batch. Randomising it to avoid the primary-key collision would break that correlation - Aggregated spend has no idempotency key where spend logs do; that gap is wider than this PR ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/2386b54878924291841e76da29322c9c Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signal.title: fix(a2a): return SSE (text/event-stream) for message/stream instead of NDJSON
signal.text:
## TLDR Problem this solves: - A2A `message/stream` returned `application/x-ndjson` - Official a2a-sdk client rejects that and raises `SSEError` - Guardrail stream errors were serialized twice, arriving as strings How it solves it: - Emit `text/event-stream` with `data: <json>

` framing - Matches the SSE path already used by `tasks/resubscribe` - Guardrails yield error objects; the endpoint owns serialization ## User Flow Before: a developer using the official a2a-sdk client cannot stream from an agent behind the gateway; the call dies before the first event is read 1. They point the SDK client at `https://litellm-domain/a2a/my-agent` and call the streaming send with `Accept: text/event-stream` 2. The gateway answers `200` with `content-type: application/x-ndjson` and bare JSON-RPC objects, one per line 3. The SDK raises `SSEError` complaining the content type is not `text/event-stream`, so no Task, StatusUpdate or Message event is ever surfaced to their app 4. If a guardrail blocks the stream halfway, whatever the client does receive is a quoted JSON string rather than a JSON-RPC error, so the rejection reads as unparseable output instead of a refusal After: the same client streams the agent's events incrementally and sees blocks as real JSON-RPC errors 1. They point the SDK client at `https://litellm-domain/a2a/my-agent` and call the streaming send with `Accept: text/event-stream` 2. The gateway answers `200` with `content-type: text/event-stream; charset=utf-8` and one `data: {...}` line per event, each terminated by a blank line 3. The SDK yields Task, StatusUpdate and Message events as they arrive; with `A2A-Version: 1.0` the events carry 1.0 envelopes (`task`/`statusUpdate`/`message`, `ROLE_AGENT`) 4. signal.title: [Bug]: A2A 1.0 SendStreamingMessage still returns NDJSON instead of SSE in v1.93.0
signal.text:
### Check for existing issues - [x] I searched existing issues. - [x] This is a follow-up/regression report for #20278. PR #20365 fixed the issue, but PR #20446 reverted that fix. The problem is still reproducible in LiteLLM 1.93.0. ### What happened? LiteLLM's A2A JSON-RPC proxy returns `SendStreamingMessage` responses as newline-delimited JSON: ```http HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: application/x-ndjson ``` The response body contains multiple complete JSON-RPC objects separated by `
`: ```text {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"...","result":{"task":{...}}} {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"...","result":{"statusUpdate":{...}}} {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"...","result":{"artifactUpdate":{...}}} {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"...","result":{"statusUpdate":{...}}} ``` For the A2A 1.0 JSON-RPC binding, the official `a2a-sdk` client requests `text/event-stream` and expects SSE framing. Because LiteLLM returns NDJSON, the SDK treats the entire non-SSE body as one response and cannot parse multiple JSON-RPC objects as one event. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Register an A2A 1.0 agent that supports streaming. 2. Send this request through LiteLLM: ```bash curl --no-buffer --location 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/a2a/my-agent' \ --header 'Authorization: Bearer <LITELLM_API_KEY>' \ --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --header 'Accept: text/event-stream' \ --header 'A2A-Version: 1.0' \ --data '{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": "a2a-stream-test", "method": "SendStreamingMessage", "params": { "message": { "messageId": "msg-stream-test", "role": "ROLE_USER", "parts": [{"text": "Hello streaming"}] } } }' ``` 3. Observe `Content-Type: application/x-ndjson` and bare JSON lines. 4. Run the same call with the official Python `a2a-sdk` JSON-RPC client and observe that the multi-object response is not consumable as SSE events. ### Expected behavior LiteLLM should return: ```http Content-Type: text/event-stream ``` with each JSON-RPC response framed as an SSE event: ```text data: {"jsonrpc":"2.0",...} data: {"jsonrpc":"2.0",...} ``` This lets unmodified A2A clients receive Task, StatusUpdate, and ArtifactUpdate events incrementally. ### Environment - LiteLLM: `1.93.0` - Official image: `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-stable` - Image digest: `sha256:a1745e629abfb17d434426ff48b115f54f4f4a0f5af241de569e93c63c411e` - A2A Python SDK: `1.1.2` - A2A protocol version: `1.0` - Deployment: Docker ### Additional context The current implementation still returns: ```python StreamingResponse(stream_response(), media_type="application/x-ndjson") ``` A local compatibility build that only changes the media type to `text/event-stream` and wraps each complete JSON-RPC line as `data: <json>

` successfully produced incremental SSE events and worked through the standard A2A parsing path. Could the SSE fix and tests from #20365 be restored, or could the reason for the revert in #20446 be documented so a protocol-compatible alternative can be implemented?
