signal.title: fix: omit thinking.type=disabled for always-on thinking Claude models
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}` forwarded verbatim to Fable/Mythos models - those models 400: "thinking.type.disabled is not supported for this model" - routers retargeting requests across model generations hit this constantly How it solves it: - new cost map flag `thinking_always_on` on Fable/Mythos entries - Anthropic, /v1/messages, and Bedrock Converse transforms omit the param when flagged - omission is the API documented remedy; model thinks adaptively by default ## User Flow Before: a caller whose request was valid on Claude Sonnet 4.5 gets a 400 when a router sends the same request to Claude Fable 5 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages with `"model": "claude-fable-5"`, `"thinking": {"type": "disabled"}` 2. The response is a 400 with `"thinking.type.disabled" is not supported for this model. Thinking defaults to adaptive mode when not specified` 3. The same body against a router model group fails the whole request whenever the router picks a Fable 5 deployment, even though the request was valid on the model the caller originally targeted After: the same request succeeds; the model thinks adaptively as the API prescribes 1. They send the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages with `"model": "claude-fable-5"`, `"thinking": {"type": "disabled"}` 2. The response is a 200 with the model's normal content; the gateway omitted the unsupported param and logged a warning 3. Requests carrying `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}` to models that accept it (Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.8, Opus 5, Sonnet 5) are forwarded byte for byte, unchanged ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Setup: local proxy on :4620 from this branch, `LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True`, real Postgres, models `claude-fable-5` and `claude-sonnet-4-5` served through a live Anthropic-compatible upstream (real provider account for this repo is out of credit; the upstream is the team's live gateway hitting the real Anthropic API, so requests, money, and the 400 are real). Config: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: claude-fable-5 litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-fable-5 api_base: https://<gateway-host> api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN - model_name: claude-sonnet-4-5 litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 api_base: https://<gateway-host> api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN general_settings: master_key: sk-1234 ``` ### Before (4bb3152cc5) #### /v1/messages, claude-fable-5, thinking disabled 1. `curl -s -w "HTTP %{http_code}" -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4620/v1/messages -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"model":"claude-fable-5","max_tokens":64,"thinking":{"type":"disabled"},"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"say hi repro leg 1"}]}'` 2. `HTTP 400` with `"\"thinking.type.disabled\" is not supported for this model. Thinking defaults to adaptive mode when not specified; use \"thinking.type.enabled\" with \"budget_tokens\" for extended thinking"` #### /v1/chat/completions, claude-fable-5, thinking disabled 1. Same body against http://127.0.0.1:4620/v1/chat/completions 2. `HTTP 400`, `litellm.BadRequestError: AnthropicException` wrapping the same provider error #### /v1/messages, claude-sonnet-4-5, thinking disabled (negative control) 1. Same body with `"model": "claude-sonnet-4-5"` 2. `HTTP 200`, normal text content (this model accepts disabled) ### After (1eb90f3d0a) #### /v1/messages, claude-fable-5, thinking disabled 1. Same curl as Before 2. `HTTP 200`, content starts with an adaptive thinking block then text; proxy log shows `Dropping thinking={'type': 'disabled'} for model=claude-fable-5: thinking is always on for this model and cannot be disabled. The model thinks adaptively when the param is omitted.` #### /v1/chat/completions, claude-fable-5, thinking disabled 1. Same curl as Before (max_tokens 2048 so text survives the thinking budget) 2. `HTTP 200`, `content: "Hi! ..."`, `model: claude-fable-5` #### /v1/messages, claude-sonnet-4-5, thinking disabled (negative control) 1. Same curl as Before 2. `HTTP 200`, normal text content, request body forwarded unchanged (no warning logged) ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Bedrock Converse arm covered by unit tests only; no AWS credentials in this rig - /v1/responses already converts `thinking` to `reasoning`, never forwards disabled - Opus 5 `disabled` plus `output_config.effort xhigh/max` is a caller contradiction, untouched - unmapped future Fable/Mythos ids covered by a `fallback_generalizations` rule ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Changes Anthropic/Bedrock request transforms and model capability metadata. Scope is narrow (only drops `thinking.type=disabled` for flagged models) but incorrect flagging would silently change thinking behavior. > > **Overview** > Stops Fable/Mythos (and unmapped family ids) from 400ing when a caller or router forwards `thinking={"type": "disabled"}`. Those models reject disabled thinking; omitting the param is the documented fallback to adaptive thinking. > > Adds a cost-map flag `thinking_always_on` on Fable/Mythos entries plus a `claude-always-on-thinking` fallback rule. Chat, `/v1/messages`, and Bedrock Converse transforms drop only that disabled shape for flagged models and leave it unchanged for models that accept it (e.g. Opus/Sonnet 5). Also hoists the duplicated `local_model_cost_map` pytest fixture into shared conftest. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 1eb90f3d0aed662f88d8138b4a317b0e599a5abb. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: test(e2e): pin query params and multipart form fields as replay match-key identity
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Replay match key ignored query params and form fields - Dropping either from canonicalize() left all 92 tests green - Two requests differing only there share one replay pool How it solves it: - Adds two identity tests to TestKeyDistinctness - Each is mutation-proved: it fails when its field is dropped ## User Flow The end user here is someone running the e2e suite in replay mode, since this is harness coverage Before: a developer records a bundle, then replays it, and one test silently asserts against a different request's response 1. They run the suite with `E2E_FIXTURE_MODE=record`, hitting `GET /v1/vector_stores?limit=100` and `GET /v1/vector_stores?limit=10` 2. Both interactions land in the bundle under the same match key, because the query string is not part of it 3. They re-run with `E2E_FIXTURE_MODE=replay`; the two calls pop each other's recorded response FIFO 4. The test asserting on the 10-item page reads the 100-item body and passes anyway, so a real behavior change never surfaces After: the same two calls keep separate identities 1. They record the same bundle 2. The two interactions land under distinct match keys 3. Replay serves each call its own recorded response 4. A genuine drift now fails with a `ReplayMiss` naming the computed key instead of passing on the wrong body ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5890 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix These are markerless harness tests over pure functions, so there is no proxy route or LLM call to curl. The evidence that matters for a coverage gap is whether the suite can tell the difference, so both sides below apply the same two mutations to `tests/e2e/fixture_canonical.py` Mutations used, one at a time: ``` "params": _canonical_flat(request.params), -> "params": {}, "form": None if request.form is None else _canonical_flat(request.form), -> "form": None, ``` Command, identical on both sides: ``` python -m pytest test_fixture_canonical.py test_fixture_transport.py test_fixture_bundle.py -q ``` ### Before (487356733c) #### params dropped from the key 1. Applied the params mutation 2. `92 passed in 1.25s` - the suite cannot tell #### form dropped from the key 1. Applied the form mutation 2. `92 passed in 1.10s` - the suite cannot tell ### After (80cb65502c) #### params dropped from the key 1. Applied the params mutation 2. `1 failed, 93 passed` - `TestKeyDistinctness::test_query_params_are_identity` #### form dropped from the key 1. Applied the form mutation 2. `1 failed, 93 passed` - `TestKeyDistinctness::test_form_fields_are_identity` #### unmutated 1. No mutation applied 2. `94 passed in 0.61s` Both mutations were reverted and `fixture_canonical.py` verified clean; only the test file changed `make lint-e2e-basedpyright`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes ## Type ✅ Test ## Caveats (if any) - Param values must survive canonicalization to prove anything - Two `/spend/logs` date ranges still collide; dates become `<date>` - No test pins that recording itself captures params or form ## QA runbook - tests/e2e/test_fixture_canonical.py::TestKeyDistinctness::test_query_params_are_identity - two GETs to one path differing only in the query string get different replay match keys - [ ] In `tests/e2e`, open a python shell and build two `RecordedRequest`s for `get /v1/vector_stores`, one with `params={"limit": "100"}` and one with `params={"limit": "10"}` - [ ] Call `canonicalize(...).key` on each and expect the two keys to differ - [ ] Edit `fixture_canonical.py` to set `"params": {}`, re-run the test, and expect it to fail; revert - [ ] Sanity check: this test makes sense to add and is not hand-wavey or potentially flaky - tests/e2e/test_fixture_canonical.py::TestKeyDistinctness::test_form_fields_are_identity - two uploads of identical bytes differing only in a multipart form field get different replay match keys - [ ] Build two `RecordedRequest`s for `upload /v1/files` with the same `file_sha256`, one `form={"purpose": "assistants"}` and one `form={"purpose": "batch"}` - [ ] Call `canonicalize(...).key` on each and expect the two keys to differ - [ ] Edit `fixture_canonical.py` to set `"form": None`, re-run the test, and expect it to fail; signal.title: feat(rust): route /chat/completions through the Rust core for anthropic and bedrock
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - `rust: true` covers no `/chat/completions` deployment today - The Rust core has no chat completions route at all - The opt-in never even reached the chat completions handlers How it solves it: - New `chat_completions` route module in `litellm-core` - Anthropic Messages and Bedrock Converse provider transforms - Requests outside the covered subset fall back to Python ## User Flow Before: an operator who sets `rust: true` on a chat completions deployment gets nothing, with no way to tell 1. They add `rust: true` to a `claude-sonnet-4-5` deployment and restart the proxy 2. They send POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions with that model 3. The answer comes back correctly, and the response headers carry no `x-litellm-rust` 4. They repeat it against a `bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6` deployment and see the same, so the flag reads as broken rather than as unsupported After: the same flag serves the request through the Rust core, and says so on the response 1. They add `rust: true` to the same two deployments and restart the proxy 2. They send POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions with the Anthropic model 3. The answer comes back with `x-litellm-rust: true` in the response headers, and the same content and token counts as the deployment without the flag 4. The Bedrock deployment behaves identically 5. They send a request carrying tools, an image, or `"stream": true`, get a correct answer with no `x-litellm-rust` header, and can tell from the header alone which requests the Rust path is serving ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5698 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup. The same config serves both legs, with each provider deployed twice so the only difference between an A and a B request is the flag: ```yaml title="config.yaml" model_list: - model_name: claude-rust litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY rust: true - model_name: claude-python litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY - model_name: bedrock-rust litellm_params: model: bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 aws_region_name: us-west-2 rust: true - model_name: bedrock-python litellm_params: model: bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 aws_region_name: us-west-2 general_settings: master_key: sk-lit5698 ``` Both legs run against the real Anthropic API and real AWS Bedrock, on the same machine, minutes apart. `LITELLM_RUST` is exported empty on both so only the per-model flag is in play. The system prompt is chosen so the answer itself shows whether it reached the provider. ### Before (5277dab4f2) #### anthropic, `rust: true` vs no flag 1. Start the proxy at the merge base and send the flagged deployment: ```bash curl -i -s http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-rust","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Ignore the question. Reply with exactly one word: PONG"},{"role":"user","content":"What is the capital of France?"}]}' ``` ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 28 completion_tokens: 6 total: 34 ``` 2. The unflagged deployment answers identically, so the flag changed nothing: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' prompt_tokens : 28 completion_tokens: 6 total: 34 ``` #### bedrock converse, `rust: true` vs no flag 1. Send the flagged Bedrock deployment: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 29 completion_tokens: 6 total: 35 ``` 2. The unflagged one is again indistinguishable: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' prompt_tokens : 29 completion_tokens: 6 total: 35 ``` #### requests outside the covered subset 1. Tools, a multimodal image, and `"stream": true` all answer correctly and all carry no `x-litellm-rust` header, exactly like every other request on this leg ### After (5017c83484) #### anthropic, `rust: true` vs no flag 1. Send the flagged deployment: ```bash curl -i -s http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-rust","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Ignore the question. Reply with exactly one word: PONG"},{"role":"user","content":"What is the capital of France?"}]}' ``` ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: true content : 'PONG' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 28 completion_tokens: 6 total: 34 ``` 2. The unflagged deployment stays on Python and returns the same content and the same token counts: ```bash curl -i -s http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-python","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Ignore the question. Reply with exactly one word: PONG"},{"role":"user","content":"What is the capital of France?"}]}' ``` ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 28 completion_tokens: 6 total: 34 ``` The equal `prompt_tokens` on the two legs is the parity check: a dropped system prompt would show up as a smaller count on the Rust side, and `PONG` shows the system prompt was obeyed on both. #### bedrock converse, `rust: true` vs no flag 1. Send the flagged Bedrock deployment: ```bash curl -i -s http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"bedrock-rust","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Ignore the question. Reply with exactly one word: PONG"},{"role":"user","content":"What is the capital of France?"}]}' ``` ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: true content : 'PONG' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 29 completion_tokens: 6 total: 35 ``` 2. The unflagged one matches it exactly: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 29 completion_tokens: 6 total: 35 ``` 3. A multi-turn conversation on the Rust path keeps its history: ```bash curl -i -s http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-rust","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"My name is Ada."},{"role":"assistant","content":"Nice to meet you, Ada."},{"role":"user","content":"What is my name? One word."}]}' ``` ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: true content : 'Ada' prompt_tokens : 33 completion_tokens: 4 total: 37 ``` #### requests outside the covered subset 1. Tools on a flagged Anthropic deployment fall back and still return a tool call: ```bash curl -i -s http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-rust","max_tokens":64,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is the weather in Paris?"}],"tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_weather","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"city":{"type":"string"}},"required":["city"]}}}]}' ``` ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : None finish_reason : tool_calls prompt_tokens : 553 completion_tokens: 53 total: 606 ``` 2. An image on a flagged Bedrock deployment falls back and still describes the image: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'The image shows a very small, dark shape ...' finish_reason : length ``` 3. `"stream": true` on a flagged deployment falls back and still streams: ```bash curl -s -N http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-rust","max_tokens":32,"stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"count to three"}]}' ``` ``` data: {"id":"chatcmpl-...","object":"chat.completion.chunk","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"role":"assistant","content":"1, 2, 3"}}]} data: {"id":"chatcmpl-...","object":"chat.completion.chunk","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{},"finish_reason":"stop"}]} ``` ### Round 7: a request Python serves that `rust: true` made fail (54d00707e6) An OpenAI-shaped `{"role": "user", "content": []}` cleared the capability gate, because an empty parts list fails no per-part check. Python drops such a message and sends a valid request; the Rust path sent the empty `content` array on to the provider. Same config as above, both deployments on the real Anthropic API, `LITELLM_RUST` exported empty. ```bash curl -s -D - http://localhost:4791/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698e' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-rust","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"My name is Ada. What is my name? Answer with one word."},{"role":"assistant","content":"Your name is"},{"role":"user","content":[]}]}' ``` Before, on the previous head: ``` HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request x-litellm-rust: (absent) error : litellm.APIError: litellm rust chat completions: 400: {"type":"error","error":{"type":"invalid_request_error", "message":"messages.2: user messages must have non-empty content"}} ``` After: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : ' Ada.' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 25 completion_tokens: 5 ``` Two controls ran in the same window on both legs. The unflagged `claude-python` deployment answered that identical body with `' Ada.'` at 25 and 5 tokens on both legs, which is what the flagged deployment now matches exactly. A plain text request on `claude-rust` returned `x-litellm-rust: true` and `'PONG'` on both legs, so the Rust path was live throughout and the fix narrows the gate rather than turning it off. ### Round 8: the configured Bedrock identity the Rust path was replacing (a76b698e84) Python reads a Bedrock deployment's `api_key` as a bearer token and signs SigV4 only when neither it nor `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK` is set. The Rust config discarded `api_key` and always signed SigV4, so a deployment carrying a bearer identity was billed and rate-limited against whatever principal the host's AWS credentials resolve to. This leg needs no AWS account. The deployment points at a stub Converse endpoint that records the `Authorization` header it is handed, and the host is given ambient AWS credentials so the capture reproduces the exact condition the finding names. ```yaml title="config.yaml" model_list: - model_name: bedrock-rust-bearer litellm_params: model: bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 api_base: http://127.0.0.1:4793/model/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6/converse api_key: bedrock-api-key-abc123 aws_region_name: us-west-2 rust: true ``` ```bash export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAHOSTPRINCIPAL000 export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=hostsecret... curl -s -D - http://localhost:4794/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698e' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"bedrock-rust-bearer","max_tokens":16,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"say pong"}]}' ``` Before, on the previous head: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: true upstream received: authorization : AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 Credential=AKIAHOSTPRINCIPAL000/20260820/us-west-2/bedrock/aws4_request, SignedHeaders=conten... x-amz-date : 20260820T031037Z ``` After: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: true upstream received: authorization : Bearer bedrock-api-key-abc123 x-amz-date : None ``` Both legs carry `x-litellm-rust: true`, so the Rust core served both and the signing identity is the only variable. The host principal appears by name in the before leg, which is what the configured bearer identity was being replaced with. ### Round 15: the Bedrock attribution the gate was not declining (4d8190c54d) `AmazonConverseConfig` resolves proxy-owned `requestMetadata` onto the Converse body out of `litellm_params`, which the core never sees. A Bedrock deployment carrying `rust: true` under an operator who armed `bedrock_request_metadata_fields` therefore reached AWS with the tenant dimension silently missing. This leg needs no AWS account either. The same stub Converse endpoint now also records the body it was handed. ```yaml title="config.yaml" model_list: - model_name: bedrock-rust-bearer litellm_params: model: bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 api_base: http://127.0.0.1:47981/model/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6/converse api_key: bedrock-api-key-abc123 aws_region_name: us-west-2 rust: true litellm_settings: bedrock_request_metadata_fields: - user_api_key_team_id - spend_logs_metadata ``` ```bash curl -s -D - http://localhost:47982/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698r15' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"bedrock-rust-bearer","max_tokens":16,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"say pong"}],"metadata":{"spend_logs_metadata":{"tenant":"tenant-a"}}}' ``` Before, on the previous head: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: true content : 'PONG' upstream received: requestMetadata on the Converse body: None ``` After: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' upstream received: requestMetadata on the Converse body: {'tenant': 'tenant-a'} ``` The identical request with the setting removed still comes back `x-litellm-rust: true`, so the decline follows the operator's opt-in rather than the provider, and the request is served on both configurations. Both legs also re-confirm round 8 at this head: the upstream sees `authorization: Bearer bedrock-api-key-abc123` and no `x-amz-date`, so the configured bearer is still the identity that signs. ### The live Anthropic leg, re-run at this head (4d8190c54d) Rounds 9 to 15 landed after the After capture above, so the headline A/B was re-run against the real Anthropic API on the current commit, same config, same prompt: ``` flagged (claude-rust) 200 x-litellm-rust: true 'PONG' 28 / 6 / 34 unflagged (claude-python) 200 x-litellm-rust: (absent) 'PONG' 28 / 6 / 34 flagged + tools 200 x-litellm-rust: (absent) answered on the Python path ``` ### The live Bedrock leg, re-run against real AWS at this head (4d8190c54d) The stub legs above prove which identity signs and which requests decline, but they cannot prove AWS accepts the signature: rounds 9, 11 and 13 all changed which headers are signed and which credential wins, and a signature AWS rejects comes back 403 rather than 200. So the Bedrock A/B was re-run against real Bedrock Converse, `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6` in `us-west-2`, on the current commit. ```bash curl -s -D - http://localhost:47987/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698live' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"bedrock-rust","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Ignore the question. Reply with exactly one word: PONG"},{"role":"user","content":"What is the capital of France?"}]}' ``` With `bedrock_request_metadata_fields` unset: ``` flagged (bedrock-rust) 200 x-litellm-rust: true 'PONG' 29 / 6 / 35 unflagged (bedrock-python) 200 x-litellm-rust: (absent) 'PONG' 29 / 6 / 35 ``` The same config with the setting armed, which is round 15 against real AWS rather than the stub: ``` flagged (bedrock-rust) 200 x-litellm-rust: (absent) 'PONG' 29 / 6 / 35 unflagged (bedrock-python) 200 x-litellm-rust: (absent) 'PONG' 29 / 6 / 35 ``` Three things this leg establishes that the stub cannot. Real AWS accepted the SigV4 signature the round 9 and round 11 filtering produces, so the signed-header subset is right rather than merely self-consistent. The token counts are identical across both paths, which exercises the round 14 `totalTokens` passthrough on a genuine Converse response instead of a fixture. And the armed leg returns 200 with the attribution on the wire, so declining to Python leaves a working request rather than trading one defect for another; Bedrock rejects malformed `requestMetadata` with a 400, so the 200 is the assertion. ### Round 16: the auth header the Rust path was adding back (4d8190c54d) Anthropic's `validate_environment` settles the auth shape before the gate is asked, and for an OAuth deployment key it pops `x-api-key` and sets `authorization` instead. The core's `Header` auth arm added `x-api-key` back whenever it was absent, so the Rust path put the credential into the very header Python had removed. Same stub upstream, recording the auth headers it is handed. No real Anthropic account needed, and the deployment key is a fake OAuth-shaped token: ```yaml title="config.yaml" model_list: - model_name: custom-rust litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 api_base: http://127.0.0.1:47984 api_key: sk-ant-oat01-stub-oauth-token rust: true - model_name: custom-python litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 api_base: http://127.0.0.1:47984 api_key: sk-ant-oat01-stub-oauth-token ``` Before, on the previous head: ``` custom-python 200 x-litellm-rust: (absent) auth headers on the wire : ['authorization'] custom-rust 200 x-litellm-rust: true auth headers on the wire : ['authorization', 'x-api-key'] x-api-key : sk-ant-oat01-stub-oauth-token ``` After: ``` custom-python 200 x-litellm-rust: (absent) auth headers on the wire : ['authorization'] custom-rust 200 x-litellm-rust: true auth headers on the wire : ['authorization'] x-api-key : None ``` The Rust leg still carries `x-litellm-rust: true`, so the core served both captures and the header set is the only variable. ### Round 17: whose credential the Rust path authenticates with (4d8190c54d) veria filed that a caller-supplied `extra_headers.X-Api-Key` outranked the deployment's resolved credential on the Rust path, so whoever sends the request could choose the Anthropic principal it bills to. Python's rule, measured across every case rather than read, is that the deployment credential always wins and `x-api-key` is dropped only for OAuth: ``` x-api-key authorization 1 normal key, no caller headers 'sk-ant-deploy' None 2 normal key + caller x-api-key 'sk-ant-deploy' None 3 OAuth deployment key None 'Bearer sk-ant-oat01-deploy' 4 normal key + unrelated authorization 'sk-ant-deploy' 'Bearer unrelated' 5 normal key + unrelated auth + caller x-api-key 'sk-ant-deploy' 'Bearer unrelated' 6 forwarded OAuth bearer, normal deploy key None 'Bearer sk-ant-oat01-fwd' ``` Live, with `forward_client_headers_to_llm_api: true` and a client sending `x-api-key: sk-ant-ATTACKER-CHOSEN` against a deployment holding `sk-ant-deployment-key`: ``` before custom-python 200 x-litellm-rust: (absent) x-api-key the provider saw: sk-ant-deployment-key custom-rust 200 x-litellm-rust: true x-api-key the provider saw: sk-ant-deployment-key after custom-python 200 x-litellm-rust: (absent) x-api-key the provider saw: sk-ant-deployment-key custom-rust 200 x-litellm-rust: true x-api-key the provider saw: sk-ant-deployment-key ``` Both legs already sent the deployment key, and that is the honest headline: through the litellm host the finding does not reproduce, because `validate_environment` builds `{**headers, **anthropic_headers}` and has already overwritten the forwarded value before the core is asked. It is still worth fixing, because the core's guarantee rested entirely on a distant caller having sanitized first, and `ai-gateway` calls the same entrypoint without running any of that. The three tests that pinned the old precedence asserted the caller's key survives, which made the defect read as deliberate. ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats - Non-streaming only; streaming falls back to Python - Text conversations only; tools and images fall back - Bedrock covers the `converse` route, not `invoke` - A response block the core cannot read is surfaced, not retried, since the provider has already billed it - Rust pre-call logging records the request before translation - An `extra_headers` value the bridge cannot serialize raises instead of declining, and Python rejects the same value at its own header encoding, so no request Python would have served is lost to it - `cargo clippy --features server` on `ai-gateway` is red on pre-existing `realtime` lints CI does not run - Rust `post_call` carries the core's normalized response, not the provider's wire body - `rust` is a deployment setting, refused in a proxy request body - Follow-ups: tools LIT-5715, streaming LIT-5716 - Docs: BerriAI/litellm-docs#923, merge that after this ## Review notes Scope of the Rust path, and why it is drawn there. Acceptance is an allowlist rather than a denylist, so a parameter or message shape the core has never seen declines by construction instead of being translated wrong. `chat_completions_decline_reason` answers that question with no credential resolution and no I/O, which is what lets the caller emit its pre-call logging exactly once on whichever path is about to run. Covered today: system, user and assistant turns whose content is a string or all-text parts, plus the sampling parameters each provider maps. Everything else declines, including tool calls, tool results, images, extended thinking, `response_format`, prompt caching, and `top_k` on either provider, which Python routes by base model through a model catalog the core cannot read. Parity is pinned rather than asserted. The shared conversation builder mirrors Python's `anthropic_messages_pt` for the surface it accepts: consecutive same-role turns merge, the final assistant turn is right-stripped, and empty text becomes the same placeholder Python substitutes. Converse diverges on both of those, so the Bedrock config declines blank text and any conversation that opens or closes on an assistant turn, which makes both divergences unreachable rather than papered over. `usage` folds cache tokens into `prompt_tokens` and reports the same `prompt_tokens_details` split Python does, so cost tracking agrees either way. The response deliberately carries no `id`, so the `chatcmpl-` id LiteLLM already minted survives. Bedrock signs with the credentials the Python handler already resolved, handed down through `optional_params`, rather than re-deriving them. Without that, an unrelated `AWS_ROLE_NAME` or `AWS_PROFILE_NAME` in the environment outranks explicit keys during classification and the two paths would sign as different principals. The Converse URL Python built is passed through untouched for the same reason, since Python encodes the model id itself. Two plumbing fixes were needed for the flag to work at all, both found on a live proxy rather than by reading. `rust` was absent from the key set `completion()` forwards into `get_litellm_params`, so the opt-in never reached the chat completions handlers and the gate was never consulted. Registering it as a litellm param elsewhere keeps it out of the provider body; this keeps it in `litellm_params`, where the handlers read it. Review round 1 found that a Rust failure re-entered the Python path after pre-call logging had already run, so callbacks fired twice for one request. The fix went at the root rather than at the symptom, because the same re-entry also re-issued the provider call and billed the customer twice for work already done. The bridge now separates the two cases: anything raised before the request goes out declines and the host serves it on Python, while a failure after it is surfaced as an `APIError` carrying the upstream status, which LiteLLM's exception mapping already understands. Since a decline is the same attempt continuing rather than a second one, the fallback no longer re-logs pre_call, so exactly one fires per request either way. Review round 2 caught the hole that fix left: a config reports the same error variants on either side of the provider call, so a response the core could not normalize (`MissingField`, or an unsupported content block) was being classed as a pre-send decline and retried. The handler now re-tags every error raised while normalizing a response the provider already answered, so the retryable set can only contain failures raised before the request went out. Round-trip tests drive a stub upstream and assert exactly that: a body missing `usage`, a body carrying a `tool_use` block, and a 429 all come back as errors the host will not retry, while a well-formed body round-trips. The route-owned `client.rs` was also flagged, and it is kept deliberately. It is part of the documented route template: `litellm-rust/ADDING_A_PROVIDER.md` and `crates/core/CLAUDE.md` both list `client.rs` as one of a route module's files, and `crates/core/src/messages/client.rs` is the reference implementation this mirrors. The core cannot reach LiteLLM's Python HTTP handler, which lives in the host; `core/CLAUDE.md` puts serving and transport concerns outside the core on purpose. It follows the workspace's Network I/O rules: one client behind a `OnceLock` rather than one per request, with both a connect and a full-request timeout, and rustls. Round 3 found the same lifecycle defect on the synchronous Anthropic path, which the earlier fix had only closed for the async one. It is closed the same way and pinned by three mutation checks, including one that the ordinary path still logs, so the suppression cannot swallow a log it was never meant to. Every invariant above is pinned by a mutation check: 39 mutants, 39 killed. Round 4 took the veria finding that the opt-in was request-controlled. `rust` is a litellm param, `route_llm_request` splats a proxy request body straight into the router, and the gate reads the merged `litellm_params`, so an authenticated caller could send `rust: true` and pick a transport and a callback surface the deployment never chose. A spy on the gate settled it rather than reading: driven with the kwarg it saw `litellm_params["rust"] is True`, and the control without it saw the key absent. The flag now sits in `_BANNED_REQUEST_BODY_PARAMS`, so it is a deployment decision again, liftable only by the same admin opt-in as the rest of that list, and covered under `extra_body` for free. The check runs in `pre_db_read_auth_checks`, so it also closes the same caller-controlled path on `/v1/messages`, where `_maybe_rust_anthropic_messages` has read this flag since before this PR: the same spy, driven through `litellm.anthropic_messages`, saw the caller's `rust=True` arrive there too. The responses-websocket route is not affected in either direction, since it builds its request body server-side and no caller field ever reached its gate. Deleting the entry fails three of the five new tests. One knock-on is worth naming rather than leaving to be found. `_config_base_for_health_check` reads the same list, and treats any banned param in a connection-test body as "this request describes its own connection", so it drops the configured credentials. A `/health/test_connection` body that echoes a Rust deployment's `litellm_params` verbatim now probes without them. No dashboard flow sends the field, and the Add Model wizard has no config base to drop from, so this reaches a hand-written caller only. Narrowing that set is the surgical fix if it ever bites; weakening the ban is not. The LIT002 count is resolved rather than argued, so `lint` is green. It counted twelve new dict literals. Ten of them the bridge JSON-encodes or logging callbacks consume as dicts, and `MappingProxyType` breaks both at runtime (`json.dumps` rejects a mappingproxy, and the response converter rewrites the dict it is handed), so those carry a `# mutable-ok` naming the reason: nine comments, since one line holds a nested literal. The last two went for real, by deleting the `rust_kwargs` bundles and passing the nine arguments by keyword instead. `**dict` unpacking is unchecked, so writing them out also drops twenty basedpyright errors across the three files. Round 5 is the same lifecycle defect once more, on the synchronous Bedrock path. Round 3 closed it for Anthropic by capturing the gate's answer and guarding the Python-path `pre_call` with it; Bedrock still called the gate inline, so nothing downstream could tell that the request had already been logged, and a synchronous call that the gate accepted and the core then declined logged twice. It is closed the same way, with the same comment explaining why the async branch does not need it. Two mutation checks, run separately: removing the guard fails the decline test, and inverting it also fails the control that an ordinary request with no opt-in still logs exactly once, so the suppression cannot swallow a log it was never meant to. Round 6 closed the second half of veria's original sentence, which the ban did not touch: the Rust path emitted no `post_call` at all. That is not conditional on who set the flag, so an operator's own `rust: true` lost it too, since `post_call` is raised inside the provider transform the core replaces. Measured rather than read: a `CustomLogger` on a Router deployment with `rust: true` and no request kwarg observed `['pre_api_call', 'success']` and no `post_api_call`, with the other two events as the positive control that the logger was wired and reachable. So `original_response` was unset on every Rust-served request, which OTel, Arize and two guardrail hooks read. The bridge now takes a `ResponseObserver` and calls it on success only, from both `chat_completions` and `achat_completions`, so the two paths cannot drift the way the pre_call suppression twice did. `response_logger` builds the observer, so the handlers share one implementation rather than each growing a closure, and hoisting it out of `completion` is also what keeps that function under the C901 ceiling. A decline never calls it, because the Python path that serves the request raises its own. Each hook site was mutated separately rather than both at once: dropping the synchronous one fails the two synchronous tests, dropping the asynchronous one fails only the asynchronous test, and the decline tests hold either way. The payload is the core's normalized response rather than the provider's wire body, which is the closest thing that crosses the bridge; the `/v1/messages` Rust route still has this gap and is out of scope here. Round 7 took the empty-content-parts finding, which is the one open bot finding that is a real defect. `unsupported_message` checked every part and therefore accepted a message with no parts at all, and Bedrock's blank-text scan skipped it for the same reason, so a request that Python serves fine came back 400 once the deployment carried the flag. The guard goes in the shared gate, so both providers get it from one place, and each provider's test file pins its own side with a positive control that a one-part text message still accepts. Removing the guard fails both tests. The other two open findings are answered rather than taken. The redundant-documentation one is partly right: the route's module header duplicated what `Unsupported`'s own doc comment in `transformation.rs` says, so that paragraph is deleted and only the entrypoint description remains, which is what `messages/mod.rs` carries for the reference route. The route-owned `client.rs` stays, and the honest version of that argument is not a claim about tunability. The two core clients hold identical values today, `MESSAGES_TIMEOUT_SECS` and `CHAT_COMPLETIONS_TIMEOUT_SECS` both 600 with both connect timeouts at 10, so folding them would be behavior-neutral right now and would collapse four constants into two. The reason not to is that `constants.rs` documents each pair as mirroring its own Python default, so one constant would then serve two parity contracts and have to be unpicked the day those defaults diverge, and `crates/core/CLAUDE.md` lists `client.rs` among a route module's six files with `src/messages` as the reference, so deleting it is a change to the documented template rather than to this route alone. The workspace already carries five independently configured production clients and they are not one shape: `ai-gateway/src/client.rs` sets no connect timeout, the OCR document fetch builds one per call with `redirect::Policy::none()`, and the log shipper sets no bounds at all. What this route copies is the one the docs point at. The shared-helper work the finding reaches for is in this PR already, since `core/src/http_utils.rs` is new and `messages/common_utils.rs` gave up 42 lines consuming it. None of that changes the last point, which is that Python's `HTTPHandler` lives in the host and is unreachable from the core crate by design. The Bedrock synchronous double `pre_call` finding was filed against `90f4bd0e6c` and fixed in `296fa843dd`, one commit later. `converse_handler.py` guards the Python-path `pre_call` with `if not serves_via_rust`, the same shape Anthropic uses. Round 8 took veria's remaining finding, that the Bedrock config ignored `api_key` and always selected SigV4. It is real and it is the same defect class this PR already fixed once, where ambient `AWS_ROLE_NAME` or `AWS_PROFILE_NAME` state could make the two paths sign as different principals: the Python handler resolves host credentials and hands them down regardless of the bearer token, so the Rust path signed with them and the bearer identity's account and quota boundary was bypassed. The config now mirrors `get_request_headers` exactly rather than approximating it, and each precedence rule is a separate row in one test. A caller-supplied key is the bearer token and outranks the env; with no key the env supplies it; an empty key is not a bearer token and deliberately does not reach for the env, which is what Python's `is not None` check does. An all-whitespace token stays a bearer token because Python sends it too, and treating it as absent would silently sign as the host principal instead, which is the swap this branch exists to prevent. Four mutants, run separately, each killed: dropping the bearer branch, letting an empty key reach the env, trimming whitespace to absent, and letting the env outrank the caller. No handler change was needed, since `prepare` already attaches an `authorization` header for the `Bearer` variant and `signed_headers` already returns the headers untouched for anything that is not SigV4. The existing `prepares_a_bedrock_call_without_resolving_credentials` test turned red on this change, which is itself the reachability argument: its fixture passes an `api_key` that was being discarded. It now pins the no-key SigV4 case, with a sibling pinning that a configured key leaves prepare as a bearer token. Round 9 took bugbot's finding that the Bedrock SigV4 path signed every upstream header. Python signs only the AWS set (`host`, `content-type`, `date`, and the `x-amz-` / `x-amzn-` prefixes) and reattaches the rest afterwards, precisely so a header a caller forwarded cannot change the canonical request. The Rust handler passed the whole map to the signer, so a forwarded header joined `SignedHeaders` and any rewrite or drop of it on the wire would 403 a deployment that works on Python. `aws_signature_headers` now mirrors that allowlist, applied at the chat completions call site, with every original header still going out alongside the computed SigV4 ones. The claim this paragraph originally ended on, that the computed ones win on collision, was wrong; round 11 measured it and fixed what it found. The first version of this fix is worth naming, because its mutation check caught it rather than the tests: the new test drove the helper directly, so reverting the actual call site back to signing everything left the suite green. Patching the thing the fix plumbs into is what makes a plumbing test vacuous at the far end. The test now drives `signed_headers` through the real `prepare`, asserts the forwarded header is absent from the signature and present on the wire, and all three mutants die: reverting the call site, making the filter a passthrough, and dropping the `x-amzn-` prefix. Fixing that surfaced a second defect this PR had already shipped, which CI cannot see. Adding `CoreError::Unsupported` made `ai-gateway`'s `routes/messages` error match non-exhaustive, so `cargo clippy -p litellm-ai-gateway --features server` fails to compile. CI runs `cargo clippy --workspace` with no `--features server`, so that file is never built and the rust job stays green. It now has an explicit arm returning 400 with the decline reason, chosen over a wildcard so the next variant is a compile error rather than a silent 500. Three `collapsible_if` errors remain in `realtime/service.rs` and `realtime/streaming.rs` under that same feature; those files are untouched by this PR and identical to the base, so they are a pre-existing condition of a check CI does not run, and not something to fix here. Round 10 is a bugbot finding that is half wrong and half worth stating plainly, so it is answered rather than taken. It reads that an Anthropic `refusal` block is classed as an already-sent error and fails after billing, where Python would return the completion. `refusal` is a `stop_reason`, not a content block type. The content of a refused response is ordinary text, so it normalizes on the Rust path exactly as it does on the Python one, and `response_utils::FINISH_REASONS` already maps it to `content_filter`, the same value Python's `_FINISH_REASON_MAP` gives it. A test now drives a refusal end to end and asserts both the `content_filter` finish reason and the preserved text; deleting the mapping fails it. The residual half is real and is a deliberate choice rather than an oversight. If a provider returns a content block the core cannot read, on a request whose parameters the gate accepted, that failure is raised after the provider has already answered, so it is surfaced instead of being retried. Retrying is what round 1 and round 2 removed: it re-issues a provider call that has already completed and bills the customer twice. The narrow window that remains needs a provider to volunteer a block shape for a request that asked for none, since tools, thinking, images and `reasoning_config` are all declined before the call goes out. Closing it properly means handing the raw upstream body back to Python to transform rather than making the error retryable, which is a larger change than this PR should carry and is worth its own follow-up. Round 11 is a defect round 9 introduced and no bot has filed, found by re-reading the least reviewed code on the branch with a probe rather than with an argument. Round 9 filtered the headers that get SIGNED and reattached the rest, which is the half Python does in its filter. It missed the half Python does in its reattach loop: `SIGV4_COMPUTED_HEADERS` names the four headers the signer emits itself, and the loop skips them precisely so a caller's copy cannot land next to the computed one. The Rust handler chained every original header onto the signature into a `Vec`, and `reqwest`'s `RequestBuilder::header` appends rather than replaces, so nothing deduplicated and both copies went on the wire. Measured, not reasoned. A probe driving `signed_headers` with `Authorization`, `x-amz-date` and `x-amz-security-token` forwarded reported `AUTHORIZATION_COUNT=2` and `XAMZDATE_COUNT=2`, with the caller's `Bearer` value sitting next to a real `AWS4-HMAC-SHA256` signature. Bedrock rejects that pair, so a deployment that works on Python would 403 once it carried the flag, which is the same failure round 9 set out to remove. The `x-amz-date` case is worse than a duplicate: that name is inside the signed allowlist, so the caller's value joined the canonical request while a different computed value went on the wire, guaranteeing a mismatch. The fix declines rather than imitates. Dropping the caller's copy would match Python's loop but not Python's behaviour, because Python then deliberately prefers a forwarded non-AWS4 `Authorization` over the signature it just computed, and reproducing that here would let a request body pick the identity a Bedrock deployment signs as, which is the finding round 4 closed. So a request forwarding any of those four headers now declines before credentials are resolved and Python serves it whole, with its own semantics, which is what the allowlist posture in this PR says should happen to anything the core cannot serve faithfully. The regression test drives all four names through the real `prepare` and asserts the decline is `Unsupported`, since that is the only variant the host falls back on. Removing the guard fails it, and the mutant's own panic output is the evidence above: two `Authorization` headers in one request. The existing forwarded-header test kept passing throughout, because its fixture uses `x-request-id`, a name that cannot collide, which is why the suite could not find this. Round 12 is a sweep of the two categories a silent wrong answer could still hide in, the request gate and the response transform, run against the Python transforms field by field rather than against the branch's own tests. Six defects, none of them filed by a bot, all fixed here with a mutation check each. They share one root cause worth stating: the parity work was checked against the Anthropic transform and generalized, so every place Converse differs, or where Python does something below the gate, went unexamined. `top_k` was in the Anthropic allowlist and should never have been. `temperature` and `top_p` reach the gate already resolved, because `map_openai_params` applies `_apply_sampling_param` to them first; `top_k` bypasses `map_openai_params` entirely and Python gates it inside `transform_request`, the function this route replaces. On a model that removed sampling params (Opus 4.7, 4.8, Fable 5) Python drops it under `drop_params` and succeeds, while the Rust path sent it and took a 400 after the call, which is post-send and therefore not retryable, so a working request became a hard failure. Bedrock already declined `topK` for exactly this reason and the two providers now agree. `content_filtered` mapped to `stop`, and two tests asserted that was correct. Python's `_FINISH_REASON_MAP` maps it to `content_filter`, and `content_filter` itself was missing too. Both now map, so a filtered completion no longer reports as a normal one to anything keying on the finish reason. The tests are the more interesting half: one was named `defaults_an_unmapped_reason_to_stop_like_python` and used `content_filtered` as its example of an unmapped reason, and the other sat in a table called `maps_converse_stop_reasons_python_maps` asserting the same wrong value. Both were checked against the Rust map rather than the Python one, so reverting the fix would have left them green. The first test now uses a reason genuinely absent from Python's map. Bedrock returned `content: null` for an empty answer where Python returns `""`. The type carried a comment stating "Python emits `content: None` … for parity" as a cross-provider invariant, and it is not one: Anthropic ends on `merged_text or None`, Converse assigns `chat_completion_message["content"] = content_str` unconditionally. A caller calling `.strip()` on the result would break on the Rust path alone, reachable through a filtered or guardrail-intervened response whose content list is empty. Same shape as the round 7 finding, one level down: a per-element check that an empty list passes vacuously. An Anthropic `litellm_params["metadata"]["user_id"]` was silently dropped. `transform_request` promotes it into the Messages body, below the gate and inside the replaced function, and the core is handed `optional_params` only, so it could not see the key and had no way to decline. The request went to Anthropic with the abuse-detection attribution missing. The gate now declines it, deliberately as a superset of Python's condition, which also validates the id: declining a request Python would not have attributed anyway costs only the Rust path, while missing one loses the attribution with no signal. The OpenAI `user` param was never affected, since `map_openai_params` puts it in `optional_params["metadata"]`, which the gate already declined. A connection that was never established was classed as already-sent. Every `reqwest` send failure collapsed into `CoreError::Network`, which the bridge maps to `RustUpstreamError`, so a DNS failure, a refused connection or a TLS rejection surfaced as a 500 with no fallback. Nothing was billed in any of those cases, which makes it a decline by this PR's own central invariant. It matters most for the deployments whose transport is configured only on the Python client, a corporate proxy or a custom `ssl_verify` among them, where Python would have connected fine. A new `CoreError::Connect` carries it, `is_connect()` and `is_builder()` select it, and a timeout deliberately does not, since the provider may have received and answered the request already. The test binds a port, drops the listener and calls the closed port. Last is a bug this PR did not write but did move, so it is in the diff and worth fixing here rather than leaving for someone to file. `bedrock_model_id_and_region` came out of `audio_transcription.rs` unchanged, and it strips the `arn:` prefix before taking `split(':')` field 3. Python's `_get_aws_region_from_model_arn` splits the whole ARN and takes field 3, so stripping first shifts every field down one: field 3 after the strip is the account id, and the region is field 2. It reads an account id as a region for any ARN-shaped model. Chat completions never reaches it, since `converse_handler` injects the resolved region and passes a complete URL, but the audio transcription route does. Nine mutants, each applied on its own and each killed. The driver refuses a verdict when its selector runs zero tests, which caught three of its own runs: the Bedrock and `aws_base` tests are behind the `bedrock-auth` feature, so without it those mutants read as survivors when nothing had been compiled to catch them. `CoreError::Connect` also had to be added to three exhaustive matches in `ai-gateway`, one of them under the `server` feature CI does not build, so the feature-gated clippy from `litellm-rust/CLAUDE.md` was run again to confirm no `E0004`. Round 13 took bugbot's Bedrock bearer finding, which is real and is the third variant of the same defect this PR keeps producing: the Rust path and the Python path resolving a request to different AWS identities. Round 8 was the config ignoring `api_key` and signing as the host principal. Round 11 was a forwarded header duplicating the computed one. This one is a forwarded `Authorization` that the Rust path preferred over the deployment's own bearer token. `prepare` added the resolved bearer only `if !has_bearer_auth(&headers)`, so a caller who forwarded any bearer kept it and the deployment's token was never applied. Python does the opposite: `get_request_headers` assigns `headers["Authorization"]` unconditionally once a bearer resolves from `api_key` or `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK`, and it is handed the same `headers` dict the Rust call receives as `extra_headers`, so both paths see the caller's value and only one of them overwrites it. The effect is that a Bedrock deployment carrying `rust: true` authorizes and bills against whatever identity the caller supplied. The fix mirrors Python rather than declining, which is the opposite of the round 11 decision and for a reason worth stating: there, Python itself prefers the caller's non-AWS4 `Authorization`, so reproducing it would have let a request body choose the signing identity and declining was the only safe option. Here Python's own behaviour is the safe one, so matching it is both faithful and closes the hole. Scope matters more than usual on this one, because the obvious generalization is wrong. `ChatCompletionsAuth::Bearer` is produced only by the Bedrock config; Anthropic produces `Header`, and its `if !has_header` precedence is deliberate, because `process_anthropic_headers` honours a forwarded OAuth bearer and pops the configured `x-api-key` when it sees one. So the two arms now carry opposite precedence on purpose, and both directions are pinned: one test asserts the Bedrock deployment token is the only authorization on the wire, another asserts an Anthropic caller-supplied `x-api-key` still wins. Two mutants, each killed separately, and the second exists specifically to fail if someone later generalizes the Bedrock rule onto the `Header` arm. Round 14 closes the one divergence found in the round 12 sweep that was deliberately left open, so that nothing in this PR ships as an unstated gap. Converse reports `totalTokens` and Python passes it straight through (`transform_usage`, a bare `usage["totalTokens"]` lookup), while the Rust path recomputed it as input plus output. Anthropic genuinely does compute `prompt_tokens + completion_tokens` in Python, so the two providers disagree on purpose and only Bedrock overrides now; struct-update syntax over the shared `usage_from_parts` result keeps that to one field and leaves Anthropic on exactly the path it was on. The missing-key case is the part worth stating. Python raises a `KeyError` on a body without `totalTokens`, so there is no Python behaviour to mirror; a bare field read would have reported `total_tokens: 0`, which is a worse divergence than the one being fixed. It falls back to the computed total instead, pinned by its own test. This changes no live number today, and saying so is the point. Converse only reports cache token counts when the request carries a `cachePoint` block, and the gate cannot emit one, since it requires every content part to be exactly `{"type": "text", "text": ...}`. With both cache counters structurally zero the provider total and the computed one agree by arithmetic. The blast radius if that ever changes is a reporting field rather than billing, because cost tracking reads `prompt_tokens_details` and the prompt and completion counts and never `total_tokens`. So this is insurance, and it ships with the tripwire that makes the insurance legible: a test asserting the gate declines a `cache_control`-bearing part. Whoever widens the gate to admit prompt caching gets a red test pointing at the usage mapping rather than a silent number change in production. Three mutants, each killed separately, and the third is the tripwire's own positive control: relaxing the content-part check makes the decline test fail, so the tripwire is known to fire rather than assumed to. Round 15 took veria's Bedrock attribution finding, which is real and is the second variant of the defect round 4 opened, a `litellm_params` key the core cannot see. Round 4 was Anthropic's `metadata["user_id"]`. This one is `bedrock_request_metadata_fields`: `AmazonConverseConfig` resolves proxy-owned `requestMetadata` onto the Converse body and, once the operator arms the setting, also evicts a caller-supplied one. The core is handed `optional_params` only, so it can do neither. The gate now decides per provider instead of by set membership, and the Bedrock arm asks the production predicate `bedrock_request_metadata_is_owned()` rather than restating its rule, so the two cannot drift apart. Ownership is the condition rather than "did anything resolve", because owned-but-empty has to mean absent on the wire: a caller who suppresses the resolver by omitting the allow-listed fields must not thereby earn the Rust path. Two mutants, killed separately, are reverting the Bedrock arm to `False` and declining every Bedrock request. The sweep that finding earns comes back clean, and it is worth showing rather than asserting, since a clean result only counts if it reads as a real sweep. Driving the compiled gate directly rather than reading it, every Bedrock optional param that mutates the outgoing body already declines with "unrecognized request parameter": `guardrailConfig`, `additionalModelRequestFields`, `performanceConfig`, `requestMetadata`, `toolConfig`, `promptVariables`, and a nested `inferenceConfig`. So the caller-supplied half of this field was covered from the start and only the proxy-resolved half was open. `ensure_alternating_roles`, `user_continue_message` and `assistant_continue_message` are applied in `main.py` above the provider handler, so both paths receive the same message list, and Bedrock's own continue-message insertion fires only on a leading or trailing assistant turn, which the gate already declines by conversation shape ("conversation does not run user turn to user turn"). The rest of round 15 is the `lint` job, which was red on the test-quality budget rather than on anything in the diff's behaviour: four of the new logging tests asserted on `logging_obj.<hook>.call_count`, which TQ002 reads as a test restating the implementation back at itself. They now record each hook's payload in a real list and assert on that, which also makes two of them stronger than a count was: the surviving `pre_call` on a declined Rust attempt is identified by the `complete_input_dict` it carries, so the test distinguishes which path logged rather than only how often. All four still fail on unfixed code, checked one mutant at a time. Round 16 is a defect no bot filed, found by chasing a scout's lead that turned out to name the wrong entry point. The lead was `litellm_params["use_bearer_for_custom_base"]`, which `validate_environment` reads to send `authorization` instead of `x-api-key` for a third-party base. That one does not reproduce from a proxy config, and measuring rather than reading is what settled it: the knob is in neither `all_litellm_params` nor `get_litellm_params`, so it leaks into `optional_params`, where the allowlist declines it. The live capture shows Python itself ignoring the setting, which is a separate pre-existing gap and not this PR's to fix. The mechanism behind the lead was real, though, and its reachable entry point is the OAuth one. `optionally_handle_anthropic_oauth` pops `x-api-key` and sets `authorization` whenever the deployment's `api_key` is an `sk-ant-oat` token, which needs no dead knob and no forwarded header. `prepare.rs` then re-added `x-api-key` because it was absent, so the Rust path put the OAuth credential into the header Python had just removed. The fix is in the core rather than in another gate decline, because a per-knob denylist cannot be completed: the `Header` arm now skips its header when an `authorization` header is already present, which covers the OAuth key, a forwarded OAuth bearer, and the custom-base knob should it ever start working. Two tests, and the second exists to fail if someone generalizes the first. One asserts a forwarded `authorization` suppresses the resolved `x-api-key`; the other asserts that a caller-forwarded non-OAuth `authorization` alongside Python's own `x-api-key` leaves both intact, because that is what Python sends there and the guard must not start dropping one. The mutant reverting the guard kills only the first, which is the point. Round 17 took veria's precedence finding, and the interesting part is that its suggested patch would have reintroduced round 16. The suggestion was to replace any existing `x-api-key` unconditionally, with the note that forwarded OAuth "uses Authorization and is unaffected". That holds for a forwarded bearer and not for an OAuth deployment key, where `auth()` still returns the `Header` arm and the unconditional push puts the OAuth token straight back into `x-api-key`. The finding is right; the patch and the round 16 guard are each half of the rule. The rule both halves were approximating is one line of Python, `{**headers, **anthropic_headers}`, plus the `pop("x-api-key")` in the two OAuth branches. Measured, that is: the deployment credential always replaces a forwarded one, and the only exception is an OAuth bearer. My round 16 guard deferred on ANY `authorization` header, which is too broad, since Python sends the deployment's `x-api-key` alongside an unrelated forwarded `Authorization`; veria's patch deferred on none, which is too narrow. Deferring exactly on an OAuth bearer satisfies all six cases above. Where it lives matters as much as what it says. `prepare.rs` is shared across providers and `crates/core/CLAUDE.md` forbids provider-specific branching there, so the core now asks `config.defers_to_forwarded_auth(&headers)`, defaulting to false, and the Anthropic config owns the one scheme it hands off to. That also deletes round 16's special case rather than adding to it, which is the shape a converging fix has. Three mutants, each killed separately, and the third is the one that matters: restoring the caller-wins precedence kills the two deployment-credential tests, never deferring kills the two OAuth tests, and deferring to ANY bearer kills the unrelated-`authorization` test. That last mutant is precisely the round 16 over-generalization, so the boundary is now pinned rather than argued. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **High Risk** > Adds a new provider-call path for chat completions, including credential selection, SigV4 signing, and fallback vs. fail-after-bill semantics. A mismatch with Python can change which principal is billed or drop proxy attribution. > > **Overview** > Opted-in `/chat/completions` deployments for **Anthropic** and **Bedrock Converse** can now run through the Rust core instead of Python. Enable with `rust: true` on the deployment (or `LITELLM_RUST`); successful Rust responses carry `x-litellm-rust: true`. > > The new core route translates text-only conversations, calls the provider, and normalizes OpenAI-shaped usage (including cache token split). Anything outside the allowlist—streaming, tools, images, thinking, `top_k`, proxy-owned Anthropic `user_id` / Bedrock `requestMetadata`—declines **before** the provider is called and Python serves the same request. Failures after the call (HTTP, unreadable response) are **not** retried, so the customer is not billed twice. > > Auth is meant to match Python: deployment credentials win over forwarded keys, Anthropic OAuth bearers still suppress `x-api-key`, Bedrock bearer tokens outrank SigV4, and SigV4 signs only the AWS header set. `rust` is forwarded into `litellm_params` and banned from proxy request bodies so callers cannot pick the transport. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 4d8190c54d91b5aedc3d6a1ac0c6ac2e7a5efc40.
