signal.title: test(e2e): pin prompt-cache, service-tier, and cost-header billing as permanent regressions
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Six shipped billing fixes had zero e2e coverage - Cache-read, cache-write, and tier rates could silently regress - Per-component cost headers and breakdown rows went unasserted How it solves it: - Six live tests, one per shipped fix, real OpenAI caching - Each deployment gets distinct per-component rates, so wrong-rate bills cannot pass - Assert the row's gross input and the header's net components separately ## User Flow Before: back when these regressions were live, a customer running a long cached prompt through the gateway read back a bill that was wrong in several places at once, and nothing in the suite would have caught any of them coming back 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with a ~3.6k-token prefix and see `"cache_write_tokens": 3627` come back under `usage.prompt_tokens_details` 2. They read GET https://litellm-domain/spend/logs?request_id={id} and the whole prompt is billed at the plain input rate, with nothing on the row separating what the cache write cost 3. They send the same prefix again, get `"cached_tokens": 2816` back, and the row still shows no cache-read cost, so the discounted tokens bill at full input price 4. They repeat that second call with `"stream": true` and the usage comes back with the cached-token count dropped, so a streamed cache hit costs the same as a cold one 5. They send the same prefix to POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages against a Responses-only model; the reply says `"cache_read_input_tokens": 7936` but the spend row records zero cached tokens 6. They add `"service_tier": "priority"`, the reply confirms `"service_tier": "priority"`, and the reasoning tokens inside the answer are still billed at the standard output rate 7. They read the `x-litellm-response-cost-*` headers off any of those replies and the per-component values do not add up to `x-litellm-response-cost` After: every one of those readings is right today, and this PR is what holds them there, since each step above is now asserted by a live test that goes red if the number moves 1. The same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions returns `"cache_write_tokens": 3627` 2. GET https://litellm-domain/spend/logs?request_id={id} shows the cache-write tokens priced at the cache-creation rate, listed separately from the fresh input tokens 3. The repeat call's row prices the 2816 cached tokens at the cache-read rate and the rest at the input rate 4. The streamed repeat keeps its cached-token count, so it bills at the same discount as the non-streamed one 5. The POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages call's `"cache_read_input_tokens": 7936` shows up on the spend row and is billed at the cache-read rate 6. The priority call bills input, output, and the reasoning tokens inside output at the priority rates, and the row records `"service_tier": "priority"` 7. The `x-litellm-response-cost-*` component headers add up exactly to `x-litellm-response-cost` ## Relevant issues Pins the fixes for #34046, #31686, #34812, #34957, #35923, #35925, and #36965 ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5869 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix This PR adds tests only, so no product code differs between the two sides. Before is the merge base showing the behaviors have no coverage; After is the live run at the tip proving the numbers those tests assert are the numbers a real proxy produces Shared setup: a proxy from this branch on `http://localhost:48206` against a local Postgres, and four deployments registered at runtime, each with rates ~100x canonical and distinct per component so a bill computed from the wrong rate cannot match: input `4e-05`, output `8e-05`, cache-read `1e-05`, cache-creation `5e-05`, and on the tier deployment priority input `6e-05` and priority output `1.6e-04`. All calls use a virtual key from `POST /key/generate`, and all traffic hits real OpenAI. The two legs that assert on reasoning cost send `"reasoning_effort": "high"`, the same as the tests do ### Before (0b374541bb) 1. `uv run pytest tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking --collect-only -q | tail -3` -> the suite collects nothing for prompt-cache billing, service-tier pricing, cost headers, or passthrough stream cost 2. `python -m coverage_registry.collector` -> the six registry rows added here are absent, so none of these behaviors counts as covered and a regression in any of them ships with a green suite ### After (975a6806c3) #### Case 1: cache-write tokens bill at the cache-creation rate (#34046) 1. `curl -s $P/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -d @qa3_write.json` -> `id chatcmpl-EEt11sR342HaQnD4X7rd2g7a9AKCA`, `"prompt_tokens": 3630`, `"cache_write_tokens": 3627` 2. `curl -s "$P/spend/logs?request_id=chatcmpl-EEt11sR342HaQnD4X7rd2g7a9AKCA" -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234"` -> `"cache_creation_cost": 0.18135` (3627 x 5e-05), `"input_cost": 0.18147`, so the 3 fresh tokens are the remaining `0.00012` at 4e-05, and `"total_cost": 0.18395` equals input plus the `0.00248` output #### Case 2: the breakdown itemizes cache-read and reasoning (#31686) 1. `curl -s $P/chat/completions ... -d @qa10_read_prime.json` then `-d @qa10_read_measure.json`, both bodies carrying `"reasoning_effort": "high"` -> the measured call returns `"cached_tokens": 2816`, `"reasoning_tokens": 67` 2. `curl -s "$P/spend/logs?request_id=chatcmpl-EEuyXBfTmaempDNVgnKQ16C4nB7TU" ...` -> `"cache_read_cost": 0.02816` (2816 x 1e-05), `"reasoning_cost": 0.00536` (67 x 8e-05) sitting inside `"output_cost": 0.00624`, and `"input_cost": 0.0608` less the cache-read cost leaves the 816 fresh tokens at 4e-05 Priming at a different `reasoning_effort` than the measured call produces no cache read at all, so both bodies carry the same value. That is why the test sends it on its prime call too #### Case 3: a streamed cache read keeps its discount (#34812) 1. `curl -s $P/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -d @qa9_prime.json` primes a fresh 1200-word prefix -> `cached_tokens 0` 2. `curl -sN $P/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -d @qa9_stream.json` sends the same prefix with `"stream": true` and no `stream_options` -> first chunk `id chatcmpl-EEtJmzT2FmyV0Db1tP6Bh2jj2GVvs` 3. `curl -s "$P/spend/logs?request_id=chatcmpl-EEtJmzT2FmyV0Db1tP6Bh2jj2GVvs" -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234"` -> `"cache_read_input_tokens": 2816` survived the stream, `"cache_read_cost": 0.02816` (2816 x 1e-05), and the 815 fresh tokens are `0.0326` at 4e-05, so `"input_cost": 0.06076` is exactly those two added together and `"total_cost": 0.06212` is that plus the `0.00136` output. At full input price this call would have billed `0.14524`, so the discount is worth 2.3x here OpenAI's implicit caching is best-effort, so this leg was driven with the same retry-with-a-fresh-prefix loop the test uses; it hit on the first attempt above, and a separate control run put a plain stream and an `include_usage` stream on one warm prefix to confirm the discount does not depend on the client asking for usage #### Case 4: cache tokens survive the /v1/messages bridge onto a Responses-only model (#34957) 1. `curl -s $P/v1/messages -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -d @qa3_bridge_prime.json` -> `"input_tokens": 9030` 2. `curl -s $P/v1/messages -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -d @qa3_bridge_read.json` -> `"input_tokens": 1095`, `"cache_read_input_tokens": 7936` 3. `curl -s "$P/spend/logs?api_key=$KEY" ...` -> the bridged row carries `cache_read` 7936 with `"cache_read_cost": 0.07936` and an `"input_cost"` whose remainder after the cache read is the fresh tokens at 4e-05 #### Case 5: priority tier bills every component at the priority rate, reasoning included (#35923, #35925) 1. `curl -s $P/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -d @qa10_tier.json` -> `"service_tier": "priority"`, `"prompt_tokens": 34`, `"completion_tokens": 51`, `"reasoning_tokens": 40` 2. `curl -s "$P/spend/logs?request_id=chatcmpl-EEuyiqkNSoFQX30mN5FdHZQLBXlcb" ...` -> `"service_tier": "priority"` on the row, `"input_cost": 0.00204` (34 x 6e-05), `"output_cost": 0.00816` (51 x 1.6e-04), and `"reasoning_cost": 0.0064` (40 x 1.6e-04). The standard rates would have billed 0.00136 and 0.00408, so none of the three landed on the default tier #### Case 6: the per-component cost headers add up to the total (#36965) 1. `curl -s -D- $P/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -d @qa10_read_measure.json` -> `x-litellm-response-cost: 0.06704`, `-input: 0.03264`, `-output: 0.00624`, `-cache-read: 0.02816`, `-tool-usage: 0.0` 2. `0.03264 + 0.00624 + 0.02816 + 0.0 = 0.06704`, equal to the total header. Note the header's input component is net of cache while the spend row's `input_cost` is gross (`0.0608` on the same call), which is why the two surfaces are asserted differently All six tests also ran green against this same proxy at this commit: `6 passed in 139.10s` ## Type ✅ Test ## Caveats (if any) - Two sibling behaviors are not e2e reachable and stay unit-covered, see below - OpenAI caching is best-effort, so cache tests retry with a fresh prefix Two behaviors from the same batch were investigated and deliberately left out, both because no live proxy can reach them: - The scientific-notation cost coercion (#33556) cannot be triggered through any public route. `POST /model/new` and `POST /model/update` bind the body to a model whose cost fields are typed `float | None`, so pydantic coerces `"3e-06"` at the HTTP boundary, and the boot-config path is coerced too before it is ever read. The PR's own unit tests have to patch the reader to inject a string, which the e2e harness forbids - The blocked-response usage on `/v1/responses` (#36907) only differs from the old behavior on a post-call block that carries the upstream response. Every guardrail available in-tree either answers 400 outright or blocks pre-call with no upstream response, which yields zeros both before and after the fix. Reaching the fixed branch needs Bedrock with `disable_exception_on_block`, Straiker, or Rubrik, all external and credentialed A seventh registry row, `quota_management.spend_tracking.passthrough_stream.injects_usage_cost`, ships uncovered on purpose. The behavior it names (#36503) only shows up with `litellm_settings.include_cost_in_streaming_usage` turned on, and that is a boot-time setting the shared e2e stack does not enable today, so a test written against that stack now cannot reach the branch it is meant to pin. That is observed rather than assumed: an earlier commit on this branch did carry such a test, and it came back from CI with `cost=None` on the final usage frame, which is exactly the pre-fix reading. A change to the stack's configuration is open and has to land first. The row stays in the registry so the collector keeps reporting it as a gap instead of letting the behavior quietly disappear from the denominator One doc nit found on the way, not changed here: the `input_cost` field comment in `litellm/types/utils.py` reads "Cost of raw (non-cached) input tokens only", which is true of the response header but not of the spend row, where the same name is gross of cache ## QA runbook - tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_cache_cost_accounting_e2e.py::TestCacheCostAccounting::test_cache_write_tokens_billed_at_cache_creation_rate - a fresh ~3.6k-token prompt's cache-write tokens bill at the cache-creation rate, not the input rate - [x] POST /model/new with `openai/gpt-5.6-luna` and `input_cost_per_token` 4e-05, `cache_creation_input_token_cost` 5e-05 - [x] POST /v1/chat/completions with a ~1200-word unique prefix and expect the spend row to carry cache-creation tokens above zero - [x] GET /spend/logs?request_id={id} and expect `cache_creation_cost` to equal those tokens times 5e-05, with `input_cost` minus that leaving the fresh tokens at 4e-05 - [x] Sanity check: this test makes sense to add and is not hand-wavey (e.g., assert actual expected spend instead of just spend > 0) or potentially flaky - tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_cache_cost_accounting_e2e.py::TestCacheCostAccounting::test_cost_breakdown_reports_component_costs - the row itemizes cache-read and reasoning cost, with reasoning a subset of output - [x] POST /model/new with `openai/gpt-5.5` and the four distinct rates - [x] POST /v1/chat/completions twice with the same prefix, a different trailing question each time, and expect the second call's row to carry cached tokens - [x] GET /spend/logs?request_id={id} and expect `cache_read_cost` at 1e-05 per cached token, `reasoning_cost` at 8e-05 per reasoning token, and `reasoning_cost` no greater than `output_cost` - [x] Sanity check: this test makes sense to add and is not hand-wavey (e.g., assert actual expected spend instead of just spend > 0) or potentially flaky - tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_cache_cost_accounting_e2e.py::TestCacheCostAccounting::test_streaming_cache_read_billed_at_cache_read_rate - a streamed cache hit gets the same discount as a non-streamed one - [x] Prime the prefix with a non-streamed call, then send the same prefix with `"stream": true` - [x] Take the id off the first SSE chunk and GET /spend/logs?request_id={that id} - [x] Expect a non-zero cached-token count on the row priced at 1e-05, not at the 4e-05 input rate - [x] Sanity check: this test makes sense to add and is not hand-wavey (e.g., assert actual expected spend instead of just spend > 0) or potentially flaky - tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_cache_cost_accounting_e2e.py::TestCacheCostAccounting::test_messages_bridge_keeps_cache_tokens - cache tokens survive the anthropic-messages to Responses bridge and keep their discount - [x] POST /model/new with `openai/gpt-5.3-codex`, which is Responses-only and so forces the bridge - [x] POST /v1/messages twice with a ~3000-word shared prefix and expect `cache_read_input_tokens` above zero on the second - [x] GET /spend/logs?api_key={key} and expect a row for the key carrying cache-read tokens with `cache_read_cost` at 1e-05 each (the bill is filed under a different id than the response's, so query by key) - [x] Sanity check: this test makes sense to add and is not hand-wavey (e.g., assert actual expected spend instead of just spend > 0) or potentially flaky - tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_service_tier_pricing_e2e.py::TestServiceTierPricing::test_priority_tier_bills_priority_rates - a priority call bills input, output, and reasoning at the priority rates - [x] POST /model/new with both standard rates and `input_cost_per_token_priority` 6e-05, `output_cost_per_token_priority` 1.6e-04 - [x] POST /v1/chat/completions with `"service_tier": "priority"` and a reasoning question, and expect the response to echo `"service_tier": "priority"` - [x] GET /spend/logs?request_id={id} and expect `service_tier` priority on the row, output and reasoning at 1.6e-04, input at 6e-05 - [x] Sanity check: this test makes sense to add and is not hand-wavey (e.g., assert actual expected spend instead of just spend > 0) or potentially flaky - tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_cost_headers_e2e.py::TestCostHeaders::test_component_cost_headers_sum_to_total - the per-component cost headers add up to the total header - [x] POST /model/new with `openai/gpt-5.5` and the same four distinct rates - [x] POST /v1/chat/completions twice with a shared ~1200-word prefix, priming first, and pass `-D-` so the measured call's headers are visible (the test reads them off the raw transport, which the typed client drops) - [x] Read `x-litellm-response-cost` and the `-input`, `-cache-read`, `-cache-creation`, `-output`, `-tool-usage` components - [x] Expect the five components to sum to the total, the cache-read header at 1e-05 per cached token, and the input header covering only the fresh tokens at 4e-05 (these are net of cache, unlike the spend row's gross `input_cost`) - [x] Sanity check: this test makes sense to add and is not hand-wavey (e.g., assert actual expected spend instead of just spend > 0) or potentially flaky CI note, so the red gate is not mistaken for this diff: every e2e run at this tip came back `1 failed, 640 passed, 58 skipped`, and the one failure is `llm_translation/test_audio_transcriptions_e2e.py::TestAudioTranscriptions::test_missing_model_returns_error`, which fails the same way on every PR that runs the suite today. All six tests added here passed against the shared stack. #37565 carries the one-line assertion fix for that test, so this gate goes green once it merges. Separately, `buildkite/e2e-tests` is not one of `litellm_internal_staging`'s required checks, so the red X does not block merging ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR CHECKED: live-pr-risk at 975a6806c3. Five of the six files are new or registry-only, and the one shared file is `tests/e2e/models.py`, where every change is additive: `AnthropicMessagesResponse.usage` plus four optional cost fields on `LiteLLMParamsBody`, all defaulting to None, with no field renamed, retyped, or given a new default. Request bodies serialize with `exclude_none=True`, so no existing suite's call changes on the wire, and no suite outside this PR reads `.usage` off a `/v1/messages` response. The full e2e suite collects clean on the head (695 of 697, two deselected, 0 errors), the coverage collector runs `--strict` without a failure, basedpyright over `tests/e2e` reports 0 errors, and all six cases were driven live against a real proxy, database, and OpenAI - [x] 975a6806c3 passes flake test (ran 4 times). Residual risk is flaky live OpenAI prefix-cache and spend-log polling, not a production behavior change. > > **Overview** > Pins six shipped spend-tracking fixes with live OpenAI e2e tests that register per-deployment custom rates so a wrong-rate bill cannot pass. > > **Cache accounting** now asserts cache-write tokens bill at the cache-creation rate, spend-row `cost_breakdown` itemizes cache-read/creation/reasoning, streamed usage keeps the cache-read discount, and `/v1/messages` through a Responses-only model keeps cached tokens on the bill. > > **Priority `service_tier`** bills input, output, and reasoning at `*_priority` rates and records the tier on the spend row. **`x-litellm-response-cost-*` headers** must sum to the total, with input net of cache (unlike the row’s gross `input_cost`). > > Coverage registry rows are added for those behaviors; passthrough stream cost is registered as an intentional gap until the shared stack enables `include_cost_in_streaming_usage`. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 975a6806c318976efd1d9adc6ee44aed4d8ff8d4. signal.title: fix(stagger): keep every replica of an elected job on one instant
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - A staggered elected job runs once per replica, not once - Its lease dedupes for the body's runtime, not the TTL - A 10-pod fleet can run a daily job ~10 times a day - Staggering these bought nothing: one replica does the work How it solves it: - An elected job offsets by job id alone, not by pod - Every replica shares one instant, so the election settles it - Different jobs keep different offsets, so the burst stays broken up - Cost pollers excluded: role-gated but take no lock ## User Flow Before: an operator running ten replicas finds their daily key rotation scanning the key table once per replica instead of once, and the only visible symptom is database load 1. They set `LITELLM_KEY_ROTATION_ENABLED=true` and roll out 10 replicas 2. Each replica registers `key_rotation_job` on a 24h interval and is given a phase offset up to 300s apart from its peers 3. The first replica to fire takes the Redis lock, rotates whatever is due in a few seconds, and releases it 4. The second replica fires up to 300s later, finds the lock free, and runs the same job again 5. This repeats for every replica, so the fleet performs ten daily scans of the key table where one was intended 6. Nothing errors and nothing is logged as wrong, because each later pass correctly finds nothing due After: the same deployment runs it once 1. They set `LITELLM_KEY_ROTATION_ENABLED=true` and roll out 10 replicas 2. Every replica computes the same phase offset for `key_rotation_job`, because the offset no longer depends on which pod it is 3. All ten fire at the same instant and contend for the Redis lock 4. One wins and logs `litellm_key_rotation_job: pod <id> owns this run`; the other nine cost one Redis read each and return 5. The key table is scanned once 6. `spend_log_cleanup_job`, `reset_budget_job` and the rest still fire at their own distinct offsets, so they do not land together ## Relevant issues Follows #36589, which introduced the stagger, and #36618, which introduced the election helpers this depends on. ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix The discriminating measurement is how far apart the stagger places two replicas of the same job. For an elected job any spread wider than the body's runtime permits a second run, so the target is exactly 0, while a per-pod job must keep its spread or this would be a regression rather than a fix. Ten replicas, same job ids, same settings, run against each tree. **Before**, on `2d0823abf7`: ``` ### BEFORE (2d0823abf7, stagger as merged in #36589) (10 replicas) elected jobs, spread across replicas in seconds (0 means they contend on the lease): spend_log_cleanup_job 214s REPLICAS DIVERGE, each can run key_rotation_job 279s REPLICAS DIVERGE, each can run ptu_flat_cost_rollup_job 147s REPLICAS DIVERGE, each can run per-pod jobs, spread must stay non-zero: update_spend_job 203s STILL SPREAD periodic_reload_job 267s STILL SPREAD update_gateway_requests_job 208s STILL SPREAD ``` **After**, on this branch: ``` ### AFTER (this branch) (10 replicas) elected jobs, spread across replicas in seconds (0 means they contend on the lease): spend_log_cleanup_job 0s ONE INSTANT key_rotation_job 0s ONE INSTANT ptu_flat_cost_rollup_job 0s ONE INSTANT weekly_spend_report_job 0s ONE INSTANT lockless jobs, must STAY spread (they are not elected): reset_budget_job 264s STILL SPREAD check_batch_cost_job 228s STILL SPREAD per-pod jobs, spread must stay non-zero: update_spend_job 203s STILL SPREAD periodic_reload_job 267s STILL SPREAD update_gateway_requests_job 208s STILL SPREAD ``` Only the elected jobs move. The per-pod values are identical across the two runs at 203s, 267s and 208s, and `reset_budget_job` holds its 264s, which is the part showing this is surgical rather than the stagger being switched off. ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Stacked on #36618, merge that first - The set is a list of ids and can drift - Cost pollers stay spread until they take a lock ## Review notes **Greptile round 1, 4/5, and it caught a real one.** The first version of this PR listed `reset_budget_job` as single-owner. It is not: its election lives in #36497 and #36311, neither merged, so on this base it takes no lock at all. Pinning it to one instant would have had every replica start the full budget sweep simultaneously, which is the exact thundering herd that work exists to remove, so the change would have made the thing it was fixing worse. It is removed, and the test that pins the exclusion now asserts the behaviour rather than just the membership: a lockless job must still come out spread across replicas. Re-adding it fails that test. This is the same misclassification I had already guarded against for the cost pollers and did not apply here, which is why the rule in the docstring is now stated as "membership is: this job elects an owner", not "a serving pod skips it". `reset_budget_job` joins the set when its own entry point elects, and that is worth doing as part of whichever reset-budget PR lands. **Why not a dedupe bound.** `DEFAULT_CRON_DEDUPE_SECONDS` already bounds how far apart replicas of its three cron ids may be placed, and the obvious fix was to add the interval jobs to it. That does not work. The bound's own docstring said the value is "how long each job's leader-election lock stays held", and that premise is false for any job using `run_as_single_owner`, which releases the lease when the body returns. The dedupe span is the body's runtime, which is seconds and not knowable statically, so no non-zero bound is safe. Worth noting `PTU_ROLLUP_JOB_ID` is in that map today with a horizon taken from its lock TTL and it releases on completion too, so that entry rested on the same premise; it is now covered by the pod-invariant rule instead, and the bound is left in place as a second line of defence with its comment corrected. **Why this costs nothing.** Staggering exists to stop every replica hitting Postgres at the same moment. For an elected job only the winner touches Postgres and the losers cost one Redis read, so the burst being prevented was never there. Every one of these jobs takes its lock before any database work: verified per job rather than assumed. **Why the set is narrower than the role gate.** It would be tempting to reuse "the jobs a serving pod skips" from #36618, and that set is wrong here. `check_batch_cost_job` and `check_responses_cost_job` are role-gated but take no lock, so pinning them to one instant would have every replica poll the provider simultaneously, which is worse than what they do now. A test pins that exclusion so the two sets cannot be conflated later. **Drift.** The set is ids, so a future elected job added without updating it silently gets pod-varying offsets and the bug returns. The tests reduce but do not remove this: every id in the set is asserted pod-invariant, the known per-pod jobs are asserted still spread, and the pollers are asserted excluded. Deriving the set from a lock-taking property rather than a name list would remove the drift entirely and is worth doing when there is a registry to derive it from. **Mutation check.** Reverting the one-line change to `identity=identity` fails 8 of the parametrized tests, one per elected job id. The existing 22 stagger tests pass unchanged either way, which is the point: none of them covered this. ## QA runbook ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: fix(router): give auto prompt caching deployment affinity (LIT-5535)
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Auto prompt caching got zero deployment affinity - Multi deployment groups paid cache writes every call - Affinity only worked for client sent `cache_control` How it solves it: - Router now reproduces the auto injected breakpoints - Affinity key matches the messages actually sent - Repeated cacheable prompts pin to one deployment ## User Flow Before: a developer calling a model group backed by two Bedrock deployments of the same Claude model with `enable_anthropic_prompt_caching: true` keeps paying the cache write premium as routing bounces between them 1. The proxy admin configures one `model_name` with two Bedrock deployments of the same Claude model, `litellm_settings.enable_anthropic_prompt_caching: true` and `router_settings.optional_pre_call_checks: ["prompt_caching"]` 2. The developer sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions eight times with the same ~4.1k token system prompt and no `cache_control` of their own 3. The `x-litellm-model-id` header alternates between the two deployments, and every call that lands on a deployment for the first time comes back with `cache_creation_input_tokens: 4106` and `cache_read_input_tokens: 0` 4. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs and see the 1.25x write premium charged once per deployment instead of once per prompt, so a group of N deployments costs N writes for the same prompt After: the same eight calls stay on one deployment, so only the first pays for the write and the rest read the warm cache 1. The proxy admin configures one `model_name` with two Bedrock deployments of the same Claude model, `litellm_settings.enable_anthropic_prompt_caching: true` and `router_settings.optional_pre_call_checks: ["prompt_caching"]` 2. The developer sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions eight times with the same ~4.1k token system prompt and no `cache_control` of their own 3. `x-litellm-model-id` is identical on all eight, the first response reports `cache_creation_input_tokens: 4106`, and calls two through eight report `cache_read_input_tokens: 4106` with `cache_creation_input_tokens: 0` 4. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs shows one write and seven reads, so caching delivers the 0.1x read discount it promises ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5535 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v` - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup, used identically by both legs 1. Two deployments of Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Bedrock, one on the US cross region inference profile and one on the global profile, in the same account and region. `/tmp/lit5535/config.yaml`: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: claude-sonnet-4-5 litellm_params: model: bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 aws_region_name: us-east-1 model_info: id: bedrock-us-inference-profile - model_name: claude-sonnet-4-5 litellm_params: model: bedrock/global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 aws_region_name: us-east-1 model_info: id: bedrock-global-inference-profile litellm_settings: enable_anthropic_prompt_caching: true router_settings: optional_pre_call_checks: ["prompt_caching"] general_settings: master_key: sk-lit5535 ``` 2. Bedrock keeps a separate prompt cache per inference profile, so the two deployments genuinely cannot serve each other's warm prefix. Without this the whole A/B would be vacuous, so it is checked first, straight against Bedrock with no LiteLLM in the path: ```bash python3 -c ' import json prefix = "Distinct preflight two: silver herons wade the shallow estuary while the tide retreats. " * 220 print(json.dumps({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": prefix}, {"cachePoint": {"type": "default"}}, {"text": "Reply with the single word OK."}]}], "inferenceConfig": {"maxTokens": 16}})) ' > /tmp/converse.json for round in 1 2; do for mid in us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0; do echo "round=$round $mid -> $(aws bedrock-runtime converse --region us-east-1 --model-id $mid --cli-input-json file:///tmp/converse.json | jq -c .usage)" done done ``` ``` round=1 us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 -> {"inputTokens":9,"outputTokens":1,"totalTokens":4415,"cacheReadInputTokens":0,"cacheWriteInputTokens":4405,"cacheDetails":[{"ttl":"5m","inputTokens":4405}]} round=1 global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 -> {"inputTokens":9,"outputTokens":1,"totalTokens":4415,"cacheReadInputTokens":0,"cacheWriteInputTokens":4405,"cacheDetails":[{"ttl":"5m","inputTokens":4405}]} round=2 us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 -> {"inputTokens":9,"outputTokens":1,"totalTokens":4415,"cacheReadInputTokens":4405,"cacheWriteInputTokens":0} round=2 global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 -> {"inputTokens":9,"outputTokens":1,"totalTokens":4415,"cacheReadInputTokens":4405,"cacheWriteInputTokens":0} ``` The global profile paid a full write in round 1 even though the US profile had just written the identical prefix, and each profile then read only its own copy in round 2 3. The payload, a ~4.1k token system prompt with no client `cache_control` anywhere, so every breakpoint in the request is one LiteLLM injected. `$NONCE` differs per leg so each leg starts against a cold Bedrock cache: ```bash python3 -c ' import json, sys prefix = f"Runbook {sys.argv[1]}. " + ("The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the riverbank at dawn. " * 240) print(json.dumps({"model": "claude-sonnet-4-5", "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": prefix}, {"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the single word OK."}], "max_tokens": 16})) ' "$NONCE" > /tmp/lit5535.json ``` 4. The eight call loop, printing the deployment that served each call next to its cache accounting: ```bash for i in $(seq 1 8); do body=$(curl -sS -D /tmp/h -X POST http://localhost:4499/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5535' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @/tmp/lit5535.json) printf 'call %s deployment=%-34s %s\n' "$i" \ "$(grep -i '^x-litellm-model-id:' /tmp/h | tr -d '\r' | awk '{print $2}')" \ "$(printf '%s' "$body" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; u=json.load(sys.stdin)["usage"]; print("cache_creation_input_tokens=%-5s cache_read_input_tokens=%-5s prompt_tokens=%s" % (u.get("cache_creation_input_tokens"), u.get("cache_read_input_tokens"), u.get("prompt_tokens")))')" done ``` Both legs run from a directory outside any LiteLLM checkout with `PYTHONPATH` pointed at the tree under test, so the proxy really imports the commit named in the heading. The two trees were diffed before the run and differ in exactly the four files this PR touches ### Before (cb4eb82249) 1. Start the proxy on the parent commit: ```bash PYTHONPATH=/tmp/lit5535/before python -m litellm.proxy.proxy_cli --config /tmp/lit5535/config.yaml --port 4499 --num_workers 1 ``` 2. Confirm the tree really lacks the fix: ```bash grep -c messages_with_default_injections /tmp/lit5535/before/litellm/router_utils/pre_call_checks/prompt_caching_deployment_check.py ``` ``` 0 ``` 3. Run the eight call loop: ``` call 1 deployment=bedrock-us-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=4106 cache_read_input_tokens=0 prompt_tokens=4109 call 2 deployment=bedrock-us-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 3 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=4106 cache_read_input_tokens=0 prompt_tokens=4109 call 4 deployment=bedrock-us-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 5 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 6 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 7 deployment=bedrock-us-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 8 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 ``` Eight identical requests spread across both deployments, and the prompt was written to the cache twice, on call 1 and again on call 3, because the second deployment had never seen it. The affinity check never fired: routing keyed off the unmarked messages while the success event keyed off the marked ones, so the two keys never matched ### After (469a688de9) 1. Start the proxy on this PR's tip, same config, same port: ```bash PYTHONPATH=/tmp/lit5535/after python -m litellm.proxy.proxy_cli --config /tmp/lit5535/config.yaml --port 4499 --num_workers 1 ``` 2. Confirm the tree carries the fix: ```bash grep -c messages_with_default_injections /tmp/lit5535/after/litellm/router_utils/pre_call_checks/prompt_caching_deployment_check.py ``` ``` 1 ``` 3. Run the same eight call loop against a fresh nonce: ``` call 1 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=4106 cache_read_input_tokens=0 prompt_tokens=4109 call 2 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 3 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 4 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 5 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 6 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 7 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 call 8 deployment=bedrock-global-inference-profile cache_creation_input_tokens=0 cache_read_input_tokens=4106 prompt_tokens=4109 ``` All eight land on one deployment, the prompt is written once, and `cache_read_input_tokens` is non-zero from call 2 onward. Which deployment wins is still whatever the strategy picks first, the fix only makes the rest follow it ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Only the default Anthropic and Bedrock breakpoints are reproduced - Custom `cache_control_injection_points` still route as before - Before leg warms both caches, so later calls do read ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/d9190d9ed8a04fbfb6fa4c4165f8dbff Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signal.title: perf(prometheus): render /metrics off the event loop and coalesce concurrent scrapes
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - `/metrics` rendered the registry on the event loop - Big registries stalled every other in-flight request - Concurrent scrapes each re-rendered the whole registry - `?name[]=` was silently ignored, returning everything How it solves it: - Render and gzip in a worker thread - Share one render across scrapes wanting the same output - Stream the payload in 64 KiB chunks - Apply the `name[]` filter that was being dropped ## User Flow Before: an operator running Prometheus against a busy proxy sees unrelated requests stall every scrape interval 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions traffic across many models, plus requests with misspelled model names, growing the exposition payload 2. Their scraper sends GET https://litellm-domain/metrics every 15s, several scrapers at once 3. During each scrape, GET https://litellm-domain/health/liveliness that normally answers in under 1 ms takes up to 252 ms, and chat completions in flight slow down by the same amount 4. Overlapping scrapes make it worse, because each one pays the full serialization cost again 5. They narrow a scrape with GET https://litellm-domain/metrics?name[]=litellm_proxy_total_requests_metric_total to cut the payload, and get the entire registry back anyway After: the same scrapes return the same payload while the rest of the proxy keeps answering at normal speed 1. They send the same traffic mix to POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions 2. The same scrapers send GET https://litellm-domain/metrics every 15s 3. GET https://litellm-domain/health/liveliness stays in the low milliseconds through the scrape, 15 ms at worst, and chat completions are unaffected 4. Overlapping scrapes finish in half the wall time, since scrapers asking for the same payload share one render instead of repeating it, and each still gets a complete, fresh payload 5. GET https://litellm-domain/metrics?name[]=litellm_proxy_total_requests_metric_total now returns only that metric 6. `Accept-Encoding: gzip` behaves exactly as before, so existing scrape configs need no change ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5357 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup, run identically for both sides against a proxy started with `python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config <config> --port 4099` and `callbacks: ["prometheus"]`: ```bash # real Anthropic call (costs real $) curl -s -X POST http://localhost:4099/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"anthropic-haiku-4-5","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"say hi in 3 words"}]}' # grow cardinality the way misspelled model names do in production for b in $(seq 0 99); do ( for i in $(seq $((b*4+1)) $((b*4+4))); do curl -s -o /dev/null -m 5 -X POST http://localhost:4099/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d "{\"model\":\"typo-model-$i\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"x\"}]}" & done; wait ) done # load: 20 concurrent scrapes split across two spellings of the same Accept-Encoding, # which is what two different scrapers (Prometheus sends "gzip", curl sends "gzip, deflate") look like start=$(python3 -c 'import time;print(time.time())') for i in $(seq 1 10); do curl -sL -o /dev/null -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" http://localhost:4099/metrics & done for i in $(seq 1 10); do curl -sL -o /dev/null -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate" http://localhost:4099/metrics & done sleep 0.05 for i in $(seq 1 10); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "liveliness during scrape: %{time_total}s\n" http://localhost:4099/health/liveliness; done | sort -t: -k2 -n wait echo "20 mixed-spelling concurrent scrapes wall time: $(python3 -c "import time;print(f'{time.time()-$start:.3f}s')")" ``` Both sides were health-gated at the open and close of the measurement, and both served a 1.4 MB payload ### Before (cb4eb82249) #### Unrelated requests during 20 concurrent scrapes 1. `curl -sL -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" http://localhost:4099/metrics | wc -c` ``` 1446872 ``` 2. Load script output (sorted by latency) ``` liveliness during scrape: 0.000936s liveliness during scrape: 0.000972s liveliness during scrape: 0.000984s liveliness during scrape: 0.001031s liveliness during scrape: 0.001061s liveliness during scrape: 0.001065s liveliness during scrape: 0.012704s liveliness during scrape: 0.061474s liveliness during scrape: 0.063679s liveliness during scrape: 0.252407s 20 mixed-spelling concurrent scrapes wall time: 0.637s ``` A 1.4 MB payload already stalls the loop for 252 ms. The reported 50 MB payloads scale that into multi-second stalls #### gzip negotiation 1. `curl -sL -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" -o /tmp/m.gz -D- http://localhost:4099/metrics | grep -i content-encoding; wc -c < /tmp/m.gz` ``` Content-Encoding: gzip 33926 ``` #### name[] restriction 1. `curl -sL -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-1234' 'http://localhost:4099/metrics?name%5B%5D=litellm_proxy_total_requests_metric_total' | grep -c litellm_proxy_total_requests_metric_total` ``` 403 ``` 2. Same request, counting a metric that was not requested: `... | grep -c litellm_request_total_latency` ``` 25 ``` The filter is ignored: metrics nobody asked for come back anyway ### After (57e5273023) #### Unrelated requests during 20 concurrent scrapes 1. `curl -sL -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" http://localhost:4099/metrics | wc -c` ``` 1446852 ``` 2. Load script output (sorted by latency) ``` liveliness during scrape: 0.000994s liveliness during scrape: 0.001000s liveliness during scrape: 0.001033s liveliness during scrape: 0.001086s liveliness during scrape: 0.001105s liveliness during scrape: 0.001195s liveliness during scrape: 0.001252s liveliness during scrape: 0.001276s liveliness during scrape: 0.012803s liveliness during scrape: 0.015302s 20 mixed-spelling concurrent scrapes wall time: 0.316s ``` Worst case drops from 252 ms to 15 ms, and the same 20 scrapes finish in half the wall time #### gzip negotiation 1. `curl -sL -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" -o /tmp/m.gz -D- http://localhost:4099/metrics | grep -i content-encoding; wc -c < /tmp/m.gz` ``` content-encoding: gzip 33881 ``` #### name[] restriction 1. `curl -sL -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-1234' 'http://localhost:4099/metrics?name%5B%5D=litellm_proxy_total_requests_metric_total' | grep -c litellm_proxy_total_requests_metric_total` ``` 403 ``` 2. Same request, counting a metric that was not requested: `... | grep -c litellm_request_total_latency` ``` 0 ``` ## Review notes Answers to the two review threads on `litellm/integrations/prometheus_metrics_endpoint.py`, here rather than in the threads because neither fits a review comment. Treat this section as load-bearing rather than commentary: it is the standing record of why the library's own app is not used here, and anyone simplifying this module back to `make_asgi_app` would silently reintroduce the `?name[]=` defect below. **Single-slot scrape coalescing: correct, and fixed.** The slot was keyed on the raw `Accept` and `Accept-Encoding` strings, so two scrapers asking for identical bytes in different words never shared a render. Prometheus sends `Accept-Encoding: gzip` while curl and the Grafana agent send `gzip, deflate`. A single slot on top of that meant each arrival displaced the other's entry, so under exactly the load this PR targets nothing coalesced and every overlapping scrape paid a full render. The key is now what the scrape actually asks for: the encoder and content type `choose_encoder` selected, whether gzip was accepted, and the `name[]` filter. In-flight renders live in a map keyed on that rather than in one slot, and each render drops its own entry from its own done callback, so one finishing cannot evict another still running. The Before and After above are that exact scenario, 20 concurrent scrapes split across two spellings of the same encoding. **Custom metrics HTTP handler: keeping it, because the parts that look hand-rolled are imported, and the library's app cannot do the job.** Content negotiation is `prometheus_client`'s own `choose_encoder` and `gzip_accepted`, and `?name[]=` is its `restricted_registry`. Header and query parsing is Starlette's `Request`; the response is Starlette's `StreamingResponse`. The only rewritten code is the four-line body of `prometheus_client.exposition._bake_output`, which is private and cannot be called. By contrast the library's own `make_asgi_app` hand-decodes raw ASGI header bytes and hand-emits `http.response.start` and `http.response.body`, so this module is less hand-rolled than the thing it replaces. Delegating to `make_asgi_app` also is not possible without losing two capabilities. It takes `registry` and `disable_compression`, calls `_bake_output` inline in the coroutine, and exposes no seam to move that work off the loop. Measured on a registry the size LIT-5357 reports, 600k samples and a 72.8 MB exposition, rendering inline froze the loop for 1691 ms and let a 5 ms ticker fire once, while rendering through `asyncio.to_thread` let it fire 73 times at a 12 ms median. Separately, `make_asgi_app` passes `parse_qs(scope['query_string'])` to `_bake_output`, which yields bytes keys, and `_bake_output` then tests `if 'name[]' in params` against a str key that can never match, so the library's ASGI app silently ignores `?name[]=` and returns the whole registry. That is the 25 leaked lines in the Before section, and it is why `make_wsgi_app` is unaffected: it parses a str query string. Adopting the library app would ship that bug. This looks like an upstream defect rather than a misuse, reproduced on prometheus-client 0.20.0, which is what this repo pins, and worth reporting to that project separately. Auth is not duplicated either. `/metrics` already sits behind `PrometheusAuthMiddleware`, and mounted ASGI sub-apps are an existing pattern here. ## Type 🚄 Infrastructure ## Caveats (if any) - Bounds scrape cost, does not shrink the payload - 50 MB exposition still costs 50 MB of transient memory - Render is pure Python and holds the GIL - Worker thread stops it monopolizing the loop, not using it - gzip is the part that truly parallelizes, since zlib drops the GIL - Coalescing only merges scrapes that overlap in time - Cardinality itself is unchanged, only scrape cost is - Thread offload uses the default asyncio executor ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/675dfbfab55e44f093c0d5fb93a9b0fc Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signal.title: perf(budget_reservation): tokenize each request once, off the event loop for large prompts
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Large prompts get tokenized twice per budget reservation - Tokenizing runs inline, blocking the whole event loop - Every other request on that worker stalls behind it - The size heuristic missed tool-schema property names and tool_choice How it solves it: - Count input tokens once, reuse for both cost estimates - Count large prompts (>30K chars of input) in a worker thread - Size the request on every field the tokenizer sees, keys included ## User Flow Before: a team sending a ~646KB chat completion through a budget-enforced key freezes every other in-flight request while that one is admitted 1. A user sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with 342 messages and 17 tool definitions, using a key that has a budget 2. While that request is being admitted, another user's GET https://litellm-domain/health/liveness takes 165ms to come back, against 3ms on the same idle proxy 3. With six such requests arriving together the worst wait grows to 354ms, and one call in a hundred waits longer than 166ms 4. The large request itself is also slower than the provider call alone accounts for, since its prompt is measured twice before the call is even made After: the same requests are admitted without freezing anyone else 1. A user sends the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with the same large body and the same budget-enforced key 2. The other user's GET https://litellm-domain/health/liveness now comes back in 30ms, in line with what the same request costs on a key that has no budget at all 3. With six arriving together the worst wait is 169ms rather than 354ms, and the hundredth-percentile wait drops from 166ms to 53ms 4. The large request returns the same response, with the same reserved spend visible at https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs, just sooner ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5402 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v` - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix The honest observable for an event-loop stall is not the latency of the large request itself, it is how long an unrelated request waits behind it. `GET /health/liveness` does nothing but return a string, so its round trip is the event loop's responsiveness. One `curl` process holds one connection and fires a beat every 10ms for the whole window, and the worst beat is the longest the loop was unavailable Shared setup, identical for both legs: 1. Isolated Postgres, on its own port so nothing else on the box is touched ``` docker run -d --name c9-pr37683-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=litellm -e POSTGRES_USER=litellm \ -e POSTGRES_DB=litellm -p 6329:5432 postgres:16 ``` 2. `config.yaml` ```yaml model_list: - model_name: claude-sonnet-5 litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5 api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY litellm_settings: num_retries: 0 telemetry: false ``` 3. `big_body.json`: 342 messages and 17 tool definitions, 646KB on the wire, 129,545 input tokens as counted by `litellm.token_counter`. Real Anthropic calls, roughly $0.26 of input per request 4. Both legs run from a scratch directory outside the repo with `PYTHONPATH` pointed at the tree under test, so `load_dotenv()` cannot reach the repo's `.env` and the proxy cannot silently import a different checkout. `RIG/before/litellm` is byte-identical to `litellm/` at the merge base and `RIG/after/litellm` to `litellm/` at the PR tip, and they differ in exactly one file: ``` $ diff -rq RIG/before/litellm RIG/after/litellm Files RIG/before/litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py and RIG/after/litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py differ ``` 5. Launch, one worker so there is one event loop to stall ``` PYTHONPATH=$RIG/<leg> python -m litellm.proxy.proxy_cli --config config.yaml --port 4093 --num_workers 1 ``` 6. Two keys, so the reservation path can be turned on and off without changing anything else ``` curl -X POST :4093/key/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" \ -d '{"max_budget": 500, "models": ["claude-sonnet-5"]}' # $BKEY curl -X POST :4093/key/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" \ -d '{"models": ["claude-sonnet-5"]}' # $UKEY, no budget ``` 7. The probe, and the load ``` curl -s --rate 100/s -K liveness_x12000.txt -w '%output{>>probe.txt}%{time_total}\n' & for n in $(seq 1 $CONC); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}\n' -X POST :4093/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @big_body.json & done ``` ### Before (9432f40145) ``` budget_reservation.py : RIG/before/litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py has the fix : False API keys in env : ['ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'] DATABASE_URL : 127.0.0.1:6329/litellm proxy pid=4803 live on :4093 after 11s, 1 worker budgeted key $BKEY: {"max_budget":500.0,"spend":0.0} no-budget key $UKEY: {"max_budget":null,"spend":0.0} warmup http=200 1.964812s ``` #### One large request, budget-enforced key 1. Probe the idle proxy for a floor ``` $ curl -s --rate 100/s -K liveness_x400.txt -w '%output{>>idle.txt}%{time_total} ' idle beats=400 p50=0.001s p99=0.001s MAX=0.003s 5 slowest: 0.003 0.001 0.001 0.001 0.001 ``` 2. Send one 646KB request with `$BKEY` while the probe runs ``` $ for n in $(seq 1 1); do curl -X POST :4093/v1/chat/completions -d @big_body.json & done chat http_200 x1 slowest=1.8s under load beats=268 p50=0.001s p99=0.002s MAX=0.165s 5 slowest: 0.165 0.003 0.002 0.001 0.001 ``` 3. One beat waited 165ms while every other beat stayed at the idle floor. That single beat is the reservation tokenizing the prompt on the loop #### One large request, key with no budget (control) 1. Probe the idle proxy ``` $ curl -s --rate 100/s -K liveness_x400.txt -w '%output{>>idle.txt}%{time_total} ' idle beats=400 p50=0.001s p99=0.001s MAX=0.005s 5 slowest: 0.005 0.004 0.001 0.001 0.001 ``` 2. Send the same 646KB request with `$UKEY`, which has no budget so no reservation runs ``` $ for n in $(seq 1 1); do curl -X POST :4093/v1/chat/completions -d @big_body.json & done chat http_200 x1 slowest=1.9s under load beats=279 p50=0.001s p99=0.001s MAX=0.003s 5 slowest: 0.003 0.002 0.001 0.001 0.001 ``` 3. 3ms, not 165ms. The same body, parsed and forwarded the same way, costs nothing when the reservation path is skipped, so the stall is the reservation and not the payload #### Six concurrent large requests, budget-enforced key 1. Probe the idle proxy ``` $ curl -s --rate 100/s -K liveness_x400.txt -w '%output{>>idle.txt}%{time_total} ' idle beats=400 p50=0.001s p99=0.001s MAX=0.001s 5 slowest: 0.001 0.001 0.001 0.001 0.001 ``` 2. Send six of them at once with `$BKEY` ``` $ for n in $(seq 1 6); do curl -X POST :4093/v1/chat/completions -d @big_body.json & done chat http_200 x6 slowest=3.3s under load beats=339 p50=0.001s p99=0.166s MAX=0.354s 5 slowest: 0.354 0.343 0.180 0.166 0.004 ``` 3. The worst wait is 354ms and one beat in a hundred is over 166ms ``` end of leg: liveness http=200, pid 4803 still the same live process, tracebacks in proxy log: 0 ``` ### After (c5b678acf5) ``` budget_reservation.py : RIG/after/litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py has the fix : True API keys in env : ['ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'] DATABASE_URL : 127.0.0.1:6329/litellm proxy pid=52898 live on :4093 after 9s, 1 worker budgeted key $BKEY: {"max_budget":500.0,"spend":0.0} no-budget key $UKEY: {"max_budget":null,"spend":0.0} warmup http=200 1.865320s ``` #### One large request, budget-enforced key 1. Probe the idle proxy for a floor ``` $ curl -s --rate 100/s -K liveness_x400.txt -w '%output{>>idle.txt}%{time_total} ' idle beats=400 p50=0.001s p99=0.001s MAX=0.003s 5 slowest: 0.003 0.001 0.001 0.001 0.001 ``` 2. Send one 646KB request with `$BKEY` while the probe runs ``` $ for n in $(seq 1 1); do curl -X POST :4093/v1/chat/completions -d @big_body.json & done chat http_200 x1 slowest=2.0s under load beats=290 p50=0.001s p99=0.021s MAX=0.030s 5 slowest: 0.030 0.027 0.021 0.007 0.006 ``` 3. 165ms becomes 30ms and the outlier is gone. What is left is the counting thread taking its GIL slices, not the loop waiting out a whole tokenization #### One large request, key with no budget (control) 1. Probe the idle proxy ``` $ curl -s --rate 100/s -K liveness_x400.txt -w '%output{>>idle.txt}%{time_total} ' idle beats=400 p50=0.001s p99=0.001s MAX=0.003s 5 slowest: 0.003 0.002 0.001 0.001 0.001 ``` 2. Send the same 646KB request with `$UKEY` ``` $ for n in $(seq 1 1); do curl -X POST :4093/v1/chat/completions -d @big_body.json & done chat http_200 x1 slowest=2.3s under load beats=344 p50=0.001s p99=0.001s MAX=0.018s 5 slowest: 0.018 0.004 0.003 0.001 0.001 ``` 3. Unchanged, as it should be: this path never reserved and so was never touched #### Six concurrent large requests, budget-enforced key 1. Probe the idle proxy ``` $ curl -s --rate 100/s -K liveness_x400.txt -w '%output{>>idle.txt}%{time_total} ' idle beats=400 p50=0.001s p99=0.001s MAX=0.002s 5 slowest: 0.002 0.001 0.001 0.001 0.001 ``` 2. Send six of them at once with `$BKEY` ``` $ for n in $(seq 1 6); do curl -X POST :4093/v1/chat/completions -d @big_body.json & done chat http_200 x6 slowest=2.7s under load beats=321 p50=0.001s p99=0.053s MAX=0.169s 5 slowest: 0.169 0.084 0.078 0.053 0.053 ``` 3. 354ms becomes 169ms and the p99 drops from 166ms to 53ms ``` end of leg: liveness http=200, pid 52898 still the same live process, tracebacks in proxy log: 0 ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Threshold is a constant, 30K chars of input text - Estimators still self-count when called without precomputed counts - Six concurrent counting threads still contend for the GIL ## Review notes The size heuristic renders each sized field rather than walking it. Rendering counts mapping keys, which is what a tool schema's property names are, and it keeps the function non-recursive, which `tests/code_coverage_tests/recursive_detector.py` requires. It also sizes every field `_count_input_tokens` hands the tokenizer, `tool_choice` included, so the offload decision and the work being offloaded can no longer drift apart The stall the ticket describes is hundreds of milliseconds per large request, not seconds. It scales with the prompt and with the number of pricing candidates the request is priced against: a model group with tiered pricing has one candidate per deployment table plus the group's flat rates, and before this change every candidate re-tokenized the prompt, twice over, once for the max-cost estimate and once for the input-cost estimate. `test_reservation_tokenizes_the_prompt_once` pins that against a real tiered model Every new test was mutation-checked against seven mutants of the source: ignoring mapping keys, never offloading, always offloading, dropping `tools` or `tool_choice` from the sized fields, discarding the precomputed counts in either estimator, and recounting instead of reusing them. All seven were killed, each by the test written for it. The tool-schema fixture is sized so its values alone come to 4,358 characters while counting its keys brings it to 67,581, straddling the 30,000 threshold, so a keys-ignoring heuristic sends it inline and the test fails ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/269f766e7cf345689b409ebae290e37b Requested by: @yassin-berriai

signal.title: fix(logging): bound oversized error payloads written to stdout
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Failed requests echo the whole payload to stdout - One bad 100K char request wrote 714KB of logs - That formatting and I/O blocks the event loop How it solves it: - Cap INFO-and-higher log lines and tracebacks - Keep head and tail, drop the middle - `MAX_STRING_LENGTH_STDOUT_LOG` tunes it, 0 disables ## User Flow Before: an agent framework sends a large tool-heavy request that gets rejected, and the operator watching proxy stdout gets buried in copies of the payload 1. The agent sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with a ~100K char messages array, with request/response logging turned off 2. The request is rejected, and the caller gets back a 400 whose error text quotes the request body 3. The operator tails proxy stdout and sees that same 100K char body printed several times for the one request, once as the router's exception line and again inside the re-raised exception's traceback 4. Under a burst of such requests the proxy gets slower for everyone, since writing those lines happens inline on the request path After: the same rejected request logs bounded lines, so stdout stays readable and the write cost stays flat 1. The agent sends the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with the same ~100K char messages array 2. The request is rejected, and the caller gets back the same 400 with the same error text, unchanged 3. The operator tails proxy stdout and sees each error string capped at 4096 chars, keeping the start and end of the error with a `litellm_truncated` marker in the middle saying how many chars were skipped. The marker is paid for out of that 4096, so the cap is a real ceiling rather than a floor the marker is added on top of 4. An operator who wants the whole payload back runs with `--detailed_debug`, or raises the cap with `MAX_STRING_LENGTH_STDOUT_LOG`, and logging callbacks like OTEL or Datadog keep receiving the untruncated data either way ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5374 ## Review notes The cap covers the log record's own message and traceback text. A handler's formatter still prepends its fixed timestamp, level, and source location prefix, 77 chars for the default plain formatter, so a physical stdout line reads as the capped string plus that prefix Redaction ordering was checked in both directions, since truncation runs as a logger filter and secret redaction runs as a handler filter. Truncating first then redacting is safe because redaction reads `record.exc_text` rather than reformatting from `exc_info`, and redacting first then truncating is safe because truncation reads the same field. Neither order reintroduces an unredacted payload, and truncation cannot widen exposure on a handler that never had redaction, since that handler was formatting the full traceback itself before this change ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup, a real proxy on `litellm/proxy/dev_config.yaml` (Anthropic keys, no mocks) with its stdout tee'd to a log, and a single ~100K char request the provider path rejects, so the error string carries the payload. Both runs below are from one sitting on the same machine, same payload, with `/health/liveliness` asserted immediately before and after each request so the two logs cannot straddle different processes ```bash python3 -c " import json big = 'p' * 100000 print(json.dumps({'model': 'anthropic-haiku-4-5', 'messages': [{'role': 'bogus_role', 'content': big}]})) " > payload.json uv run python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config litellm/proxy/dev_config.yaml --port 4000 2>&1 | tee litellm.log ``` ### Before (d556fac56b) 1. `wc -c < litellm.log` right before the call, prints `17744` 2. `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @payload.json`, prints `400` 3. `wc -c < litellm.log` right after, prints `731985`, so the one rejected request wrote 714241 chars of stdout 4. `awk '{print length}' litellm.log | sort -n | tail -1`, prints `100287`, the payload echoed whole on a single line 5. `awk 'length > 4096' litellm.log | wc -l`, prints `7`, so seven separate lines blow past what the cap would allow 6. `grep -o "litellm_truncated skipped [0-9]* chars" litellm.log | tail -1`, prints nothing, since no truncation happens ### After (12316f61d4) 1. `wc -c < litellm.log` right before the call, prints `17744` 2. The same curl, prints `400` with the same error body as before 3. `wc -c < litellm.log` right after, prints `31965`, so the same request wrote 14221 chars, a 50x reduction 4. `awk '{print length}' litellm.log | sort -n | tail -1`, prints `4136`, which is a 4059 char capped string plus the plain formatter's 77 char timestamp and source-location prefix 5. `awk 'length > 4096' litellm.log | wc -l`, prints `1`, that same line, and stripping the 77 char formatter prefix from every line puts the longest logged string at `4059`, inside the 4096 cap 6. `grep -o "litellm_truncated skipped [0-9]* chars" litellm.log | tail -1`, prints `litellm_truncated skipped 504038 chars`, and the surviving line still shows the head and tail of the real error ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Cap applies to LiteLLM's own loggers only - Cap bounds the record's string, not the formatter's prefix - Truncation is char-based, so it can split JSON ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/4ee3d6770cae4873b26d1041603a6138 Requested by: @yassin-berriai

  1. Switch to a new branch from main.
  2. Run npm test to ensure all tests are passing.
  3. Update the version in https://github.com/actions/cache/blob/main/package.json.

  10. Draft a new release https://github.com/actions/cache/releases use the same version number used in package.json
    1. Create a new tag with the version number.

v8.0.1

What's Changed

Full Changelog: https://github.com/actions/download-artifact/compare/v8...v8.0.1

v8.0.0

v8 - What's new

[!IMPORTANT] actions/download-artifact@v8 has been migrated to an ESM module. This should be transparent to the caller but forks might need to make significant changes.

[!IMPORTANT] Hash mismatches will now error by default. Users can override this behavior with a setting change (see below).

Direct downloads

To support direct uploads in actions/upload-artifact, the action will no longer attempt to unzip all downloaded files. Instead, the action checks the Content-Type header ahead of unzipping and skips non-zipped files. Callers wishing to download a zipped file as-is can also set the new skip-decompress parameter to true.

Enforced checks (breaking)

A previous release introduced digest checks on the download. If a download hash didn't match the expected hash from the server, the action would log a warning. Callers can now configure the behavior on mismatch with the digest-mismatch parameter. To be secure by default, we are now defaulting the behavior to error which will fail the workflow run.

ESM

To support new versions of the @actions/* packages, we've upgraded the package to ESM.

signal.title: fix(proxy): capture requester IP in 401 and auth-time 429 failure logs
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - 401 and budget 429 failure logs carry no caller IP - those failures usually have no key or user identity either - operators cannot see or block repeated bad-key traffic How it solves it: - stamp the caller IP into the failure log for auth rejections - honors `use_x_forwarded_for` and keeps any IP already recorded ## User Flow Before: an operator watching a burst of rejected requests cannot tell who is sending them 1. A caller sends POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions with `Authorization: Bearer sk-bad-key` and gets back 401 with "Invalid proxy server token passed" 2. The operator opens http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=logs, filters to failures, and opens that 401 row 3. The row shows no user and no key owner, and its IP field is empty, so there is nothing to rate limit or block on 4. Same for a key that blew its budget: the caller gets 429 "Budget has been exceeded!" and the log row again shows no IP After: the same rejected requests are attributable to an IP 1. A caller sends the same POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions with `Authorization: Bearer sk-bad-key` and gets back the same 401 2. The operator opens http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=logs, filters to failures, and opens that 401 row 3. The row now shows the caller IP, so the operator can spot the source of repeated 401s and block it upstream 4. Same for the budget 429: its log row also shows the caller IP ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-4839 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v` - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup, run against a live proxy hitting real OpenAI (`gpt-4o-mini`, real spend). Port 4707 instead of 4000 because another proxy already held 4000 on this box: ```bash docker run -d --name lit4839-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=litellm -e POSTGRES_USER=litellm -e POSTGRES_DB=litellm -p 6407:5432 postgres:16 export DATABASE_URL=postgresql://litellm:litellm@127.0.0.1:6407/litellm .venv/bin/prisma db push --schema=./litellm/proxy/schema.prisma --accept-data-loss --skip-generate DISABLE_SCHEMA_UPDATE=True python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config litellm/proxy/dev_config.yaml --port 4707 READ_LOGS() { curl -s -G "http://localhost:4707/spend/logs/ui" -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" \ --data-urlencode "start_date=2026-08-20 00:00:00" --data-urlencode "end_date=2026-08-22 00:00:00" \ --data-urlencode "status_filter=failure" --data-urlencode "page_size=3" \ | python3 -c " import sys,json for r in json.load(sys.stdin)['data']: print(r['metadata']['error_information']['error_code'], r.get('requester_ip_address'))" } ``` `/spend/logs/ui` is what http://localhost:4707/ui/?page=logs reads, so the IP column an operator sees is exactly this field. Each leg ran on its own empty database, and `/health/liveliness` returned 200 immediately before and after every case ### Before (4af59d7c6e) #### 401, unknown key 1. `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST http://localhost:4707/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-bad-key-lit4839" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"model":"gpt-4o-mini","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'` prints `401` with `Authentication Error, Invalid proxy server token passed. Received API Key = sk-...4839` 2. `READ_LOGS` shows that row as `401 None`, so the rejected caller is unattributable #### 429, key over budget 1. A key from `curl -s -X POST http://localhost:4707/key/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"models":["gpt-4o-mini"],"max_budget":0.0000001}'` spends `6.599999999999999e-06` on one real `gpt-4o-mini` call, then the next identical call returns `429` with `Budget has been exceeded! Key=key (sk-...Skcg) Current cost: 6.599999999999406e-06, Max budget: 1e-07` 2. `READ_LOGS` shows that row as `429 None` ### After (5115e91b55) #### 401, unknown key 1. The same `curl` prints `401` with the same `Authentication Error, Invalid proxy server token passed. Received API Key = sk-...4839` 2. `READ_LOGS` shows that row as `401 127.0.0.1` #### 429, key over budget 1. A key from the same `/key/generate` call spends `6.599999999999999e-06` on one real `gpt-4o-mini` call, then the next identical call returns `429` with `Budget has been exceeded! Key=key (sk-...LmAA) Current cost: 6.599999999999406e-06, Max budget: 1e-07` 2. `READ_LOGS` shows that row as `429 127.0.0.1` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - only covers rejections raised at the auth gate - rate limit 429s past auth already logged the IP ## Review notes On the bare `dict` annotation: `request_data` is the parsed request body, which spans every proxy route, so there is no single Pydantic model to validate it against. It is now `dict[str, object]` on the helper and on `_handle_authentication_error`, which is the honest shape and, unlike `dict[str, Any]`, forces narrowing at every read. The two reads narrow explicitly, the metadata bucket with `isinstance(metadata, Mapping)` and the budget model with `isinstance(budget_model, str)`, and the parameterized test's case arguments are typed too That stays inside the lint ceilings. basedpyright on `auth_exception_handler.py` goes from 23 diagnostics to 8, and the one rule that moves the wrong way anywhere is `reportUnknownArgumentType`, +2 at the two `user_api_key_auth.py` call sites that still hand over a bare `dict`, paid for by -2 in this file plus dropping the redundant `False` default on the `use_x_forwarded_for` lookup that `_get_request_ip_address` already compares with `is True` On where the IP comes from: `_get_request_ip_address` is pre-existing and gated on `general_settings.use_x_forwarded_for`, the same helper and the same operator switch the IP allowlist gate uses and the same rule `add_litellm_data_to_request` applies on the success path. With the switch off only the socket peer is used, so `X-Forwarded-For` cannot forge the logged IP. With it on, the deployment is asserting it sits behind a trusted load balancer, exactly as it already does for every successful request. Tightening the header chain further, the way the MCP surface does with `trusted_proxy_ranges`, would be a change to that shared helper rather than to this fix On redaction: the IP lands in the same `metadata` or `litellm_metadata` bucket the success path writes, so it reaches loggers through the standard payload and answers to the same switches, with no new bypass. Neither `turn_off_message_logging` nor `redact_user_api_key_info` has ever masked `requester_ip_address` on either path ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/b7d4e62082704377a178e62387d4e60d Requested by: @yassin-berriai
